legal_text:
On its incorporation as a charitable incorporated organisation, the objects of the Trust must include―
(a) the preservation of the Common as a place for peaceful open air public recreation and enjoyment; and
(b) the conservation, protection and improvement of the physical and natural environment of the Common for the benefit of the public, having regard to the requirements of good forestry and the desirability of conserving flora and fauna.
In this Act, those objects are referred to as the “primary objects”.
The objects of the Trust and any transferee under section 12 must always include the primary objects.
The Trust and any transferee may have other objects but they must be charitable objects.
Any alteration to the objects of the Trust or of a transferee requires the written consent of the Charity Commission.
simplified_text:
Upon becoming a charitable incorporated organization, the Trust's purposes must include:
Preserving the Common as a space for peaceful outdoor recreation and enjoyment by the public.
Conserving, protecting, and enhancing the physical and natural environment of the Common for the benefit of the public, while considering good forestry practices and the importance of preserving flora and fauna.
These purposes are known as the "primary objects" in this law. The Trust and any party to whom it transfers its responsibilities must always maintain these primary objects. While the Trust and any transferee can have additional purposes, these must also be charitable purposes. Any changes to the Trust's or a transferee's purposes require the written consent of the Charity Commission.

legal_text:
On the appointed day―
(a) the Common and all other property which immediately before that
date was the property of the Churchwardens and was used or held in
connection with the Common; and
(b) all rights and liabilities of the Churchwardens subsisting immediately
before that date which were acquired or incurred in connection with
the Common, are transferred to and vest in the Trust free of any trusts established under the 1777 Act.
simplified_text:
Transfer of Property and Rights: On the specified date:
The property and all other assets that previously belonged to the Churchwardens and were used for or associated with the Common, as well as
All the rights and obligations of the Churchwardens related to the Common before that date, are transferred to and become the responsibility of the Trust. This transfer is not subject to any obligations established under the 1777 Act.

legal_text:
Whilst the Common is in its ownership―
(a) the Trust must remain a charity;
(b) the objects of the Trust must include the primary objects.
From the appointed day the Churchwardens shall not be liable for any act, event, failure to act or omission so far as the act, event, failure to act or omission relates to the Common and occurred before the appointed day.
Where the transfer and vesting of the Common or any part of the Common effected by subsection (1) is a registrable disposition under the Land Registration Act 2002, the Trust must apply to the Chief Land Registrar for registration in the register of title of a restriction to reflect section 12(2).
simplified_text:
While the Common is owned by the Trust:
The Trust must continue to operate as a charity.
The Trust's mission must include the main objectives.

From the appointed day, the Churchwardens will not be responsible for any actions, events, failures to act, or omissions related to the Common that occurred before the appointed day.

If the transfer of the Common or any part of it is a registrable transaction under the Land Registration Act 2002, the Trust must request the Chief Land Registrar to register a restriction in the title register to reflect section 12(2).

legal_text:
On and after the appointed day the Trust shall be responsible for the management of the Common.
Without prejudice to the generality of subsection (1), the Trust may―
(a) do any works necessary for preserving, restoring, planting and maintaining the turf, trees, shrubs, plants and grass for landscaping and temporarily fence off such parts of the Common as it thinks
necessary;
(b) execute works of draining, raising or levelling for the preservation
and maintenance of the Common and fence off dangerous places;
(c) construct, place or erect and maintain, or permit the construction, placing or erection and maintenance of buildings, seats, fences, notice
boards, gates and other structures.
simplified_text:
Responsibilities of the Trust: After a certain date, the Trust will be in charge of managing the Common. 
Specific Powers of the Trust: The Trust has the authority to perform various actions for the upkeep and preservation of the Common, including carrying out necessary works, construction, and maintenance of various elements within the Common.

Restrictions on Erecting Fences: Only certain purposes are allowed for putting up fences, unless subsection (5) says otherwise. These purposes are:

Conservation and Recreation: To protect and enhance the natural and physical environment of the Common and make it suitable for recreational activities.
Tree Preservation: To safeguard the trees on the Common.
Fire Prevention: To minimize the risk of fires on the Common.
Safety: To prevent accidents, injuries, or health risks in areas that the Trust considers dangerous on the Common.
Other Necessary Purposes: For any other reasons that the Trust believes are essential for achieving its main goals.

legal_text:
On and after the appointed day the Trust may, over any part of the Common, grant to an owner or occupier of any land adjoining the Common easements, licences or other rights for access (with or without vehicles), maintenance or services to or in connection with the land as the Trust thinks fit.
Easements, licences or other rights may be granted on such terms (including the payment of charges, whether periodic or otherwise) and subject to such conditions as the Trust thinks fit.
Nothing in this Act affects any rights of owners and occupiers of land adjoining the Common in respect of gates, ways or passages lawfully erected or used before the appointed day.
Nothing in this section affects the application of sections 117 to 123 of the Charities Act 2011 (restrictions on dispositions of land) in relation to the Trust.
simplified_text:
Granting Rights to Land Adjacent to the Common: After a certain day, the Trust has the authority to give landowners or occupants next to the Common permissions, licenses, or other rights for access, maintenance, or services related to their land, as the Trust sees fit. These rights may include access with or without vehicles.
Terms and Conditions: These rights can be granted with certain terms, such as payment of charges (either periodically or otherwise) and subject to specific conditions that the Trust finds appropriate.
Existing Rights: Any existing rights of landowners and occupants regarding gates, ways, or passages that were lawfully established or used before the appointed day are not affected by this law.
Charities Act: This law does not change how the Trust is subject to sections 117 to 123 of the Charities Act 2011, which deal with restrictions on land dispositions.

legal_text:
Agreements with highway authorities and traffic authorities
(1) The Corporation may enter into an agreement with a highway authority or
traffic authority about the exercise of their respective functions as they relate to
an open space.
(2) An agreement under subsection (1) may include agreement for―
(a) the provision, installation or maintenance of signs, fences, gates, cattle-
grids, road-humps, traffic-calming works, or any other works or
equipment;
(b) the restriction or regulation of traffic; or
(c) the making, or dedication to the public, of a road or path.
(3) In exercising the power in subsection (1), the Corporation must have regard to
the amenity of the open space and the interests of persons resorting to it, and
to the interests of inhabitants of the locality of the open space and other persons
using the highways in that locality.
simplified_text:
Agreements with Authorities Regarding Open Spaces:
The Corporation has the authority to make agreements with highway authorities or traffic authorities concerning the management of their respective responsibilities related to an open space.
These agreements may involve:
- Providing, installing, or maintaining signs, fences, gates, cattle-grids, road-humps, traffic-calming works, or any other works or equipment.
- Regulating or restricting traffic.
- Creating or dedicating a road or path to the public.
When exercising this power, the Corporation must consider the well-being of the open space, the needs of individuals who use it, and the interests of local residents and others who utilize the local highways.

(b) the restriction or regulation of traffic; or

Agreements with Authorities Regarding Open Spaces:
The Corporation has the authority to make agreements with highway authorities or traffic authorities concerning the management of their respective responsibilities related to an open space.

legal_text:
Ban on grant or assignment of certain long residential leases of houses

1Ban on grant or assignment of certain long residential leases of houses
(1)A person may not grant or enter into an agreement to grant a long residential lease of a house on or after the day on which this section comes into force, unless it is a permitted lease (see section 7).
(2)A person may not assign or enter into an agreement to assign the whole or a part of a lease which was granted on or after the day on which this section comes into force if—
(a)at the time of the assignment the lease is a long residential lease of a house, but
(b)at the time of the grant the lease was not a long residential lease of a house.
(3)This section does not affect—
(a)the validity of a lease granted, or an assignment entered into, in breach of this section, and does not affect the powers of a person to grant or assign such a lease (whether under section 23(1) of the Land Registration Act 2002 or otherwise);
(b)any contractual rights of a party to an agreement entered into in breach of this section.
simplified_text:
Ban on grant or assignment of certain long residential leases of houses
(1) Prohibition on Granting Leases: No one can grant or agree to grant a long residential lease for a house after the date this section becomes effective, unless it is a permitted lease (see section 7).
(2) Prohibition on Assigning Leases: Furthermore, no one can transfer or agree to transfer the entire lease or a part of it, which was granted after the effective date of this section, if at the time of the transfer, the lease is a long residential lease for a house but was not initially granted as such.
(3) Exceptions: This ban does not invalidate a lease granted or an assignment made in violation of this section, nor does it affect the legal authority to grant or transfer such leases (whether under section 23(1) of the Land Registration Act 2002 or otherwise). It also does not impact the contractual rights of a party who entered into an agreement in violation of this section.

legal_text:
Leases which have a long term
(1)A lease has a “long term” in any of cases A to D.
(2)Case A: the lease is granted for a term certain exceeding 21 years.
(3)Case B: section 149(6) of the Law of Property Act 1925 applies to the lease (lease granted for life or until marriage or civil partnership) and the lease accordingly takes effect with a term fixed by law.
(4)Case C: the lease is granted with a covenant or obligation for perpetual renewal and accordingly takes effect with a term fixed by law - unless it is a sub-lease with a term fixed by law of 21 years or shorter.
(5)Case D: the lease is capable of forming part of a series of leases whose terms would extend beyond 21 years (see section 4).
(6)In determining whether a lease has a long term, it is irrelevant if the lease is, or may become, terminable by notice, re-entry or forfeiture.
simplified_text:
Leases with Long Terms
(1) A lease is considered to have a "long term" in any of the following cases:

Case A: The lease is granted for a certain period exceeding 21 years.
Case B: The Law of Property Act 1925 applies to the lease, and it is granted for life or until marriage or civil partnership, thus having a term set by law.
Case C: The lease is granted with a covenant or obligation for perpetual renewal, thus having a term fixed by law, unless it is a sub-lease with a term fixed by law of 21 years or less.
Case D: The lease is capable of being part of a series of leases whose terms would extend beyond 21 years (see section 4).

(6) Whether a lease has a long term is determined without considering whether the lease is, or may become, terminable by notice, re-entry, or forfeiture.

legal_text:
Series of leases whose term would extend beyond 21 years
(1)A lease (“the original lease”) is “capable of forming part of a series of leases whose terms would extend beyond 21 years” if conditions A to C are met at the time when the original lease is granted.
(2)Condition A: the original lease does not have a long term under section 3(2), (3) or (4).
(3)Condition B: provision for the grant of another lease of the same house (the “new lease”) is included in—
(a)the original lease, or
(b)any related arrangements.
(4)Condition C: the total duration of—
(a)the term of the original lease,
(b)the term of the new lease (if granted), and
(c)the term or terms of any subsequent leases (if granted),
would exceed 21 years.
(5)In a case where the provision for the grant of the new lease, or for the grant of any subsequent lease, allows for the possibility of the term of the lease being one of a number of differing durations, the reference in condition C to the term of the lease is to the longest of those possible durations.
(6)A lease is a “lease of the same house” if the lease demises one house, being the house comprised in the original lease, with or without any appurtenant property, and nothing else.
(7)Arrangements are “related arrangements” if they are entered into in connection with the grant of the original lease (whether or not they are entered into in writing).
(8)A lease is a “subsequent lease” if—
(a)it is not the new lease,
(b)it is a lease of the same house, and
(c)provision for the grant of the lease—
(i)is included in the original lease or any related arrangements,
(ii)would be included in the new lease (if granted), or
(iii)would be included in any other lease that (if granted) would itself be a subsequent lease.
simplified_text:
Creating a Series of Leases: A lease is considered as part of a series of leases that would last for over 21 years if certain conditions are met when the original lease is granted.

Conditions for Part of a Series: 
Condition A: The original lease does not have a long term under specific sections of the law.
Condition B: The original lease includes provisions for granting another lease for the same property, or these provisions are included in related arrangements.
Condition C: The total duration of the original lease, the new lease (if granted), and any subsequent leases (if granted) would add up to more than 21 years.

Details of the Leases: If the provisions allow for different durations, condition C refers to the longest possible duration.
Definition of Terms: The lease must only demises one property and related arrangements are those connected to the granting of the original lease.

Subsequent Leases: A subsequent lease is one that is not the new lease, is for the same property, and includes provisions that were in the original lease or related arrangements.

Houses
(1)A “house” is a separate set of premises (on one or more floors) which—
(a)forms the whole, or part, of a building, and
(b)is constructed or adapted for use for the purposes of a dwelling.
(2)But where the separate set of premises forms part of a building, it is not a house if the whole of or a material part of the set of premises lies above or below some other part of the building.
simplified_text:

  Definition of a House: A "house" is a separate set of premises, whether on one or more floors, that is part of a building and is built or modified to be used as a residence.

legal_text:
Permitted leases: certification by the appropriate tribunal
(1)The appropriate tribunal must, on an application by a person, issue a certificate (a “permitted lease certificate”) in relation to a new long residential lease of a house, where the tribunal is satisfied that the lease is or will be a permitted lease falling within Part 1 of Schedule 1.
(2)An application under this section may be made and determined whether or not the application includes a draft of the instrument creating the new lease.
(3)The appropriate tribunal may issue a permitted lease certificate on such terms and conditions as it considers appropriate, but the certificate must—
(a)identify the house or the land on which the house will be built, and
(b)state the category or categories set out in Part 1 of Schedule 1 into which the lease will fall.
(4)If an application under this section relates to two or more leases, the appropriate tribunal may issue just one certificate relating to some or all of those leases.
simplified_text:
Certificate for New Leases: The right tribunal must provide a certificate, called a "permitted lease certificate," for a new long residential lease of a house, as long as it fits the criteria in Schedule 1. 

Application Process: A person can apply for the certificate, and the tribunal will consider the application even if it doesn't include the lease document.

Certificate Conditions: The tribunal can set conditions for the certificate, but it must include the details of the house or land and the category of the lease. If the application is for multiple leases, the tribunal can issue one certificate covering some or all of those leases.

legal_text:
Permitted leases: marketing restrictions
(1)This section applies in relation to the marketing of a house where—
(a)the house is to be comprised in a new lease, and
(b)the lease will be a long residential lease of the house.
(2)A person (“a promoter”) may not make any material marketing the house to be comprised in the lease available to any person, unless the permitted lease information relating to the lease is included in or provided with that material.
(3)The “permitted lease information”, in relation to a lease, means—
(a)if the lease falls or will fall into one or more of the categories set out in Part 1 of Schedule 1, a copy of the permitted lease certificate together with a statement identifying that category or those categories,
(b)if to the best of the knowledge and belief of the promoter at the time the material is made available the lease falls or will fall into one or more of the categories set out in Part 2 of Schedule 1, a statement identifying that category or those categories, or
(c)if both paragraphs (a) and (b) apply to the lease, the information required under both those paragraphs.
(4)“Marketing” includes any form of advertising or promotion.
simplified_text:
Permitted Leases and Marketing Restrictions: 
(1) This rule applies when promoting a house that will be part of a new long-term lease. 
(2) The promoter cannot share any information promoting the house unless it includes or provides the necessary lease information.
(3) The "permitted lease information" means: 
(a) A copy of the permitted lease certificate and a statement showing the lease category, if it falls into one of the categories listed in Part 1 of Schedule 1. 
(b) A statement identifying the lease category, if the promoter believes the lease falls into one or more categories listed in Part 2 of Schedule 1. 
(c) Both types of information if the lease falls into categories from both Part 1 and Part 2. 
(4) "Marketing" includes any advertising or promotion.

legal_text:
Permitted leases: transaction warning conditions
(1)A person may not, on or after the day on which section 1 comes into force—
(a)enter into an agreement to grant a permitted lease unless the transaction warning conditions are met in relation to the agreement, or
(b)subject to subsection (5), grant a permitted lease unless the transaction warning conditions are met in relation to the lease.
(2)The “transaction warning conditions” are as follows—
(a)at least 7 days before the relevant date the grantor must give a warning notice relating to the permitted lease—
(i)to the proposed tenant, or
(ii)where there is more than one proposed tenant, to each of them;
(b)a notice of receipt of the warning notice must be given to the grantor—
(i)by the proposed tenant, or
(ii)where there is more than one proposed tenant, jointly by all of the proposed tenants;
(c)a reference to the warning notice and the notice of receipt must be included in or endorsed on the relevant instrument in the specified manner.
(3)A “warning notice” is a notice provided in a specified form and manner and containing—
(a)sufficient information to identify the house to be comprised in the lease,
(b)if the lease falls within Part 1 of Schedule 1, a copy of the permitted lease certificate,
(c)if the lease falls into one or more of the categories set out in Part 2 of Schedule 1, a statement identifying that category or those categories,
(d)if both paragraphs (b) and (c) apply to the lease, the information required under both those paragraphs, and
(e)such other information as may be specified.
(4)A “notice of receipt” is a notice provided in a specified form and manner and containing such information as may be specified.
(5)A person does not breach subsection (1) in relation to the grant of a lease if—
(a)the person previously entered into an agreement to grant that lease,
(b)the transaction warning conditions were met in relation to that agreement, and
(c)a reference to the warning notice and the notice of receipt relating to that agreement is included in or endorsed on the instrument creating the lease.
(6)This section does not apply to the grant of a permitted lease which falls within paragraph 6 of Schedule 1 (leases agreed before commencement).
(7)This section does not affect—
(a)the validity of a lease granted in breach of subsection (1), and does not affect the powers of a person to grant such a lease (whether under section 23(1) of the Land Registration Act 2002 or otherwise);
(b)any contractual rights of a party to an agreement entered into in breach of subsection (1).
(8)In this section—
“grantor”, in relation to a lease, means the person proposing to grant the lease (whether or not that person holds the freehold or leasehold title out of which the lease will be granted);
“proposed tenant”, in relation to a lease, means the proposed tenant of the house to be comprised in the lease;
“relevant date” means—
(a)
in the case of an agreement to grant a lease, the day on which the agreement is entered into, and
(b)
in the case of a grant of a lease, the day on which the lease is granted;
“relevant instrument” means—
(a)
in the case of an agreement to grant a lease, that agreement, and
(b)
in the case of a grant of a lease, the instrument creating that lease;
“specified” means specified or described in regulations made—
(a)
in relation to a lease of a house in England, by the Secretary of State;
(b)
in relation to a lease of a house in Wales, by the Welsh Ministers.
(9)A statutory instrument containing regulations under this section is subject to the negative procedure.
simplified_text:
Permitted Leases: Transaction Warning Conditions

Leasing Restrictions:
After a certain date, a person cannot:
- Make an agreement to lease a property unless they satisfy certain conditions, or
- Actually lease a property unless they satisfy certain conditions (with some exceptions).

The conditions are as follows:
- The person leasing the property must provide a warning notice to the proposed tenant(s) at least 7 days before the agreement or lease date.
- The tenant(s) must acknowledge receipt of the warning notice.
- The warning notice and receipt of acknowledgement must be included in the lease agreement in a specified way.

Warning Notice:
The warning notice should include information about the property, a copy of the lease certificate if applicable, and other specified information.

Notice of Receipt:
The notice of receipt should include specified information about the acknowledgement of the warning notice.

Exceptions:
The leasing restrictions do not apply to certain leases that were agreed upon before the restrictions came into effect.

Effect on Leases:
Breach of the leasing restrictions does not invalidate the lease, and the person involved may still have the power to lease the property.

legal_text:

(a)a lease with a long term only by virtue of falling within section 3(5);
(b)a lease which takes effect as a deemed surrender and regrant of a lease.

legal_text:
Restriction on title
(1)Subsection (3) applies where—
(a)the Chief Land Registrar approves an application for registration of a lease (the “registered lease”),
(b)section 11 applies to the registered lease, but
(c)the registered lease does not contain a statement made in accordance with subsection (2) or (3) of that section.
(2)An “application for registration of a lease” is an application for—
(a)completion by registration of a disposition of registered land, if that disposition is the grant of a lease, or
(b)registration of a lease within section 4(1)(c) of the Land Registration Act 2002.
(3)The Chief Land Registrar must enter in the register a restriction that no registrable disposition, other than the grant of a legal charge, of the registered lease is to be completed by registration.
(4)The restriction under subsection (3) may be removed if the registered lease is varied to include a statement made in accordance with section 11(2) or (3).
(5)Subsection (6) applies where—
(a)a restriction has been entered in the register in accordance with subsection (3) in relation to a registered lease, and
(b)the Chief Land Registrar approves an application for registration of a deed of variation relating to the lease by virtue of which a new lease takes effect as a deemed surrender and regrant of the lease.
(6)The Chief Land Registrar must enter in the register a restriction that no registrable disposition, other than the grant of a legal charge, of the new lease is to be completed by registration.
(7)The restriction under subsection (6) may be removed if the Chief Land Registrar is satisfied that the new lease—
(a)is not a long residential lease of a house, or
(b)is a permitted lease.
(8)An expression used in this section and in the Land Registration Act 2002 has the same meaning in this section as in that Act.
simplified_text:
Restriction on Title:
 
When the Chief Land Registrar approves an application for registration of a lease (called the "registered lease"), but the registered lease does not include a specific statement required by law, the Chief Land Registrar must enter a restriction in the register. This restriction prevents any other transfer or action related to the registered lease from being completed by registration, except for granting a legal charge.

This restriction can be removed if the registered lease is changed to include the required statement. If a new lease is created through a deed of variation, the Chief Land Registrar must also enter a similar restriction in the register for the new lease, but it can be removed if the Chief Land Registrar determines that it is not a long residential lease of a house or is a permitted lease.

Any terms used in this section have the same meaning as in the Land Registration Act 2002.

simplified_text: Ending the Right to Buy: The ability to buy the property ceases in certain situations. This includes when the lease ends or is terminated. legal_text:
Redress: general provision
(1)A lease to which section 13 applies is not as a result of any right to acquire—
(a)registrable under the Land Charges Act 1972, or
(b)to be taken to be an estate contract within the meaning of that Act.
(2)An agreement relating to a long residential lease of a house (whether or not contained in the instrument creating the lease or made before the grant of the lease) is of no effect to the extent that it makes provision—
(a)excluding or modifying the right to acquire, or
(b)providing for the surrender or termination of the lease, or for the imposition of any penalty, in the event of the rights holder taking steps to exercise the right to acquire.
(3)Subsection (2) does not prevent a tenant under a long residential lease of a house from—
(a)surrendering the lease,
(b)terminating the lease, or
(c)entering into an agreement to acquire the freehold estate in the land comprised in the lease, or any superior leasehold estate or estates in that land, other than by way of exercising the right to acquire.
(4)The right to acquire in relation to a long residential lease of a house is not capable of subsisting apart from the lease.
(5)In this section, “rights holder” has the meaning given by section 13.
simplified_text:
Addressing Disputes: General Rules

(1) If section 13 applies to a lease, then no one has the right to buy it if that right needs to be recorded under the Land Charges Act 1972, or if it's considered to be an estate contract under that Act.

(2) Any agreement related to a long residential lease of a house (whether it's in the lease itself or made before the lease is approved) isn’t valid if it tries to: 
   (a) Stop or change the right to buy the house, or
   (b) Arrange for the lease to end or for a penalty to be imposed if the person with the right to buy tries to use that right.
   
(3) Paragraph (2) doesn't mean a tenant with a long residential lease of a house can't:
   (a) End the lease,
   (b) Terminate the lease, or
   (c) Make an agreement to buy the land that the lease covers, or any leases related to it, without using the right to buy.

(4) You can't have the right to buy a house without also having the lease for it.

(5) In this section, "rights holder" has the meaning explained in section 13.

Redress Regulations: Rights for Buying a Leasehold House
The Secretary of State may create rules (known as "redress regulations") to guide and facilitate the process of a leaseholder exercising their right to buy a long residential lease for a house.
These regulations may include details about:
- The time limit for exercising the right to buy
- How the leaseholder must notify the landlord or other specified individuals about their intention to buy the lease, including the required format and timing of the notification
- Registration of the notification under specific land laws
- The landlord's acknowledgment or rejection of the leaseholder's right to buy, including the format and timing of this acknowledgment or rejection
- The relevant payment for costs in connection with the right to buy
- The legal process for determining the leaseholder's right to buy if there is disagreement between the leaseholder and the landlord
These regulations may also address situations where the leaseholder’s right to buy relates to multiple landlords, and the responsibilities of the landlords in such cases.
The regulations may make use of or modify existing laws, and they can also change or revoke any current laws. Any rules created as part of these regulations are subject to a specific process for approval by the government.

legal_text:
Enforcement by trading standards authorities
(1)It is the duty of every local weights and measures authority in England or Wales (an “enforcement authority”) to enforce the leasehold house restrictions in its area.
(2)In this section and in sections 18 to 23 the “leasehold house restrictions” means—
(a)section 1(1) so far as it relates to an agreement to grant a lease,
(b)section 1(1) so far as it relates to the grant of a lease,
(c)section 1(2) so far as it relates to an agreement to assign a lease,
(d)section 1(2) so far as it relates to the assignment of a lease,
(e)section 9(2) (marketing restrictions on permitted leases),
(f)section 10(1)(a) (conditions on agreement to grant permitted lease), and
(g)section 10(1)(b) (conditions on grant of permitted lease).
(3)For the purposes of this section and sections 18 to 23, a breach of a leasehold house restriction is taken to occur in the area in which the house in question is located (and if the house is located in more than one area, the breach is taken to have occurred in each of those areas).
(4)The duty in subsection (1) is subject to sections 19(4) (enforcement by another enforcement authority) and 22 (enforcement by the lead enforcement authority).
simplified_text:
Enforcing Leasehold House Restrictions: Every local authority responsible for weights and measures in England or Wales (an "enforcement authority") must uphold the restrictions on leasehold houses in its area.

What the Restrictions Include: In this section and in sections 18 to 23, "leasehold house restrictions" refer to:

Agreements to grant a lease under section 1(1)
The actual granting of a lease under section 1(1)
Agreements to assign a lease under section 1(2)
The assignment of a lease under section 1(2)
Marketing restrictions on permitted leases as per section 9(2)
Conditions on agreements to grant permitted leases under section 10(1)(a)
Conditions on the grant of permitted leases under section 10(1)(b)

Location of Breach: For the purposes of this section and sections 18 to 23, a violation of a leasehold house restriction is considered to have taken place in the area where the house is situated. If the house is in more than one area, the breach is considered to have occurred in each of those areas.

Limitations of Duty: The duty described in subsection (1) is subject to the provisions of sections 19(4) (enforcement by another enforcement authority) and 22 (enforcement by the lead enforcement authority).

legal_text:
Financial penalties
(1)An enforcement authority may impose a financial penalty on a person if the authority is satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the person has breached a leasehold house restriction.
(2)The amount of a penalty for a breach is to be such amount as the authority determines but—
(a)is not to be less than £500, and
(b)is not to be more than £30,000.
(3)Conduct within any one of the following paragraphs is to be regarded as a single breach of one leasehold house restriction—
(a)entering into an agreement to grant a lease in breach of section 1(1) and subsequently granting the lease in breach of that provision;
(b)entering into an agreement to assign a lease in breach of section 1(2) and subsequently assigning the lease in breach of that provision;
(c)entering into an agreement to grant a lease in breach of section 10(1)(a) and subsequently granting the lease in breach of section 10(1)(b).
Subsection (5) is to be read in accordance with this subsection.
(4)A person who makes marketing material available in relation to the same lease on more than one occasion in breach of section 9(2) is to be regarded as committing only one breach of that provision.
(5)The following are to be regarded as separate breaches—
(a)breaches by the same person of the same leasehold house restriction in relation to different leases, and
(b)breaches by the same person of different leasehold house restrictions in relation to the same lease,
and accordingly an enforcement authority may impose a separate penalty in relation to each breach (or may impose a single penalty of an amount equal to the total of the amounts of the penalties that could have been separately imposed).
(6)The Secretary of State may by regulations amend an amount for the time being specified in subsection (2) to reflect a change in the value of money.
(7)A statutory instrument containing regulations under subsection (6) is subject to the negative procedure.
(8)Schedule 2 contains further provision about financial penalties under this section.
simplified_text:
Financial Penalties:

(1) Imposing a Penalty: An enforcement authority can impose a financial penalty on a person if the authority is certain that the person has violated a leasehold house restriction.

(2) Amount of Penalty: The penalty amount is determined by the authority and must not be less than £500 or more than £30,000.

(3) Define Breach: Certain actions, like entering into an agreement or making marketing material available, are considered as a single breach of a leasehold house restriction.

(4) Multiple Occasions: Making marketing material available more than once for the same lease is considered as one breach.

(5) Separate Breaches: Breaches of the same leasehold house restriction for different leases, or breaches of different restrictions for the same lease, are considered separate breaches and may result in separate penalties.

(6) Adjustment of Amount: The Secretary of State can change the specified penalty amounts to account for changes in the value of money.

(7) Regulations: Any regulations made under this section are subject to review by the negative procedure.

(8) Further Details: More details about financial penalties under this section can be found in Schedule 2.

legal_text:
Financial penalties: cross-border enforcement
(1)An enforcement authority may impose a penalty under section 18 in respect of a breach of a leasehold house restriction which occurs outside that authority’s area (as well as in respect of a breach which occurs within that area).
(2)If an enforcement authority (“LA1”) proposes to impose a penalty in respect of a breach which occurred in the area of a different enforcement authority (“LA2”), LA1 must notify LA2 that it proposes to do so.
(3)If LA1 notifies LA2 under subsection (2) but does not impose the penalty, LA1 must notify LA2 of that fact.
(4)If an enforcement authority receives a notification under subsection (2), the authority is relieved of its duty under section 17(1) in relation to the breach unless the authority receives a notification under subsection (3).
(5)If an enforcement authority (“LA1”) imposes a penalty in respect of a breach which occurred in the area of a different enforcement authority (“LA2”), LA1 must notify LA2 of that fact.
simplified_text:
Penalties in Different Areas: If an enforcement authority wants to penalize someone for breaking a restriction on a leasehold house that happened outside of their area, they can do so. They also have to let the authority in the area where the breach occurred know about their plans.

Notification: If an authority notifies another authority about the penalty but doesn't actually impose it, they have to inform the notified authority.

Relief of Duty: If an authority receives notification about a proposed penalty but the penalty isn't actually imposed, the authority doesn't have to take any action unless they receive notification that the penalty won't be imposed.

Cross-Authority Penalties: If an enforcement authority imposes a penalty for a breach that occurred in another authority's area, they must inform the authority where the breach occurred.

legal_text:

simplified_text:
Updating Legislation: Looking Ahead

Lead Enforcement Authority

In this part of the law and in sections 21 to 23, the "lead enforcement authority" means:

a) the Secretary of State, or
b) a person who the Secretary of State has chosen to be the lead enforcement authority as per subsection (2).

The Secretary of State can arrange for a local weights and measures authority in England or Wales to be the lead enforcement authority instead of the Secretary of State.

The arrangements may include provisions for payments by the Secretary of State and about ending the arrangements.

The Secretary of State can make regulations to provide for transitional or saving measures in case there is a change in the lead enforcement authority.

These regulations can relate to a specific change in the lead enforcement authority or to changes that might occur from time to time.

A formal document containing regulations under subsection (4) is subject to the negative procedure.

legal_text:
General duties of lead enforcement authority
(1)It is the duty of the lead enforcement authority to oversee the operation of the relevant provisions of this Part in England and Wales.
(2)The “relevant provisions of this Part” means the provisions of this Part except sections 11 and 12 (statements in leases and restriction on title).
(3)It is the duty of the lead enforcement authority to issue guidance to enforcement authorities about their enforcement of the leasehold house restrictions (and if the lead enforcement authority is not the Secretary of State, the Secretary of State may give directions as to the content of the guidance).
(4)It is the duty of the lead enforcement authority to provide information and advice to the public in England and Wales about the operation of the relevant provisions of this Part, in such form and manner as it considers appropriate.
(5)The lead enforcement authority may disclose information to an enforcement authority for the purposes of enabling that authority to determine whether there has been a breach of a leasehold house restriction.
(6)If the lead enforcement authority is not the Secretary of State, the lead enforcement authority must keep under review and from time to time advise the Secretary of State about—
(a)the operation of the relevant provisions of this Part, and
(b)social and commercial developments relating to the grant or assignment of long residential leases of houses in England and Wales.
simplified_text:
Responsibilities of Lead Enforcement Authority: The lead enforcement authority in England and Wales has several duties:

1. Overseeing Relevant Provisions: The authority must supervise the implementation of the laws in this part, except for sections 11 and 12.

2. Issuing Guidance: It must provide guidance to enforcement authorities regarding the enforcement of leasehold house restrictions. If the lead enforcement authority is not the Secretary of State, the Secretary of State can provide directions on the content of the guidance.

3. Providing Information to the Public: The lead enforcement authority must offer information and advice to the public in England and Wales about the relevant laws in this part, in a suitable form and manner.

4. Sharing Information: The authority can disclose information to an enforcement authority to help them determine if there has been a breach of a leasehold house restriction.

5. Advising the Secretary of State: If the lead enforcement authority is not the Secretary of State, it must regularly review and advise the Secretary of State on the implementation of the relevant laws in this part and on social and commercial developments related to the granting or assignment of long residential leases of houses in England and Wales.

legal_text:
Enforcement by lead enforcement authority
(1)The lead enforcement authority may—
(a)take steps to enforce the leasehold house restrictions if it considers it is necessary or expedient to do so;
(b)for that purpose, exercise any powers that an enforcement authority may exercise for the purpose of the enforcement of the leasehold house restrictions.
(2)If the lead enforcement authority proposes to take steps in respect of a breach (or suspected breach) of a leasehold house restriction, it must notify the enforcement authority for the area in which the breach occurred (or may have occurred) that it proposes to do so.
(3)If the lead enforcement authority notifies an enforcement authority under subsection (2) but does not take the proposed steps, the lead enforcement authority must notify the enforcement authority of that fact.
(4)If an enforcement authority receives a notification under subsection (2), the authority is relieved of its duty under section 17(1) in relation to the breach unless the authority receives a notification under subsection (3).
(5)But the lead enforcement authority may require the enforcement authority to assist the lead enforcement authority in taking steps to enforce the leasehold house restriction referred to in subsection (2).
simplified_text:
Enforcement by Lead Enforcement Authority  

The lead enforcement authority has the power to:
- Take action to enforce the leasehold house restrictions if it believes it is necessary or helpful to do so
- Exercise any powers that an enforcement authority can use to enforce the leasehold house restrictions for this purpose  

If the lead enforcement authority intends to take action regarding a breach (or suspected breach) of a leasehold house restriction, it must inform the enforcement authority for the area where the breach occurred (or may have occurred) about its intention.

If the lead enforcement authority informs an enforcement authority under the above condition but does not take the planned action, it must notify the enforcement authority about this.

If an enforcement authority receives a notification under the above condition, it is no longer obligated to carry out its duty in relation to the breach, unless it receives a notification that the lead enforcement authority did not take the proposed action.

However, the lead enforcement authority can ask the enforcement authority to help it in taking action to enforce the leasehold house restriction mentioned in the notification.

legal_text:
Meaning of “victim”
(1)In this Part, “victim” means a person who has suffered harm as a direct result of—
(a)being subjected to criminal conduct, or
(b)one or more of the circumstances mentioned in subsection (2).
(2)The circumstances are—
(a)where the person has seen, heard, or otherwise directly experienced the effects of, criminal conduct at the time the conduct occurred;
(b)where the person’s birth was the direct result of criminal conduct;
(c)where the death of a close family member of the person was the direct result of criminal conduct;
(d)where the person is a child who is a victim of domestic abuse which constitutes criminal conduct.
(3)The reference in subsection (2)(d) to a child who is a victim of domestic abuse is to be read in accordance with Part 1 of the Domestic Abuse Act 2021.
(4)For the purposes of this Part—
(a)“harm” includes physical, mental or emotional harm and economic loss;
(b)“criminal conduct” means conduct which constitutes an offence.
(5)It is immaterial for the purposes of subsection (4)(b) that—
(a)no person has reported the offence;
(b)no person has been charged with or convicted of the offence.
(6)In section 52(3)(a) of the Domestic Violence, Crime and Victims Act 2004, for “complaint has been made about” substitute “person has reported”.

The victims’ code
(1)The Secretary of State must issue a code of practice as to the services to be provided to victims by persons appearing to the Secretary of State to have functions of a public nature relating to—
(a)victims, or
(b)any aspect of the criminal justice system.
(2)In this Part, the “victims’ code” means the code of practice issued under this section that is for the time being in operation (but see subsection (13)).
(3)The victims’ code must make provision for services which reflect the principles that victims require—
(a)information to help them understand the criminal justice process;
(b)access to services which support them (including, where appropriate, specialist services);
(c)the opportunity to make their views heard in the criminal justice process;
(d)the ability to challenge decisions which have a direct impact on them.
(4)The Secretary of State may by regulations make further provision about the victims’ code, including about matters that the code must include.
(5)But the Secretary of State may make regulations under subsection (4) only if satisfied that provision made in the code in compliance with the regulations would not result in—
(a)a significant reduction in the quality or extent of the services provided in accordance with the victims’ code, or
(b)a significant restriction in the description of persons to whom services are provided in accordance with the victims’ code.
(6)The victims’ code may restrict the application of its provisions to—
(a)victims of specified descriptions (including those who are victims by virtue of specified conduct or conduct constituting specified offences);
(b)specified persons who have functions of a kind mentioned in subsection (1).
(7)The victims’ code may include provision requiring or permitting the services which are to be provided to a victim to be provided to one or more other persons—
(a)instead of the victim (for example, where the victim has died);
(b)as well as the victim.
(8)The victims’ code may make different provision for different purposes, including different provision for—
(a)victims of different descriptions;
(b)persons who have different functions of a kind mentioned in subsection (1).
(9)The victims’ code may make different provision for different areas.
(10)In considering whether to exercise the power in subsection (8)(a), the Secretary of State must have regard to the particular needs of victims who are under the age of 18 or who have protected characteristics within the meaning of the Equality Act 2010.
(11)The victims’ code may not require anything to be done by—
(a)a person acting in a judicial capacity, or on the instructions of or on behalf of such a person;
(b)a person acting in the discharge of a prosecution function, if that function involves the exercise of a discretion.
(12)In this section, “specified” means specified in the victims’ code.
(13)Until the first code of practice issued under this section is in operation, references in sections 5 to 12 and 32 to the “victims’ code” are to the code of practice issued under section 32 of the Domestic Violence, Crime and Victims Act 2004 that is for the time being in operation.
simplified_text:
Simplified text:

Laws for Helping Victims: The Secretary of State must create a set of rules outlining the services victims should receive. These rules apply to public organizations involved with victims or the criminal justice system.

Support for Victims: The rules must ensure that victims have access to information about the legal process, support services, and the chance to express their opinions. They should also be able to challenge decisions that directly affect them.

Additional Rules: The Secretary of State can make more rules about the services for victims. However, these rules should not reduce the quality of services or limit who can receive them.

Specific Cases: The rules can apply to specific types of victims and the organizations that provide services to them. They may also require services to be provided to other people related to the victim.

Consideration for Different Situations: The rules can be different for different types of victims, organizations, and areas. The Secretary of State must also consider the needs of victims who are under 18 or have certain characteristics under the Equality Act 2010.

Exceptions: The rules cannot force someone in a judicial role to do anything, or someone involved in prosecution to make a decision against their discretion.

Previous Rules: Until the first code of practice under these rules is in place, the rules from the Domestic Violence, Crime and Victims Act 2004 will be used.

legal_text:
Preparing and issuing the victims’ code
(1)This section applies in relation to the code of practice required to be issued under section 2.
(2)The Secretary of State must prepare a draft of the code.
(3)In preparing the draft the Secretary of State must consult—
(a)the Attorney General,
(b)the Commissioner for Victims and Witnesses, and
(c)the Welsh Ministers.
(4)After preparing the draft the Secretary of State must—
(a)publish the draft, and
(b)specify a period during which representations about the draft may be made to the Secretary of State.
(5)The Secretary of State must—
(a)consider, in consultation with the Attorney General, any representations about the draft made to the Secretary of State before the end of the period specified in accordance with subsection (4)(b), and
(b)if the Secretary of State thinks it appropriate, modify the draft in the light of any such representations.
(6)After carrying out the duties under subsection (5), the Secretary of State must lay the draft code before Parliament.
(7)When the draft code has been laid before Parliament in accordance with subsection (6), the Secretary of State must bring it into operation on such day as the Secretary of State appoints by regulations.
(8)A requirement under any of subsections (2) to (5) may be met by steps taken before (as well as after) this section comes into force.
simplified_text:
Victims' Code Preparation and Issuance
This section applies to the code of practice required to be issued under section 2.
The Secretary of State must create a draft of the code.
In creating the draft, the Secretary of State must consult with:
- the Attorney General
- the Commissioner for Victims and Witnesses
- the Welsh Ministers
After creating the draft, the Secretary of State must:
- make the draft public
- specify a period during which feedback about the draft can be submitted to the Secretary of State
The Secretary of State must:
- consider any feedback about the draft submitted before the specified period ends, after consulting with the Attorney General
- modify the draft if deemed appropriate in light of the feedback
After completing the duties under subsection (5), the Secretary of State must present the draft code to Parliament.
Once the draft code has been presented to Parliament, the Secretary of State must put it into effect on a date decided by the Secretary of State through regulations.
A requirement from subsections (2) to (5) can be fulfilled by actions taken before, as well as after, this section becomes effective.

legal_text:
Revising the victims’ code
(1)The Secretary of State may from time to time revise the victims’ code.
(2)But the Secretary of State may revise the victims’ code only if satisfied that the proposed revisions would not result in—
(a)a significant reduction in the quality or extent of the services provided in accordance with the code, or
(b)a significant restriction in the description of persons to whom services are provided in accordance with the code.
(3)The procedure in section 3 applies to a revision of the victims’ code, except that if the Secretary of State considers that all of the revisions are minor the procedure in subsection (5) may be used instead.
(4)Revisions are minor if—
(a)they make corrections or clarifications, or
(b)they are consequential on changes to the law, practice or procedure relating to any aspect of the criminal justice system.
(5)The procedure in this subsection is that the Secretary of State must—
(a)consult the Attorney General, the Commissioner for Victims and Witnesses and the Welsh Ministers about the proposed revisions,
(b)lay a draft of the revised code before Parliament, and
(c)when the draft revised code has been laid before Parliament, bring it into operation on such day as the Secretary of State appoints by regulations.
simplified_text:
Revising the victims’ code

Making Changes to the Victims’ Rights Document: The Secretary of State has the power to update the victims’ code as needed. However, these updates can only be made if the Secretary of State is certain that they will not significantly reduce the quality or scope of the services provided under the code, or significantly limit the types of people who can receive these services.

Process for Revising the Code: The process for revising the victims’ code follows certain steps, unless the Secretary of State believes that all the changes are minor. Minor changes include corrections or clarifications, as well as changes that are a result of new laws, practices, or procedures related to the criminal justice system.

Consultation and Implementation: In the case of minor revisions, the Secretary of State must consult with the Attorney General, the Commissioner for Victims and Witnesses, and the Welsh Ministers. The revised code must also be presented to Parliament, and once it is laid before Parliament, it can come into effect on a date specified by the Secretary of State through regulations.

legal_text:
Code compliance
(1)Where the victims’ code makes provision about a service to be provided to victims by a person, the person must provide the service in accordance with the code unless the person has good reasons not to.
(2)Any person who is subject to the duty in subsection (1) and is not an individual must ensure that procedures are in place by which other persons may complain about an alleged failure to comply with the duty.
(3)If a person fails to act in accordance with the victims’ code, the failure does not of itself make that person liable to criminal or civil proceedings.
(4)But the victims’ code is admissible in evidence in criminal or civil proceedings, and a court may take into account a failure to act in accordance with the code in determining a question in the proceedings.
simplified_text:
Complying with the Victims' Code:

1. Service Provision: If the victims' code outlines a service to be provided to victims by a certain person, that person must follow the code when delivering the service, unless there are valid reasons not to do so.

2. Complaint Procedures: Any non-individual subject to the duty in point 1 must have procedures in place for others to file complaints if they believe there has been a failure to comply with the duty.

3. Legal Consequences: Failing to act in line with the victims' code doesn't automatically result in criminal or civil proceedings.

4. Admissible Evidence: The victims' code can be used as evidence in criminal or civil proceedings, and a court can consider a failure to act in accordance with the code when making decisions in these proceedings.

Raising Awareness and Ensuring Compliance: Organizations involved in the criminal justice system in a particular police area must take reasonable steps to make the public aware of the victims' code and ensure that their services comply with the legal duty outlined in section 5(1).

Specific Duties for Criminal Justice Bodies: These organizations are required to undertake specific activities, as prescribed by regulations. This includes gathering and sharing information about the services they provide with other relevant bodies and the local policing authority. They must also review this shared information with the concerned bodies.

Regulations and Consultation: The detailed requirements for collecting and sharing information are determined by regulations set by the Secretary of State. Before creating these regulations, the Secretary of State must consult with the Commissioner for Victims and Witnesses and other relevant individuals or organizations.

Definition of Criminal Justice Body: A "criminal justice body" includes the chief police officer for the area, the Crown Prosecution Service, the Lord Chancellor, the Secretary of State, youth offending teams, and probation services.

legal_text:
Arrangements for collection of victims’ feedback
(1)This section applies where the Secretary of State has made arrangements with a person for the collection by the person of information which—
(a)relates to the characteristics or experiences of users of services provided by a relevant criminal justice body in a police area, and
(b)is collected for the purposes of assessing whether and how those services are provided in accordance with the duty in section 5(1).
(2)The Secretary of State and the Attorney General may by a joint direction require the body to provide specified information to the person for the purposes of enabling or assisting the performance of the arrangements.
(3)A relevant criminal justice body which is directed to provide information under this section must provide it—
(a)in such form and manner as may be specified, and
(b)at such times or within such periods as may be specified.
(4)In this section—
“relevant criminal justice body” means a criminal justice body falling within paragraphs (a), (b) or (e) of the definition of “criminal justice body” in section 6(6);
“specified” means specified in the direction.
simplified_text:
Collecting Feedback from Victims: This rule applies when the Secretary of State has a deal with someone to gather information about the users of services provided by a relevant criminal justice body in a police area. This information is collected to check if the services are being provided according to the law.

Directing the Provision of Information: If necessary, the Secretary of State and the Attorney General can order the body to provide specific information to the person who is collecting the feedback.

Obligation to Provide Information: The relevant criminal justice body must provide the specified information in the way and at the times specified in the order.

Definition: "Relevant criminal justice body" refers to specific types of criminal justice bodies, and "specified" means mentioned in the order.

legal_text:
Reviewing code compliance: elected local policing bodies
(1)The elected local policing body for a police area must keep under review whether and how criminal justice bodies which provide services in the police area provide those services in accordance with the duty in section 5(1).
(2)The elected local policing body for a police area must, in particular, undertake the following activities in such manner as may be prescribed—
(a)provide the Secretary of State with information shared with it under section 6(2)(b), or such of that information as may be prescribed;
(b)participate in any review under section 6(2)(c);
(c)provide the Secretary of State with such reports, on such matters in connection with a review under section 6(2)(c), as may be prescribed.
(3)In subsection (2), “prescribed” means prescribed in regulations made by the Secretary of State.
(4)Regulations under subsection (2) may, in particular—
(a)prescribe the times at which, or periods within which, information or a report must be provided;
(b)prescribe the form in which information or a report must be provided, or require information or a report to be provided in such form as may be specified in a notice issued from time to time by the Secretary of State.
(5)Before making regulations under this section, the Secretary of State must consult the Commissioner for Victims and Witnesses and such other persons as the Secretary of State considers appropriate (and it is immaterial for these purposes whether the consultation is carried out before or after this section comes into force).
(6)In this section, “criminal justice body” has the meaning given by section 6(6).
simplified_text:
Reviewing code compliance: elected local policing bodies

Review and Oversight:
The elected local policing body for a specific police area must regularly assess whether the criminal justice bodies providing services in that area are meeting their duty as outlined in section 5(1).

Prescribed Activities:
The elected local policing body is required to undertake specific activities in the manner set out by regulations, including sharing information with the Secretary of State, participating in reviews, and providing reports to the Secretary of State concerning the reviews.

Regulations and Consultation:
"Preset" refers to rules set by the Secretary of State through regulations, which may include defining the timing, format, and method of providing information or reports. Before creating such regulations, the Secretary of State must consult the Commissioner for Victims and Witnesses and other relevant parties.

Meaning of "Criminal Justice Body":
In this section, "criminal justice body" has the meaning given by section 6(6).

Code Awareness and Compliance Review: British Transport Police

Definitions:
- "the Authority" refers to the British Transport Police Authority  
- "the Chief Constable" is the Chief Constable of the British Transport Police Force  
- "relevant services" are services provided in England and Wales by the Chief Constable  

Duties of the Chief Constable and the Authority:
1. The Chief Constable is required to take reasonable steps to promote awareness of the victims’ code among users of relevant services and the public.
2. The Chief Constable and the Authority are responsible for reviewing whether and how relevant services are provided in accordance with the duty in section 5(1).  
3. The Chief Constable is specifically required to:
    a. Collect prescribed information about the provision of relevant services
    b. Share prescribed information about the provision of relevant services with the Authority
    c. Review with the Authority the information shared under paragraph (b).  

The Authority is specifically required to:
    a. Provide the Secretary of State with the information shared with it under subsection (4)(b), or such of that information as may be prescribed
    b. Participate in any review under subsection (4)(c)
    c. Provide the Secretary of State with such prescribed reports, on such matters in connection with a review under subsection (4)(c).  

Additional Information:
- "Prescribed" refers to regulations made by the Secretary of State  
- Regulations under this section may, among other things:
    a. Prescribe different information for different services  
    b. Prescribe information relating to the characteristics or experiences of service users  
    c. Prescribe the timing and format for collecting, sharing, and reviewing information, as well as providing reports to the Secretary of State.  
- Before making regulations under this section, the Secretary of State is required to consult the Commissioner for Victims and Witnesses and other relevant persons.

Code Awareness and Reviewing Compliance: Ministry of Defence Police

Definitions:
- "Chief Constable": The head of the Ministry of Defence Police.
- "relevant services": Services provided in England and Wales by the Chief Constable.

Duties:
1. The Chief Constable must take reasonable steps to make sure that users of relevant services and the public are aware of the victims’ code.
2. The Chief Constable and the Secretary of State must regularly check if the relevant services are being provided in line with their duty as outlined in section 5(1).
3. The Chief Constable must, as prescribed, collect information about the relevant services, share it with the Secretary of State, and review it with the Secretary of State.
4. The Secretary of State must participate in any review with the Chief Constable, and prepare reports on specified matters in connection with the review.
5. "prescribed" means specified in regulations by the Secretary of State.

Regulations:
1. Regulations under this section may specify different information for different services, characteristics or experiences of service users, and the timing and form of collecting and sharing information.
2. Before making regulations, the Secretary of State must consult the Commissioner for Victims and Witnesses and other relevant parties, regardless of when the consultation occurs in relation to the section coming into force.

legal_text:
Reviewing code compliance: Secretary of State and Attorney General
(1)The Secretary of State and the Attorney General, acting jointly, must—
(a)keep under review the code compliance of the persons mentioned in subsection (6), and
(b)annually, prepare and publish a report about the code compliance of those persons in the period to which the report relates.
(2)If the Secretary of State and the Attorney General agree that the code compliance of a person mentioned in subsection (6) is unsatisfactory they may—
(a)if the person is the chief officer of police for a police area, give the elected local policing body for the area a notice setting out their reasons for being of that view;
(b)in any other case, give the person a notice setting out their reasons for being of that view.
(3)If the Secretary of State and the Attorney General give a notice under subsection (2) they must—
(a)if the notice is given under paragraph (a) of that subsection, send a copy of the notice to the chief officer of police to whom the notice relates, and
(b)in any case, publish the notice in such form and manner as they consider appropriate.
(4)The Secretary of State and the Attorney General must consult the Commissioner for Victims and Witnesses before—
(a)publishing a report under subsection (1)(b);
(b)giving a notice under subsection (2).
(5)The Secretary of State must publish such compliance information as the Secretary of State considers will enable members of the public to assess the code compliance of the persons mentioned in subsection (6) in the period to which the information relates.
(6)The persons are—
(a)each criminal justice body which provides services in a police area;
(b)the Chief Constable of the British Transport Police Force;
(c)the Chief Constable of the Ministry of Defence Police.
(7)For the purposes of this section—
(a)“compliance information” means information provided to the Secretary of State under section 8(2)(a), 9(5)(a) or 10(4)(b), or information collected under arrangements mentioned in section 7;
(b)the “code compliance” of a person is whether and how the services provided by the person in the relevant area are provided in accordance with the duty in section 5(1).
(8)In subsection (7)(b), “relevant area” means—
(a)in relation to a criminal justice body which provides services in a police area, that area;
(b)in relation to the Chief Constable of the British Transport Police Force or the Chief Constable of the Ministry of Defence Police, England and Wales.
(9)The first report under paragraph (b) of subsection (1) may relate to any 12 month period that includes the day on which that paragraph comes into force.
(10)Subsequent reports must relate to the 12 month period immediately following the 12 month period to which the previous report relates.
(11)The Secretary of State must lay each report before Parliament.
(12)Information or a report published under this section—
(a)must be published as soon as is reasonably practicable after the end of the period to which it relates;
(b)may be published in such form and manner as the Secretary of State considers appropriate.
(13)Where information published by the Secretary of State under subsection (5) relates to a particular police area, the elected local policing body for the area must take reasonable steps to make members of the public in the area aware of how to access the information.
(14)In this section, “criminal justice body” has the meaning given by section 6(6).

Monitoring Compliance with Codes of Conduct: Secretary of State and Attorney General

Review and Report: The Secretary of State and the Attorney General must work together to monitor whether certain individuals and organizations are following the rules of conduct outlined in the law. They must also prepare and share an annual report about the compliance of these parties.

Notifying Unsatisfactory Compliance: If the Secretary of State and the Attorney General agree that one of these parties is not following the rules, they may issue a notice explaining their concerns to either the elected local policing body or directly to the individual or organization.

Publishing Notices and Reports: If a notice is issued, it must be sent to the relevant party and published in an appropriate manner. The Commissioner for Victims and Witnesses must be consulted before publishing a report or issuing a notice.

Providing Information to the Public: The Secretary of State must share information that allows the public to assess the code compliance of the mentioned individuals and organizations.

Entities Covered: This review applies to various bodies involved in the criminal justice system, including those providing services in a police area, the Chief Constable of the British Transport Police Force, and the Chief Constable of the Ministry of Defence Police.

Definition of Compliance: "Compliance information" refers to information provided to the Secretary of State or collected under specific arrangements. "Code compliance" refers to whether and how services are provided in line with the duty outlined in the law.

Publishing Reports: The first report can relate to any 12-month period after the relevant provision comes into force. Subsequent reports cover the 12-month period following the previous report and must be presented to Parliament.

Publishing Information: The Secretary of State must publish information and reports as soon as possible after the relevant period ends.

Awareness of Information: The elected local policing body must take steps to inform the public about accessing the information published by the Secretary of State about their area.

Interpretation: "Criminal justice body" has the meaning outlined in the law.

Guidance for Understanding and Checking Compliance

The Secretary of State must provide instructions on how to fulfill obligations under sections 6 to 11. Anyone who has to meet these obligations must consider these instructions while doing so.

The instructions might cover:

Different ways to raise awareness about the victims' code, including specific actions for users of a company's services and for the general public.

How to gather information, especially regarding individuals under 18 or those with protected characteristics according to the Equality Act 2010.

How to share and review information, including how to conduct review meetings.

The actions that a local elected policing body must take, if a certain section applies, to ensure that the public knows how to access compliance information published by the Secretary of State that relates to their area.

Before issuing these instructions, the Secretary of State must consult the Commissioner for Victims and Witnesses and other relevant parties, whether before or after this section comes into effect.

Guidance on Code Awareness and Reviewing Compliance 

(1) The Secretary of State will create guidance on how to fulfill responsibilities under sections 6 to 11 (and anyone who has such responsibilities must take the guidance into account when fulfilling their responsibilities).
(2) The guidance may include:
(a) Different ways to make people aware of the victims’ code (including special provisions for users of services provided by an organization and other members of the public).
(b) How to collect information (especially about individuals under the age of 18 or individuals with protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010).
(c) How to share and review information (including the conduct of review meetings).
(d) Steps that an elected local policing body must take, when section 11(13) applies, to inform the public about how to access compliance information published by the Secretary of State relating to the police area.
(3) Before creating this guidance, the Secretary of State must consult with the Commissioner for Victims and Witnesses and other relevant individuals. This consultation can happen before or after this section comes into force.

simplified_text:
Victim Support Role Guidance:

The Secretary of State must create guidelines for specific victim support roles in England and, except in specific cases, in Wales.

These guidelines cannot involve matters that would be under the control of Senedd Cymru if they were included in a law passed by Senedd.

In this section, "specified" means identified in regulations made by the Secretary of State, and "victim support role" refers to activities performed by individuals that involve providing support to victims of criminal conduct.

Victim support roles can be specified based on things such as when the role is performed, the type of support provided, and the type of criminal conduct involved.

The guidance on victim support roles must cover the support provided, training and qualifications for those who perform the role, and how they work with others in the criminal justice system.

The guidelines must also address support for victims who are under 18 or have protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010.

Any person with public duties related to victims or the criminal justice system must consider these guidelines when performing their duties, unless they are acting in a judicial capacity or on behalf of a devolved Welsh authority.

Disclosures by victims that cannot be precluded by agreement

Disclosure Protections for Victims:
Agreements cannot stop victims from making certain disclosures of information. These disclosures can include:
- Speaking to law enforcement for them to address relevant wrongdoing
- Seeking legal advice from a qualified lawyer about the wrongdoing
- Getting support from a regulated profession in relation to the wrongdoing
- Seeking support from a service that assists victims in relation to the wrongdoing
- Cooperating with a regulator of a regulated profession regarding the wrongdoing
- Releasing the information into the public domain

Exceptions:
Agreements can still prevent disclosures if the primary purpose is to release the information into the public domain. The Secretary of State can make regulations to add, remove, or change the types of disclosures that agreements cannot prevent. These regulations must not apply to disclosures made by someone who is not a victim or does not relate to the relevant wrongdoing.

Definitions:
- "Entitled to practise": Qualification to practice a regulated profession
- "Law enforcement functions": Investigating or prosecuting criminal offenses
- "Partner": Someone in a significant relationship, including marriage, civil partnership, or long-term intimate personal relationship
- "Qualified lawyer": A person authorized to provide legal services
- "Regulated profession" and "regulator": Defined by the Professional Qualifications Act 2022
- "Relevant conduct": The behavior that has led the person to believe they are a victim of wrongdoing

Establishment and Conduct of Domestic Abuse Related Death Reviews

The Domestic Violence, Crime and Victims Act 2004 is changed to include domestic abuse related death reviews. These reviews look at the circumstances of a person's death if it was caused by domestic abuse and aim to learn from the situation.

The Secretary of State may ask specific organizations to set up or take part in these reviews. Those involved in the reviews must follow any guidance from the Secretary of State. Once a review is completed, a copy of the report must be sent to the Secretary of State and the Domestic Abuse Commissioner by the police, local authorities, healthcare organizations, and other relevant bodies. The Secretary of State has the power to adjust the list of organizations involved. Additionally, certain sections of the existing law are updated to align with the new domestic abuse related death review process.

The Domestic Abuse Act 2021 is changed to include a new rule. This rule says that the police must have a way to tell schools when they think a child is being abused at home.

The rule says that if a police officer has good reason to think that a child in their area is being abused at home, they should tell the school as soon as they can. But sometimes, the Secretary of State can say when the police don't have to tell the school.
