Costs: General

An RTM company and its members are not responsible for paying the expenses of any other person as a result of a claim notice issued by the company regarding any property, except as explained in this section. Any lease, transfer, contract, or agreement that says otherwise is not valid.

The RTM company is responsible for paying its members for any agreed-upon expenses incurred. Similarly, a member of the RTM company is responsible for paying the company for any agreed-upon expenses, as well as another member for their expenses.

If a court or tribunal has the authority under another law to order the RTM company or its members to pay costs, and they issue such an order, then the company or its members are indeed liable for those costs.

The RTM company and its members are responsible for the costs incurred by another person under the circumstances outlined in section 87B.

An owner of a managed dwelling can ask the estate manager in charge of the property for specific information, as laid out by the Secretary of State. This information must relate to the management of the estate.

The estate manager must provide the owner with any requested information that they have in their possession. If the estate manager doesn't have the information, but believes that another person does, they must request it from that person.

The person in possession of the requested information must provide it to the estate manager.

If a person is asked for information and they don't have it but believe another person does, they must request it from that person, who must then provide the information.

The Secretary of State has the authority to make regulations regarding the process of making requests, setting timeframes for requests, and specifying when the duty to comply with a request doesn't apply. 

Further details about making requests under this section are covered in Section 81. 

Any regulations made under this section are subject to oversight through the negative procedure.

If you own a property in a managed building and believe that someone has requested payment of fees incorrectly or that the estate manager has not provided a required report, you can ask a special court to review the situation. The court has the power to do several things, including:
- Requiring the estate manager to demand payment correctly or to provide the report within a specific time frame.
- Ordering the estate manager to compensate you for their failure.
- Making any other necessary orders related to the situation.

Similarly, if someone fails to follow requirements under section 80 or 81, another person can apply to the court. The court can then order them to comply with the requirement, pay damages for the failure, or make any other necessary orders. Damages awarded under this law cannot exceed £5,000. (a)its amount appeared for the required period on an administration charge schedule published under section 84, or
(b)its amount was determined in accordance with a method that appeared on the published administration charge schedule for the required period.
(3)“The required period” is the period of 28 days ending with the day on which the administration charge is demanded to be paid.
(4)An administration charge is not payable to an estate manager if—
(a)the charge relates to the same matter as, or a matter of a similar nature to, a matter for which an administration charge is payable by another person to the estate manager,
(b)the amount of the charge is different from the charge payable by that other person, and
(c)it is not reasonable for the amount of the charge to be different.

Limitation of Administration Charges:

1) An administration charge must be reasonable to be payable.
2) An administration charge can only be paid to an estate manager if:
   a) it was listed on a published administration charge schedule for at least 28 days, or
   b) it was determined according to a method listed on the published administration charge schedule.
3) "The required period" is the 28-day period ending on the day when the administration charge is demanded.
4) An administration charge cannot be paid to an estate manager if:
   a) it relates to the same matter, or something similar, for which another person has already paid an administration charge to the estate manager,
   b) the amount of the charge is different from what the other person paid, and

(b)the person to which it is payable,
(c)the amount which is payable,
(d)the date on or by which it is payable, and
(e)the manner in which it is payable.
(2)Subsection (1) applies whether or not any payment has been made.
(3)No application under subsection (1) may be made in respect of a matter which—
(a)relates to a dwelling, and has been agreed or admitted by every owner of the dwelling,
(b)has been, or is to be, referred to arbitration pursuant to a post-dispute arbitration agreement to which every owner of the dwelling is a party,
(c)has been the subject of determination by a court, or
(d)has been the subject of determination by an arbitral tribunal pursuant to a post-dispute arbitration agreement.
(4)But an owner of a dwelling is not to be taken to have agreed or admitted any matter by reason only of having made any payment.
(5)An agreement (other than a post-dispute arbitration agreement) is void in so far as it purports to provide for a determination—

simplified_text:
Tribunal Determination of Administration Charges

An application can be made to a tribunal to decide if an administration charge needs to be paid and, if so:
- Who needs to pay it
- Who should receive the payment
- The amount to be paid
- The deadline for payment
- The method of payment

This rule applies whether or not any payment has been made already.

However, an application cannot be made if:
- It concerns a dwelling and has been agreed or admitted to by every owner of the dwelling
- It is the subject of an arbitration agreement or has been referred to arbitration by every owner of the dwelling
- It has been decided by a court
- It has been decided by an arbitral tribunal based on an arbitration agreement

It's important to note that making a payment does not mean that an owner of a dwelling has agreed or admitted to any matter.

Also, any agreement that tries to dictate how a question can be decided in a particular way or based on particular evidence is not valid if it can be the subject of an application to the tribunal.

Appointing a Replacement Manager:

Appointment Orders: Further Provision

An appointment order can:

Make arrangements for the substitute manager to carry out their duties under the order, and any other related matters, as decided by the tribunal. This can include:
- Shifting rights and responsibilities from contracts or agreements to the substitute manager.
- Allowing the substitute manager to pursue legal claims for events that happened before or after they were appointed.
- Deciding how much the substitute manager should be paid by the estate manager.
- Specifying the timeframe during which the substitute manager can carry out their duties.

Be subject to conditions determined by the tribunal.

Be suspended according to terms set by the tribunal.

The tribunal can change or cancel an appointment order upon the request of an interested party or on its own initiative. However, this can only happen if the tribunal is satisfied that doing so won't lead to the same problems as the original appointment order, and if it seems fair and appropriate given the circumstances.

When deciding on the terms of an appointment order, or whether to change or cancel it, the tribunal must consider whether the estate manager has breached regulations that require them to be a member of a redress scheme under section 100(1).

Enforcing Sales Information Request: If someone (let's call them "C") asks for sales information and the other person ("D") doesn't comply with the request, "C" can apply to a special court called the tribunal. The tribunal can then make a few different orders:

1. They can order "D" to comply with the request within a certain time.
2. They can order "D" to pay "C" for not complying.
3. If "D" has charged "C" more than the allowed amount, the tribunal can order "D" to refund the excess amount to "C."
4. If "D" charged "C" in breach of regulations, the tribunal can also order "D" to repay the amount charged.

Limits on Damages: The damages that can be awarded under point 2(b) cannot be more than £5,000.

Changing the Limit: The government can change the £5,000 limit if it thinks it's necessary to keep up with changes in the value of money.

Regulations: Any changes to the law regarding this matter will go through a process where they are reviewed before being approved.

Voluntary Redress Schemes: Under this law, redress schemes have the option to allow individuals to join as voluntary members. These members can then have their complaints investigated or resolved through a voluntary jurisdiction, even if they are not current or former property owners under estate management. The schemes can also offer voluntary mediation services. Additionally, the schemes have the ability to exclude certain complaints from being investigated or resolved, under specific circumstances.

In this law, "complaints under a voluntary jurisdiction" refer to complaints where there is no requirement to be a member of a redress scheme, and the members involved have willingly accepted the scheme's authority. "Voluntary mediation services" are processes like mediation or conciliation that are available at the request of a member in response to complaints made against them, or complaints made by them against others. "Voluntary members" are individuals who are not obligated to be part of a redress scheme.

(4)In any notice or other document that the CMA is required to give or publish under or by virtue of this Part, the CMA may describe a digital activity by reference to the nature of the activity, brand names or both.
simplified_text:
Defining Digital Activities: In this section, "digital activities" include:

- Providing a service using the internet, whether for payment or not
- Providing one or more pieces of digital content, whether for payment or not
- Other activities done for the purpose of the activities mentioned above

Using the Internet: A service is considered to be provided via the internet even if it's provided using a combination of the internet and an electronic communications service.

Treating as Single Activity: The CMA can consider two or more activities by one company as a single digital activity if they have similar purposes or can be combined to achieve a specific goal.

Describing Digital Activities: The CMA can describe a digital activity in any notice or document by mentioning the nature of the activity, brand names, or both.

legal_text:
Link to the United Kingdom
A digital activity is linked to the United Kingdom for the purposes of section 2(1)(a) if—
(a)the digital activity has a significant number of UK users,
(b)the undertaking that carries out the digital activity carries on business in the United Kingdom in relation to the digital activity, or
(c)the digital activity or the way in which the undertaking carries on the digital activity is likely to have an immediate, substantial and foreseeable effect on trade in the United Kingdom.
simplified_text:
When a digital activity is considered to be linked to the United Kingdom according to section 2(1)(a), it means that:
- The digital activity is used by a large number of people in the UK,
- The company conducting the digital activity operates its business in the UK for that digital activity, or
- The digital activity or how the company conducts the digital activity is expected to have a direct, significant, and predictable impact on trade in the United Kingdom.

legal_text:
Substantial and entrenched market power
In order to assess whether an undertaking has substantial and entrenched market power in respect of a digital activity for the purposes of section 2(2)(a), the CMA must carry out a forward-looking assessment of a period of at least 5 years, taking into account developments that—
(a)would be expected or foreseeable if the CMA did not designate the undertaking as having SMS in respect of the digital activity, and
(b)may affect the undertaking’s conduct in carrying out the digital activity.
simplified_text:
Assessment of Market Power:
To determine if a company has significant and established market power for a digital activity under section 2(2)(a), the CMA must look ahead at least 5 years and consider how developments could impact the company's behavior in conducting the digital activity. This assessment should take into account potential developments that would occur if the CMA did not designate the company as having significant market power for the digital activity.

Significant Position: A company has a significant position in a digital activity if one or more of these things is true:

The company is big or important in the digital activity.

Many other companies use the digital activity to run their business.

The company's position in the digital activity allows it to expand its control over other activities.

The company's position in the digital activity allows it to control or greatly influence how other companies operate, in relation to the digital activity or other things.

legal_text:
The turnover condition
(1)The CMA may not designate an undertaking as having SMS in respect of a digital activity unless the turnover condition is met in relation to the undertaking.

(2)The turnover condition is met in relation to an undertaking if the CMA estimates that—

(a)the total value of the global turnover of an undertaking or, where the undertaking is part of a group, the global turnover of that group in the relevant period exceeds £25 billion, or

(b)the total value of the UK turnover of an undertaking or, where the undertaking is part of a group, the UK turnover of that group in the relevant period exceeds £1 billion.

(3)The Secretary of State may by regulations amend either of the sums mentioned in subsection (2).

(4)Regulations under subsection (3) are subject to the affirmative procedure.

(5)The CMA must—

(a)keep under review the sums mentioned in subsection (2), and

(b)from time to time advise the Secretary of State as to whether the sums are still appropriate.
simplified_text:
Setting a Condition Based on Turnover: The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) cannot designate a business as having a Strategic Market Status (SMS) for a digital activity unless the business meets a specified condition related to its turnover.

Conditions for Meeting Turnover: For a business to meet this turnover condition, the CMA must estimate that either the business's global turnover or its UK turnover in a specific period exceeds certain financial thresholds outlined in the law.

Adjusting Turnover Amounts: The Secretary of State has the authority to change the financial thresholds mentioned in the law through regulations.

Review and Advisory Role: The CMA is responsible for reviewing the mentioned financial thresholds and advising the Secretary of State periodically on whether they are still appropriate.

legal_text:
(6)In this section—

(a)the “relevant period” means—

(i)the most recent period of 12 months (“period A”) in respect of which the CMA considers that it is able to make an estimate of the total value of the relevant turnover of the undertaking or group, or

(ii)if the CMA estimates that the relevant turnover of the undertaking or group in the period of 12 months ending immediately before period A was higher than the relevant turnover of the undertaking or group in period A, that earlier period of 12 months;

simplified_text:
(6) In this section—
The "relevant period" means the most recent 12-month period (referred to as "period A") during which the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) can estimate the total value of the relevant turnover of the company or group. If the CMA estimates that the relevant turnover in the 12-month period immediately before period A was higher than in period A, then that earlier 12-month period will be considered the relevant period.
The "relevant turnover" refers to the UK turnover or global turnover of the company or group.

legal_text:
Turnover of an undertaking
(1)This section applies for the purposes of the turnover condition.

(2)The total value of the global turnover of an undertaking or group in the relevant period (as defined in section 7(6)) is, subject to regulations under subsection (4), the total value of the turnover of the undertaking or group arising in connection with any of its activities.

(3)The total value of the UK turnover of an undertaking or group in the relevant period is, subject to regulations under subsection (4), the total value of the turnover of the undertaking or group—

(a)arising in connection with any of its activities, and

(b)relating to UK users or UK customers.

(4)The Secretary of State may by regulations make provision about how the total value of the global turnover or UK turnover of an undertaking or group in a period is to be estimated for the purposes of the turnover condition.

(5)Regulations under subsection (4) may (among other things)—

(a)make provision about amounts which are, or are not, to be regarded as comprising the turnover of an undertaking or group;

(b)confer on the CMA the power to determine matters specified in the regulations (including the matter mentioned in paragraph (a)).

(6)Regulations under subsection (4) are subject to the negative procedure.
simplified_text:
Calculation of Turnover for Businesses
(1) The following rules are used to determine the value of turnover for the turnover condition.

(2) The total value of the global turnover of a business or group during the relevant period (as defined in section 7(6)) is, subject to regulations under subsection (4), the total value of the turnover arising from any of its activities.

(3) The total value of the UK turnover of a business or group in the relevant period is, subject to regulations under subsection (4), the total value of the turnover—

(a) arising from any of its activities, and

(b) related to customers in the UK.

(4) The Secretary of State may create rules about how the total value of the global turnover or UK turnover of a business or group in a period should be estimated for the turnover condition.

(5) Rules under subsection (4) may (among other things)—

(a) specify which amounts are included in turnover and which are not;

(b) give the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) the power to decide on matters specified in the rules (including what is mentioned in paragraph (a)).

(6) Rules under subsection (4) are subject to the negative procedure.

legal_text:
Initial SMS investigations
(1)The CMA may begin an initial SMS investigation where it has reasonable grounds to consider that it may be able to designate an undertaking as having SMS in respect of a digital activity in accordance with section 2.
(2)An “initial SMS investigation” is an investigation into whether to designate an undertaking as having SMS in respect of a digital activity where the undertaking is not already designated in respect of that activity (subject to section 10(4)).
(3)The CMA may begin an initial SMS investigation into whether to designate an undertaking as having SMS in respect of a digital activity even if it has previously made a decision not to designate the undertaking as having SMS in respect of that activity.
simplified_text:
Initial SMS Investigations:
The CMA can start an initial SMS investigation if it has good reason to believe it can designate a business as having SMS for a digital activity under section 2.
An initial SMS investigation is when the CMA looks into whether to designate a business as having SMS for a digital activity that it has not been designated for before (unless stated in section 10(4)).
The CMA can start an initial SMS investigation even if it previously decided not to designate the business as having SMS for that activity.

legal_text:
Further SMS investigations
(1)The CMA may begin a further SMS investigation in relation to the designation of a designated undertaking in respect of a relevant digital activity at any time during the designation period (see section 18) relating to that designation.
(2)The CMA must begin a further SMS investigation in relation to the designation of a designated undertaking in respect of a relevant digital activity not later than 9 months before the end of the designation period relating to that designation, if it is not already carrying one out at that time under subsection (1).
(3)A “further SMS investigation” is an investigation into whether—
(a)to revoke a designated undertaking’s designation in respect of the relevant digital activity or to designate the undertaking again in respect of that activity, and
(b)to make provision under section 17 (existing obligations).
(4)A further SMS investigation may also include an investigation into whether to designate the designated undertaking in respect of a digital activity that the CMA considers to be similar or connected to the relevant digital activity (whether instead of, or in addition to, the relevant digital activity).
simplified_text:
Further Investigations:
The CMA can start another investigation in relation to the designation of a specific company for a digital activity at any time during the period of designation. 

The CMA must start another investigation regarding the designation of a specific company for a digital activity at least 9 months before the end of the designated period, if it hasn't already started one earlier.

A "further investigation" is an examination into whether to remove a company's designation for a digital activity, or to re-designate the company for that activity, and to make related provisions.

The further investigation may also include a look into whether to designate the company for a digital activity that the CMA considers to be similar or connected to the relevant digital activity.

legal_text:
Procedure relating to SMS investigations
(1)When the CMA begins an SMS investigation it must give the undertaking to which the investigation relates a notice (an “SMS investigation notice”).
(2)The SMS investigation notice must state—
(a)in the case of an initial SMS investigation—
(i)the reasonable grounds mentioned in section 9(1);
(ii)that the CMA may close the investigation in accordance with section 12;
(b)the purpose and scope of the SMS investigation;
(c)the period by the end of which the CMA must give the undertaking a notice setting out its decisions as a result of the investigation (see section 14(2));
(d)the circumstances in which that period may be extended (see section 104).
(3)The statement of the purpose and scope of the investigation must include a description of the undertaking and digital activities to which the investigation relates.
(4)The CMA must give the undertaking one or more revised versions of the SMS investigation notice if it changes its view of the purpose and scope of the investigation.
(5)As soon as reasonably practicable after giving an SMS investigation notice or a revised version of an SMS investigation notice, the CMA must—
(a)publish the notice, and
(b)give a copy of the notice to the FCA, OFCOM, the Information Commissioner, the Bank of England and the PRA.
simplified_text:
Investigation Notice for Digital Activities: When the competition and markets authority (CMA) starts an investigation relating to digital activities, it must provide the company under investigation with a notice called an "SMS investigation notice."

Contents of the Notice: The notice must include the reasons for the investigation, the purpose and scope of the investigation, the deadline for the CMA to provide its decisions based on the investigation, and the circumstances under which this deadline may be extended.

Revisions to the Notice: If the CMA changes its understanding of the purpose and scope of the investigation, it must provide the company with an updated version of the investigation notice.

Notification and Publication: The CMA must promptly publish the notice and provide copies to the Financial Conduct Authority, OFCOM, the Information Commissioner, the Bank of England, and the Prudential Regulation Authority.

legal_text:
Closing an initial SMS investigation without a decision
(1)The CMA may close an initial SMS investigation at any time before it has reached a final view on the matters mentioned in paragraphs (a) and (b) of section 2(1).
(2)When the CMA decides to close an initial SMS investigation, the CMA must give the undertaking to which the investigation related a notice to that effect.
(3)The notice must include the CMA’s reasons for closing the investigation.
(4)As soon as reasonably practicable after giving a notice under subsection (2), the CMA must publish the notice.
simplified_text:
Closing an initial SMS investigation without a decision:
1) The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) can end an initial SMS investigation at any time before making a final decision on the matters mentioned in paragraphs (a) and (b) of section 2(1).
2) When the CMA chooses to close an initial SMS investigation, the CMA must provide the organization being investigated with a notice about the closure.
3) The notice must explain why the investigation is being closed.
4) The CMA must publish the notice as soon as reasonably possible after providing it.

legal_text:
Consultation on proposed decision
(1)The CMA must—
(a)carry out a public consultation on any decision that it is considering making as a result of an SMS investigation (see section 14(1)), and
(b)bring the public consultation to the attention of such persons as it considers appropriate.
(2)Consultation under subsection (1) may be carried out at the same time as consultation under section 24(1) (consultation in relation to a conduct requirement).
simplified_text:
Proposed Decision Consultation:

1. Public Consultation: 
The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) must publicly consult on any decision it is thinking about making after an investigation related to a legal duty to provide information (see section 14(1)), and inform relevant people about the public consultation.

2. Simultaneous Consultation: 
The consultation mentioned in point 1 can be done at the same time as another consultation related to a conduct requirement under section 24(1).

legal_text:
Outcome of SMS investigations
(1)The CMA must—
(a)in the case of an initial SMS investigation which it does not close under section 12, decide whether to designate the undertaking to which the investigation relates as having SMS in respect of a digital activity to which the investigation relates;
(b)in the case of a further SMS investigation, make a decision on the matters mentioned in section 10(3) and, where relevant, section 10(4).
(2)The CMA must give the undertaking a notice (an “SMS decision notice”) setting out its decisions under subsection (1) on or before the last day of the period (the “SMS investigation period”) of 9 months beginning with the day on which the SMS investigation notice is given.
(3)The giving of a revised version of an SMS investigation notice under section 11(4) does not change the day on which the SMS investigation period begins.
simplified_text:
Outcome of SMS Investigations

(1) Initial Investigation: If the CMA does not close an initial SMS investigation under section 12, it must decide whether to categorize the company being investigated as having significant market power in relation to a digital activity.

(2) Further Investigation: In the case of a subsequent investigation, the CMA must make decisions on the matters mentioned in section 10(3) and, where applicable, section 10(4).

(3) Deadline for Notice: The CMA must provide the company with a notice (referred to as an "SMS decision notice") outlining its decisions under subsection (1) on or before the last day of the 9-month period (referred to as the "SMS investigation period") starting from the day the SMS investigation notice is given.

(4) Revision: If a revised version of an SMS investigation notice is provided under section 11(4), the start date of the SMS investigation period remains unchanged.

legal_text:
Notice requirements: decisions about whether to designate
(1)Where the CMA decides as a result of an initial SMS investigation not to designate the undertaking to which the investigation relates as having SMS in respect of a digital activity to which the investigation relates, the SMS decision notice must include the CMA’s reasons for its decision.
(2)Subsections (3) to (6) apply where the CMA decides to designate an undertaking as having SMS in respect of a digital activity (whether or not that undertaking is already a designated undertaking).
(3)The SMS decision notice must include—
(a)a description of the designated undertaking,
(b)a description of the digital activity with respect to which the designation has effect,
(c)any provision that the CMA has decided to make in reliance on section 17 (existing obligations),
(d)the CMA’s reasons for its decisions under section 14(1),
(e)a statement of the period (the “designation period”) for which the designation has effect (see section 18),
(f)a statement of the circumstances in which the designation period may be extended (see section 104), and
(g)a statement of the circumstances in which the designation may be revoked before the end of the designation period (see sections 10 and 14(1)(b)).
simplified_text:
Notification Requirements for Decisions on Designation:

Deciding not to Designate: If the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) decides not to designate a company as having a Strategic Market Status (SMS) for a specific digital activity after an initial investigation, the notice must include the reasons for this decision.

Designating an Undertaking: If the CMA decides to designate a company as having SMS for a digital activity, the notice must include a description of the company and the digital activity, any obligations imposed, the reasons for the decision, the duration of the designation, circumstances for extension, and conditions for revocation.

legal_text:
Notice requirements: decisions about whether to designate
(4)The CMA may give one or more revised versions of an SMS decision notice if it changes its view of—
(a)the undertaking, or
(b)the digital activity,
provided that the undertaking or digital activity, as the case may be, remains substantially the same.
(5)The giving of a revised SMS decision notice providing for the designation of an undertaking does not affect—
(a)the day on which the designation period in relation to that designation begins, or
(b)anything done under this Part in relation to that undertaking.
(6)As soon as reasonably practicable after giving a revised SMS decision notice, the CMA must publish the revised notice.
simplified_text:
Revised Decision Notices: The CMA can issue new versions of a decision notice if it changes its opinion about a business or digital activity, as long as the business or activity remains mostly unchanged. Issuing a revised decision notice about a business doesn't change when the designation period begins or affect any actions taken in relation to that business under this Part.

Public Disclosure: The CMA must publish the revised decision notice as soon as possible after issuing it.

legal_text:
Notice requirements: decisions to revoke a designation
(1)This section applies where the CMA decides, as a result of a further SMS investigation, to revoke the existing designation of a designated undertaking in respect of a digital activity without making a further designation in respect of that digital activity under section 14(1)(b).
(2)The SMS decision notice must provide for the revocation of the existing designation—
(a)to have effect at the end of the day on which the notice is given, or
(b)to have effect from such earlier time as the CMA may specify in the notice.
(3)The SMS decision notice must include—
(a)any provision that the CMA has decided to make in reliance on section 17 (existing obligations);
(b)the CMA’s reasons for its decisions under section 14(1)(b).
simplified_text:
Revocation Notice: Decisions to Cancel a Designation

(1) This rule applies when the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) decides, after further investigation, to cancel the current designation of a designated company for a digital activity without making a new designation for that digital activity under section 14(1)(b).

(2) The decision notice must specify the cancellation of the current designation to:
  (a) take effect at the end of the day the notice is issued, or
  (b) take effect from an earlier time specified by the CMA in the notice.

(3) The decision notice must include:
  (a) any provision that the CMA has decided to make based on section 17 (existing obligations),
  (b) the CMA’s reasons for its decisions under section 14(1)(b).

legal_text:
Existing obligations
(1)Where the CMA decides, as a result of a further SMS investigation, to revoke a designated undertaking’s designation in respect of a relevant digital activity, the CMA may make transitional, transitory or saving provision in respect of any existing obligation.
(2)Provision may be made in reliance on subsection (1) only for the purpose of managing the impact of the revocation—
(a)on any person who benefited from the existing obligation, and
(b)in a way that appears to the CMA to be fair and reasonable.
(3)In Chapters 6 (investigatory powers and compliance reports) and 7 (enforcement and appeals), references to a “designated undertaking” are to be read as including an undertaking to which an existing obligation applies by virtue of provision made in reliance on subsection (1).
(4)Subsection (5) applies where the CMA decides, as a result of a further SMS investigation, to—
(a)designate an undertaking again in respect of a relevant digital activity, or
(b)designate an undertaking in respect of a different digital activity in reliance on section 10(4).
simplified_text:
Existing Obligations:
When the CMA decides, after another SMS investigation, to remove a designated company from being designated for a specific digital activity, the CMA may create new rules for any existing obligations.
These new rules can only be created to soften the impact of the removal on anyone who benefited from the existing obligation, and the CMA must do this in a way that seems fair and reasonable to them.
In Chapters 6 and 7, when it talks about a "designated company," it also includes a company to which an existing obligation applies because of the new rules created by the CMA.
If the CMA decides, after another SMS investigation, to designate a company again for a specific digital activity, or designate a company for a different digital activity, then subsection (5) applies.

legal_text:
Existing obligations
(5)Where this subsection applies, the CMA may—
(a)apply any existing obligation, with or without modification, to the designated undertaking in respect of the new designation;
(b)make transitional, transitory or saving provision in respect of any existing obligation.
(6)For the purposes of this section, an “existing obligation” is any—
(a)conduct requirement (see section 19),
(b)enforcement order (see section 31),
(c)commitment (see sections 36 and 56);
(d)final offer order see section 41(2), or
(e)pro-competition order (see section 46(3)(a)),
that is in force in relation to a designated undertaking in respect of the relevant digital activity before the revocation mentioned in subsection (1) or, as the case may be, the designation mentioned in subsection (4).
(7)Provision made in reliance on this section is to be included in an SMS decision notice.
simplified_text:
Existing Obligations:
When this rule applies, the CMA can:

Apply existing obligations to the designated company, with or without changes.
Make temporary arrangements for any existing obligations.
Definition: An "existing obligation" includes any conduct requirement, enforcement order, commitment, final offer order, or pro-competition order that is in force for the designated company regarding the relevant digital activity before any revocation or new designation.

The provisions made under this rule should be included in an SMS decision notice.

legal_text:
Designation period
(1)Where the CMA decides to designate an undertaking as having SMS in respect of a digital activity, the designation period is 5 years beginning with the day after the day on which the SMS decision notice is given.
(2)See—
(a)section 104 for circumstances in which the designation period may be extended, and
(b)sections 10 and 14(1)(b) for circumstances in which a designation may be revoked before the end of the designation period.
simplified_text:
Designation Period:
When the CMA decides to recognize a company as having significant market power in a digital activity, they have a five-year designation period, starting from the day after the decision is made. 
The rules for extending the designation period can be found in section 104, and circumstances under which a designation may be cancelled before the end of the period are outlined in sections 10 and 14(1)(b).

legal_text:
Power to impose conduct requirements
(1)The CMA may impose one or more conduct requirements on a designated undertaking by giving the undertaking a notice containing the information set out in section 21.
(2)The CMA may vary a conduct requirement imposed on a designated undertaking by giving the undertaking a revised version of that notice.
(3)“Conduct requirements” are requirements as to how the designated undertaking must conduct itself in relation to a relevant digital activity, and references in this Part to imposing conduct requirements include references to varying conduct requirements in reliance on subsection (2).
(4)As soon as reasonably practicable after giving a notice under subsection (1) or (2), the CMA must publish the notice.
(5)The CMA may only impose a conduct requirement or a combination of conduct requirements on a designated undertaking if it considers that it would be proportionate to do so for the purposes of one or more of the following objectives—
(a)the fair dealing objective,
(b)the open choices objective, and
(c)the trust and transparency objective,
having regard to what the conduct requirement or combination of conduct requirements is intended to achieve.
simplified_text:
Imposing Conduct Requirements: The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) can require a specific business to follow certain rules by sending them a notice that includes the necessary information. The CMA can also change these requirements by sending the business an updated notice.

What Are Conduct Requirements? These are rules about how the business must behave when it comes to certain digital activities. When we talk about imposing or changing these requirements, we are referring to the process outlined in (2) in this law.

Making it Public: The CMA must make the notice public as soon as reasonably possible after sending it out.

Considering Objectives: The CMA can only impose or change conduct requirements for a business if it believes it's fair to do so in order to achieve one or more of these goals: promoting fair dealing, allowing for open choices, and ensuring trust and transparency.

legal_text:
Power to impose conduct requirements
(6)The fair dealing objective is that users or potential users of the relevant digital activity are—
(a)treated fairly, and
(b)able to interact, whether directly or indirectly, with the undertaking on reasonable terms.
(7)The open choices objective is that users or potential users of the relevant digital activity are able to choose freely and easily between the services or digital content provided by the undertaking and services or digital content provided by other undertakings.
(8)The trust and transparency objective is that users or potential users of the relevant digital activity have the information they require to enable them to—
(a)understand the services or digital content provided by the undertaking through the relevant digital activity, including the terms on which they are provided, and
(b)make properly informed decisions about whether and how they interact with the undertaking in respect of the relevant digital activity.
simplified_text:
Imposing Conduct Requirements: The rules aim to ensure that people using or wanting to use a specific digital service are treated fairly and have the opportunity to engage with the company on reasonable terms.

Giving Users Choices: The objective is to allow users to freely and easily choose between the digital services offered by a particular company and those provided by other companies.

Building Trust and Transparency: The goal is to make sure that users have all the necessary information to understand the services or digital content offered by the company, including the terms of service, and to make informed decisions about engaging with the company for the relevant digital activity.

legal_text:
Power to impose conduct requirements
(8)The trust and transparency objective is that users or potential users of the relevant digital activity have the information they require to enable them to—
(a)understand the services or digital content provided by the undertaking through the relevant digital activity, including the terms on which they are provided, and
(b)make properly informed decisions about whether and how they interact with the undertaking in respect of the relevant digital activity.
(9)A conduct requirement must be of a permitted type (see section 20).
(10)Before imposing a conduct requirement or a combination of conduct requirements on a designated undertaking, the CMA must have regard in particular to the benefits for consumers that the CMA considers would likely result (directly or indirectly) from the conduct requirement or combination of conduct requirements.
(11)A conduct requirement—
(a)comes into force at a time determined by the CMA, and
(b)ceases to have effect—
(i)in accordance with a decision of the CMA to revoke the requirement (see section 22), or
(ii)subject to provision made in reliance on section 17 (existing obligations), when the designation to which the requirement relates ceases to have effect.
simplified_text:
Requirement for Clear Information: The objective of the trust and transparency rule is to ensure that users of digital platforms have the necessary information to:
a) Understand the services and digital content offered by the company through the digital platform, including the terms and conditions of their provision, and
b) Make well-informed decisions about whether and how they engage with the company on the digital platform.

Type of Requirement: Any conduct requirement must be of an approved type (see section 20).

Consideration and Implementation: Before imposing a conduct requirement or a combination of conduct requirements on a specific company, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) must carefully consider the potential benefits for consumers that would likely result directly or indirectly from such requirements.

Effect and Duration: A conduct requirement goes into effect based on a decision by the CMA and ceases to be effective in accordance with a decision to revoke the requirement or when the designation to which the requirement applies is no longer valid.

Permitted Types of Conduct Requirement:

1) Types of Requirements: Conduct requirements are allowed if they fall within subsection (2) or (3).

2) Requirements Within Subsection: Requirements fall within this section if they are meant to:

- Ensure fair and reasonable terms for trade
- Establish effective processes for handling complaints and disputes with users
- Provide clear, relevant, accurate, and accessible information about digital activity to users
- Give explanations and reasonable notice to users before making impactful changes
- Present options and default settings to users in a way that allows them to make informed decisions in their best interests

Types of Conduct Requirement: 

The following rules can be applied to prevent a designated company from:

Applying unfair terms, conditions, or policies to certain users or potential users, or certain groups of users or potential users.

Favoring its own products over those of other companies, using its position related to the relevant digital activity and access to data.

Developing other activities in a way that can significantly increase the company's dominance in the relevant digital activity.

Forcing or encouraging users or potential users of its products to use other products.

Limiting compatibility between the relevant service or digital content and products from other companies.

Restricting how users or potential users can use the digital activity, using data unfairly.

Limiting the ability of users or potential users to use products from other companies.

Amendments and Regulations: The Secretary of State can change the types of requirements through regulations. These regulations must go through the affirmative procedure.

Notice Imposing a Conduct Requirement:
A notice under section 19(1) or (2) must include, for each conduct requirement or varied conduct requirement:
- What the conduct requirement is and the digital activity it relates to.
- The reasons why the CMA imposed the conduct requirement, including:
  - The purpose for imposing it
  - The benefits expected from it
  - The type of requirement it is
- When the conduct requirement starts.
- The last day of the designation period for the related designation.
- How the conduct requirement interacts with any other conduct requirement imposed on the undertaking.

Subject: Co-ownership Schemes in Collective Investment

The government has the authority to create rules related to tax for authorized co-ownership schemes, and these rules can also apply to other co-ownership schemes, under certain conditions:

2. If it is defined as an AIF under the Alternative Investment Fund Managers Regulations 2013, 
3. If it meets specific conditions outlined in the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, such as participation being limited to professional or large investors, and 
4. If it satisfies any other conditions set forth in regulations.

The regulations may also: 
- Establish conditions regarding the scheme's connection to the United Kingdom, the diversity of its ownership, the types of property it holds, and the tax status of its participants, 
- Set other appropriate conditions for a scheme to become or remain a RIF, and 
- Address the tax implications when a co-ownership scheme meets or no longer meets the conditions for being classified as a RIF.

Transfers by closely-held companies

This law applies to prevent tax avoidance involving transfers made by closely-held companies that have a connection to certain individuals.

Qualifying Interest in a Company

An individual has a qualifying interest in a closely-held company if they or their nominee are shareholders in that company or in a closely-held company connected to the original company through a chain of ownership.

Involvement in a Company

An individual with a qualifying interest in a company is considered to be involved in the company, unless they can prove to a tax authority that they have no involvement in the company's decision-making.

Avoidance Condition

The avoidance condition is met if the shareholder did not object to the transfer and it is reasonable to conclude that they were aware or should have been aware that the transfer would result in tax avoidance.

Designated Participator

In determining involvement, the term "relevant participator" refers to the individual in most cases, or their nominee in cases where the qualifying interest arises from a nominee.

Disregarding Arrangements

Arrangements meant to keep a person uninvolved in the decision-making of a company will be disregarded if their main purpose is to avoid meeting the condition for tax avoidance. Similarly, arrangements that would avoid meeting the avoidance condition will also be disregarded.

Definitions

The term "arrangements" includes any type of agreement or transaction, while "taxation" has the meaning it has in a specific section of the law.

Meaning of “category 1 hazard” and “category 2 hazard”
(1)In this Act—

“category 1 hazard” means a hazard of a prescribed description which falls within a prescribed band as a result of achieving, under a prescribed method for calculating the seriousness of hazards of that description, a numerical score of or above a prescribed amount;
“category 2 hazard” means a hazard of a prescribed description which falls within a prescribed band as a result of achieving, under a prescribed method for calculating the seriousness of hazards of that description, a numerical score below the minimum amount prescribed for a category 1 hazard of that description; and
“hazard” means any risk of harm to the health or safety of an actual or potential occupier of a dwelling or HMO which arises from a deficiency in the dwelling or HMO or in any building or land in the vicinity (whether the deficiency arises as a result of the construction of any building, an absence of maintenance or repair, or otherwise).
(2)In subsection (1)—

“prescribed” means prescribed by regulations made by the appropriate national authority (see section 261(1)); and
“prescribed band” means a band so prescribed for a category 1 hazard or a category 2 hazard, as the case may be.
(3)Regulations under this section may, in particular, prescribe a method for calculating the seriousness of hazards which takes into account both the likelihood of the harm occurring and the severity of the harm if it were to occur.

(4)In this section—

“building” includes part of a building;
“harm” includes temporary harm.
(5)In this Act “health” includes mental health.

Definition of "Category 1 Hazard" and "Category 2 Hazard"

(1) In this law:

"Category 1 hazard" means a specific type of hazard that falls within a particular range, as determined by a calculated numerical score meeting certain criteria. The calculation is done using a prescribed method to evaluate the seriousness of hazards of this type.

"Category 2 hazard" means a specific type of hazard that falls within a different specified range, as determined by a calculated numerical score meeting specific criteria. The calculation is done using a prescribed method to evaluate the seriousness of hazards of this type, but with a lower numerical score than required for a Category 1 hazard.

"Hazard" refers to any potential risk of harm to the health or safety of someone living in or using a dwelling or house in multiple occupation (HMO). This risk results from a deficiency in the building, HMO, or in nearby buildings or land. The deficiency could arise from poor construction, lack of maintenance or repairs, or other causes.

(2) In subsection (1):

"Prescribed" means determined by regulations set by the appropriate national authority (see section 261(1)).

"Prescribed band" refers to a specified range determined by regulations for a Category 1 hazard or a Category 2 hazard, as the case may be.

(3) Regulations issued under this law may define a method for assessing the seriousness of hazards, considering both the likelihood of harm occurring and the potential severity of the harm.

(4) In this law:

"Building" includes a section of a building.

"Harm" includes temporary harm.

(5) In this law, "health" includes mental health.

- Issue an emergency prohibition order
- Issue a demolition order
- Declare the area surrounding the premises as a clearance area.

(6)The Secretary of State must not proceed with the proposed guidance or alterations if, within the period of 40 days mentioned in subsection (5), either House resolves that the guidance or alterations be withdrawn.

(7)Subsection (6) is without prejudice to the possibility of laying a further draft of the guidance or alterations before each House of Parliament.

(8)In calculating the period of 40 days mentioned in subsection (5), no account is to be taken of any time during which Parliament is dissolved or prorogued or during which both Houses are adjourned for more than four days.
simplified_text:
Guidance on Inspections and Enforcement Actions: The national authority can provide guidance to local housing authorities on how to carry out inspections, assess hazards, issue improvement notices, prohibition orders, or hazard awareness notices, as well as how to handle emergency remedial action, emergency prohibition orders, demolition orders, and slum clearance. Local housing authorities must consider and follow this guidance.

Different Types of Guidance: The national authority can provide different guidance for different situations, purposes, or types of local housing authorities, as well as for housing authorities in different areas.

Parliamentary Approval: Before issuing or revising the guidance, the Secretary of State must present a draft to both Houses of Parliament. The guidance cannot be issued or revised until 40 days have passed, and neither House has objected during that time. If either House rejects the guidance during this period, it cannot be implemented. However, the Secretary of State can present a revised draft to Parliament.

Calculation of Time: The 40-day period during which Parliament must consider the guidance does not include periods of parliamentary dissolution, prorogation, or adjournments of more than four days.

(b)no management order is in force in relation to the premises under Chapter 1 or 2 of Part 4,

(a)if the residential premises on which the hazard exists are a dwelling or HMO which is not a flat, it may require such action to be taken in relation to the dwelling or HMO;

(c)if those premises are the common parts of a building containing one or more flats, it may require such action to be taken in relation to the building (or any part of the building) or any external common parts.

Improvement Notices for Housing Hazards:
If the local housing authority determines that a hazardous situation exists in a residential property, and there is no current management order in place for that property, the authority has the power to issue an improvement notice to address the hazard.

legal_text:
Contents of improvement notices
(1)An improvement notice under section 11 or 12 must comply with the following provisions of this section.

(2)The notice must specify, in relation to the hazard (or each of the hazards) to which it relates—

(a)whether the notice is served under section 11 or 12,

(b)the nature of the hazard and the residential premises on which it exists,

(c)the deficiency giving rise to the hazard,

(d)the premises in relation to which remedial action is to be taken in respect of the hazard and the nature of that remedial action,

(e)the date when the remedial action is to be started (see subsection (3)), and

(f)the period within which the remedial action is to be completed or the periods within which each part of it is to be completed.

(3)The notice may not require any remedial action to be started earlier than the 28th day after that on which the notice is served.

(4)The notice must contain information about—

(a)the right of appeal against the decision under Part 3 of Schedule 1, and

(b)the period within which an appeal may be made.

(5)In this Part of this Act “specified premises”, in relation to an improvement notice, means premises specified in the notice, in accordance with subsection (2)(d), as premises in relation to which remedial action is to be taken in respect of the hazard.
simplified_text:
Contents of improvement notices:

An improvement notice issued under section 11 or 12 must include the following information:

1. Identification: It should state whether it is issued under section 11 or 12 and clearly describe the hazard and the residential premises affected.
2. Deficiency: It should explain what is lacking that has resulted in the hazard.
3. Action Required: It should specify the premises where action needs to be taken to address the hazard, and describe the necessary action.
4. Timeline: It should indicate when the action needs to begin (at least 28 days after the notice is served) and the deadline for completion, or the deadlines for each part of the action.
5. Appeal Rights: It should inform the recipient about the right to appeal the decision and the timeframe for filing an appeal.

In this part of the law, "specified premises" means the premises identified in the notice where remedial action is required to address the hazard.

legal_text:
Suspension of improvement notices
(1)An improvement notice may provide for the operation of the notice to be suspended until a time, or the occurrence of an event, specified in the notice.

(2)The time so specified may, in particular, be the time when a person of a particular description begins, or ceases, to occupy any premises.

(3)The event so specified may, in particular, be a notified breach of an undertaking accepted by the local housing authority for the purposes of this section from the person on whom the notice is served.

(4)In subsection (3) a “notified breach”, in relation to such an undertaking, means an act or omission by the person on whom the notice is served—

(a)which the local housing authority consider to be a breach of the undertaking, and

(b)which is notified to that person in accordance with the terms of the undertaking.

(5)If an improvement notice does provide for the operation of the notice to be suspended under this section—

(a)any periods specified in the notice under section 13 are to be fixed by reference to the day when the suspension ends, and

(b)in subsection (3) of that section the reference to the 28th day after that on which the notice is served is to be read as referring to the 21st day after that on which the suspension ends.
simplified_text:
Suspending Improvement Notices: An improvement notice can be set to be put on hold until a specific time or event occurs, as mentioned in the notice. 

Specifying the Time: This specified time could be when a specific person starts or stops occupying certain premises.

Specifying the Event: The specified event could be a reported violation of an agreement made by the local housing authority with the person receiving the notice.

Consequences of Suspension: If the improvement notice is suspended, any set time periods in the notice are based on when the suspension ends. Additionally, certain time references in the notice are adjusted based on when the suspension ends.

legal_text:
Operation of improvement notices
(1)This section deals with the time when an improvement notice becomes operative.

(2)The general rule is that an improvement notice becomes operative at the end of the period of 21 days beginning with the day on which it is served under Part 1 of Schedule 1 (which is the period for appealing against the notice under Part 3 of that Schedule).

(3)The general rule is subject to subsection (4) (suspended notices) and subsection (5) (appeals).

(4)If the notice is suspended under section 14, the notice becomes operative at the time when the suspension ends.

This is subject to subsection (5).
(5)If an appeal against the notice is made under Part 3 of Schedule 1, the notice does not become operative until such time (if any) as is the operative time for the purposes of this subsection under paragraph 19 of that Schedule (time when notice is confirmed on appeal, period for further appeal expires or suspension ends).

(6)If no appeal against an improvement notice is made under that Part of that Schedule within the period for appealing against it, the notice is final and conclusive as to matters which could have been raised on an appeal.
simplified_text:
Improvement Notices in Operation

This section explains when an improvement notice takes effect.

1) When Does it Take Effect? 
The general rule is that an improvement notice takes effect 21 days after it is served, which is the period for appealing against the notice.

2) Exceptions to the General Rule
This general rule is subject to two exceptions: suspended notices and appeals.

3) Suspended Notices
If the notice is suspended under section 14, it takes effect when the suspension ends.

4) Appeals
If an appeal against the notice is made, the notice does not take effect until a specific time outlined in the schedule.

5) If No Appeal Is Made
If no appeal is made within the appeal period, the notice becomes final and conclusive for all matters that could have been raised on appeal.

legal_text:

(1)The local housing authority must revoke an improvement notice if they are satisfied that the requirements of the notice have been complied with.

(2)The local housing authority may revoke an improvement notice if—

(a)in the case of a notice served under section 11, they consider that there are any special circumstances making it appropriate to revoke the notice; or

(a)subsection (1) is to be read as applying separately in relation to each of those hazards, and

legal_text:
Review of suspended improvement notices
(1)The local housing authority may at any time review an improvement notice whose operation is suspended.

(3)As from the changeover date, the liable person in respect of the premises is to be in the same position as if—

legal_text:
Prohibition orders relating to category 1 hazards: duty of authority to make order
(1)If—

(a)the local housing authority are satisfied that a category 1 hazard exists on any residential premises, and

(b)no management order is in force in relation to the premises under Chapter 1 or 2 of Part 4,

making a prohibition order under this section in respect of the hazard is a course of action available to the authority in relation to the hazard for the purposes of section 5 (category 1 hazards: general duty to take enforcement action).
(2)A prohibition order under this section is an order imposing such prohibition or prohibitions on the use of any premises as is or are specified in the order in accordance with subsections (3) and (4) and section 22.

(3)The order may prohibit use of the following premises—

(a)if the residential premises on which the hazard exists are a dwelling or HMO which is not a flat, it may prohibit use of the dwelling or HMO;

(b)if those premises are one or more flats, it may prohibit use of the building containing the flat or flats (or any part of the building) or any external common parts;

(c)if those premises are the common parts of a building containing one or more flats, it may prohibit use of the building (or any part of the building) or any external common parts.

Paragraphs (b) and (c) are subject to subsection (4).
(4)The notice may not, by virtue of subsection (3)(b) or (c), prohibit use of any part of the building or its external common parts that is not included in any residential premises on which the hazard exists, unless the authority are satisfied—

(a)that the deficiency from which the hazard arises is situated there, and

(b)that it is necessary for such use to be prohibited in order to protect the health or safety of any actual or potential occupiers of one or more of the flats.

(5)A prohibition order under this section may relate to more than one category 1 hazard on the same premises or in the same building containing one or more flats.

(6)The operation of a prohibition order under this section may be suspended in accordance with section 23.
simplified_text:
Prohibition Orders for Dangerous Conditions:

When a local housing authority determines that a serious hazard exists in a residential property and no management order is in place, they can issue a prohibition order to prevent the use of the property. The order can restrict the use of the property in different ways, depending on the type of property and the specific hazard. It can also apply to multiple hazards in the same property or building.

The authority can also suspend the prohibition order in certain circumstances.

legal_text:

(1)If—

(a)the local housing authority are satisfied that a category 2 hazard exists on any residential premises, and

(b)no management order is in force in relation to the premises under Chapter 1 or 2 of Part 4,

the authority may make a prohibition order under this section in respect of the hazard.
(2)A prohibition order under this section is an order imposing such prohibition or prohibitions on the use of any premises as is or are specified in the order in accordance with subsection (3) and section 22.

(3)Subsections (3) and (4) of section 20 apply to a prohibition order under this section as they apply to one under that section.

(4)A prohibition order under this section may relate to more than one category 2 hazard on the same premises or in the same building containing one or more flats.

simplified_text:
Prohibition Orders for Category 2 Hazards: Authority's Power to Make Orders
(1) If the local housing authority believes there is a category 2 hazard in any residential property, and no management order is in place for the property, they can issue a prohibition order for that hazard.
(2) The prohibition order can specify restrictions on the use of the premises, as determined by subsection (3) and section 22.
(3) The provisions of section 20, subsections (3) and (4), also apply to a prohibition order issued under this section.
(4) A prohibition order under this section can cover multiple category 2 hazards in the same property or building with one or more flats.
(5) A prohibition order under this section can be combined into a single document with an order issued under section 20 if they impose restrictions on the same property or a building with one or more flats.
(6) The enforcement of a prohibition order under this section can be paused in accordance with section 23.

legal_text:
Suspension of prohibition orders
(1)A prohibition order may provide for the operation of the order to be suspended until a time, or the occurrence of an event, specified in the order.

(2)The time so specified may, in particular, be the time when a person of a particular description begins, or ceases, to occupy any premises.

(3)The event so specified may, in particular, be a notified breach of an undertaking accepted by the local housing authority for the purposes of this section from a person on whom a copy of the order is served.

(4)In subsection (3) a “notified breach”, in relation to such an undertaking, means an act or omission by such a person—

(a)which the local housing authority consider to be a breach of the undertaking, and

(b)which is notified to that person in accordance with the terms of the undertaking.
simplified_text:
Temporary Suspension of Prohibition Orders

1) If a prohibition order is issued, it can be temporarily suspended until a specified time or event.

2) The specified time might be when a certain type of person starts or stops occupying a property.

3) The specified event might be a reported violation of a promise made to the local housing authority by a person who received a copy of the order.

4) A "notified breach" of the promise means an action or failure by the person that the local housing authority considers to be a violation of the promise and has been reported to that person in line with the terms of the promise.

legal_text:
Operation of prohibition orders
(1)This section deals with the time when a prohibition order becomes operative.

(2)The general rule is that a prohibition order becomes operative at the end of the period of 28 days beginning with the date specified in the notice as the date on which it is made.

(3)The general rule is subject to subsection (4) (suspended orders) and subsection (5) (appeals).

(4)If the order is suspended under section 23, the order becomes operative at the time when the suspension ends.

This is subject to subsection (5).
(5)If an appeal is brought against the order under Part 3 of Schedule 2, the order does not become operative until such time (if any) as is the operative time for the purposes of this subsection under paragraph 14 of that Schedule (time when order is confirmed on appeal, period for further appeal expires or suspension ends).

(6)If no appeal against a prohibition order is made under that Part of that Schedule within the period for appealing against it, the order is final and conclusive as to matters which could have been raised on an appeal.

(7)Sections 584A and 584B of the Housing Act 1985 (c. 68) provide for the payment of compensation where certain prohibition orders become operative, and for the repayment of such compensation in certain circumstances.
simplified_text:
When a Prohibition Order Takes Effect: This section explains when a prohibition order goes into effect.

Normally, the order becomes effective 28 days after it is issued, unless it is suspended or an appeal is filed.

If the order is suspended, it becomes effective when the suspension ends, unless an appeal is pending.

If an appeal is filed, the order doesn't take effect until the appeal is resolved or the suspension ends.

If no appeal is filed within the allowed time, the order is final and conclusive.

Additionally, the Housing Act 1985 addresses compensation for certain types of prohibition orders and circumstances for repayment.

legal_text:
Revocation and variation of prohibition orders
(1)The local housing authority must revoke a prohibition order if at any time they are satisfied that the hazard in respect of which the order was made does not then exist on the residential premises specified in the order in accordance with section 22(2)(b).
