7. Facts necessary to explain or introduce a fact in issue or relevant fact, or which support or rebut an inference suggested by a fact in issue or a relevant fact, or which establish the identity of anything, or person whose identity, is relevant, or fix the time or place at which any fact in issue or relevant fact happened, or which show the relation of 10 parties by whom any such fact was transacted, are relevant in so far as they are necessary
for that purpose.
Illustrations.
(a) The question is, whether a given document is the will of A. The state of A's property and of his family at the date of the alleged will may be relevant facts.
(b) A sues B for a libel imputing disgraceful conduct to A; B affirms that the matter alleged to be libellous is true. The position and relations of the parties at the time when the libel was published may be relevant facts as introductory to the facts in issue. The particulars of a dispute between A and B about a matter unconnected with the alleged libel are irrelevant, though the fact that there was a dispute may be relevant if it affected the relations between AandB.
(c) A is accused of a crime. The fact that, soon after the commission of the crime, A absconded from his house, is relevant under section 6, as conduct subsequent to and affected by facts in issue. The fact that, at the time when he left home, A had sudden and urgent business at the place to which he went, is relevant, as tending to explain the fact that he left home suddenly. The details of the business on which he left are not relevant, except in so far as they are necessary to show that the business was sudden and urgent.
(d) A sues B for inducing C to break a contract of service made by him with A. C, on leaving A's service, says to A—"I am leaving you because B has made me a better offer". This statement is a relevant fact as explanatory of C's conduct, which is relevant as a fact in issue.
(e) A, accused of theft, is seen to give the stolen property to B, who is seen to give it to A's wife. B says as he delivers it—"A says you are to hide this". B's statement is relevant as explanatory of a fact which is part of the transaction.
(f) A is tried for a riot and is proved to have marched at the head of a mob. The cries of 35 the mob are relevant as explanatory of the nature of the transaction.
simplified_text:
7. Facts necessary to explain or introduce a fact in issue or relevant fact, or which support or rebut an inference suggested by a fact in issue or a relevant fact, or which establish the identity of anything, or person whose identity, is relevant, or fix the time or place at which any fact in issue or relevant fact happened, or which show the relation of parties by whom any such fact was transacted, are relevant in so far as they are necessary for that purpose.

Illustrations:
(a) If we are trying to determine if a specific document is the will of A, then the condition of A's property and family at the time of the will may be important.
(b) When A sues B for saying something harmful about A that B claims to be true, the situation and connections of the people when the harmful statement was made may be important, but other disputes between A and B are not relevant, unless they affected their relationship.
(c) If A is accused of a crime and left home soon after the crime was committed, the fact that A left home is important. If A left due to sudden and urgent business, that can also be relevant. The exact details of the business aren't important except to show that the business was sudden and urgent.
(d) If A sues B for persuading C to break a work contract with A, the statement by C as they leave A's work is relevant to explain their actions.
(e) In a theft case, if A is seen giving the stolen property to B, and B then gives it to A's wife, the statement made by B as they give the item is relevant to understand the transaction.
(f) In a trial for a riot, if A is proven to have led a crowd, the cries of the crowd are relevant to explain the nature of the event.

legal_text:
8. Where there is reasonable ground to believe that two or more persons have conspired together to commit an offence or an actionable wrong, anything said, done or written by any one of such persons in reference to their common intention, after the time when such intention was first entertained by any one of them, is a relevant fact as against each of the persons believed to be so conspiring, as well for the purpose of proving the existence of the conspiracy as for the purpose of showing that any such person was a party to it. Illustration.
Reasonable ground exists for believing that A has joined in a conspiracy to wage war 45 against the State.
The facts that B procured arms in Europe for the purpose of the conspiracy, C collected money in Kolkata for a like object, D persuaded persons to join the conspiracy in Mumbai, E published writings advocating the object in view at Agra, and F transmitted from Delhi to
G at Singapore the money which C had collected at Kolkata, and the contents of a letter written by H giving an account of the conspiracy, are each relevant, both to prove the existence of the conspiracy, and to prove A's complicity in it, although he may have been ignorant of all of them, and although the persons by whom they were done were strangers to him, and although they may have taken place before he joined the conspiracy or after he left it.
simplified_text: Evidence of Conspiracy: If there is a reasonable belief that two or more people have conspired to commit a crime or harm someone, anything said, done, or written by any one of them after the conspiracy was formed can be used as evidence against each of them. This can be used to prove the existence of the conspiracy and to show that a person was involved in it, even if they were unaware of certain actions and even if those actions were carried out by others before or after their involvement.

legal_text:
9. Facts not otherwise relevant are relevant—
(1) if they are inconsistent with any fact in issue or relevant fact;
(2) if by themselves or in connection with other facts they make the existence or non-existence of any fact in issue or relevant fact highly probable or improbable.
Illustrations.
(a) The question is, whether A committed a crime at Chennai on a certain day. The fact that, on that day, A was at Ladakh is relevant. The fact that, near the time when the crime was committed, A was at a distance from the place where it was committed, which would render it highly improbable, though not impossible, that he committed it, is relevant.
(b) The question is, whether A committed a crime. The circumstances are such that the crime must have been committed either by A, B, C or D. Every fact which shows that the crime could have been committed by no one else, and that it was not committed by either B, C or D, is relevant.
simplified_text:
Relevance of Facts in Legal Proceedings:
Facts that are not directly related may still be important to consider in legal proceedings if:
1. They contradict or are inconsistent with a fact that is being discussed or a fact that is relevant to the case.
2. They, on their own or in combination with other facts, strongly indicate the likely presence or absence of a relevant fact in the case.

Examples:
a) If the question is whether A committed a crime in Chennai on a specific day, the fact that A was in Ladakh on that day is relevant. Additionally, the fact that A was far away from the crime scene around the time the crime occurred, making it highly unlikely (although not impossible) for him to have committed it, is also relevant.
b) If the question is whether A committed a crime and it is known that the crime could only have been committed by A, B, C, or D, any fact that demonstrates that the crime could not have been committed by B, C, or D, and could only have been committed by A, is relevant.

legal_text: 10. In suits in which damages are claimed, any fact which will enable the Court to determine the amount of damages which ought to be awarded, is relevant.
simplified_text: In cases where someone is claiming compensation for damage, any piece of information that will help the court decide how much compensation should be given is important.

legal_text:
11. Where the question is as to the existence of any right or custom, the following facts are relevant—
(a) any transaction by which the right or custom in question was created, claimed, modified, recognised, asserted or denied, or which was inconsistent with its existence;
(b) particular instances in which the right or custom was claimed, recognised or exercised, or in which its exercise was disputed, asserted or departed from.
Illustration.
The question is, whether A has a right to a fishery. A deed conferring the fishery on A's ancestors, a mortgage of the fishery by A's father, a subsequent grant of the fishery by A's father, irreconcilable with the mortgage, particular instances in which A's father exercised the right, or in which the exercise of the right was stopped by A's neighbours, are relevant facts.
simplified_text:
Relevant Facts for Proving a Right or Custom:
When determining whether a right or custom exists, the following information is important:
How the Right or Custom Was Established: Any transactions that created, claimed, changed, acknowledged, contested, or contradicted the right or custom in question.
Past Instances of Claiming or Exercising the Right: Specific examples of when the right or custom was asserted, acknowledged, or utilized, as well as instances when its use was challenged, claimed, or deviated from.
Example:
To determine if A has a right to a fishery, relevant information includes a deed that granted the fishery to A's ancestors, a mortgage of the fishery by A's father, a subsequent grant of the fishery by A's father that contradicted the mortgage, and specific instances of A's father exercising the right or facing opposition from neighbors.

legal_text:
13. When there is a question whether an act was accidental or intentional, or done with a particular knowledge or intention, the fact that such act formed part of a series of similar occurrences, in each of which the person doing the act was concerned, is relevant.
Illustrations.
(a) A is accused of burning down his house in order to obtain money for which it is insured. The facts that A lived in several houses successively each of which he insured, in each of which a fire occurred, and after each of which fires A received payment from a different insurance company, are relevant, as tending to show that the fires were not
accidental.
(b) A is employed to receive money from the debtors of B. It is A's duty to make entries in a book showing the amounts received by him. He makes an entry showing that on a particular occasion he received less than he really did receive. The question is, whether this false entry was accidental or intentional. The facts that other entries made by A in the same
book are false, and that the false entry is in each case in favour of A, are relevant.
(c) A is accused of fraudulently delivering to B a counterfeit currency. The question is, whether the delivery of the currency was accidental. The facts that, soon before or soon after the delivery to B, A delivered counterfeit currency to C, D and E are relevant, as
showing that the delivery to B was not accidental.
simplified_text:
Determining Accidental or Intentional Acts:
When there is doubt about whether an act was accidental or intentional, or done with a specific knowledge or intention, the fact that the act was part of a series of similar occurrences can be considered. These occurrences should involve the same person and be relevant to the question at hand.

Examples:
(a) A is suspected of setting fire to his house to collect insurance money. Evidence that A lived in multiple houses successively, insured each one, had fires occur in each house, and received payment from different insurance companies after each fire, can be considered to suggest that the fires were not accidental.

(b) A is responsible for collecting money from B's debtors and recording the amounts in a book. A makes a false entry in the book, claiming to have received less money than he actually did. To determine if this false entry was accidental or intentional, it is relevant that other entries in the same book made by A are also false and all in favor of A.

(c) A is accused of fraudulently giving counterfeit currency to B. It is questioned whether this delivery was accidental. Evidence that A delivered counterfeit currency to individuals C, D, and E shortly before or after the delivery to B is relevant and can indicate that the delivery to B was not accidental.

legal_text:
14. When there is a question whether a particular act was done, the existence of any course of business, according to which it naturally would have been done, is a relevant fact.
Illustrations.
(a) The question is, whether a particular letter was dispatched. The facts that it was the ordinary course of business for all letters put in a certain place to be carried to the post, and that particular letter was put in that place are relevant.
(b) The question is, whether a particular letter reached A. The facts that it was posted in due course, and was not returned through the Return Letter Office, are relevant.
simplified_text:
Determine Act: When there is uncertainty about whether a specific action was taken, the presence of any usual business practice that suggests the action would have naturally occurred is important.

Examples:
(a) If the issue is whether a certain letter was sent, it is relevant to consider if it was the regular practice for all letters placed in a certain location to be sent to the post, and if that particular letter was placed in that location.
(b) If the issue is whether a certain letter reached person A, it is relevant to consider if the letter was sent on time and was not returned through the Return Letter Office.

legal_text: 15. An admission is a statement, oral or documentary or contained in electronic form, which suggests any inference as to any fact in issue or relevant fact, and which is made by any of the persons, and under the circumstances, hereinafter mentioned.
simplified_text: An admission is a statement, whether spoken, written, or in electronic form, that implies a conclusion about a fact that is in question or is relevant. It can be made by certain individuals under specific conditions.

legal_text:
16. (1) Statements made by a party to the proceeding, or by an agent to any such party, whom the Court regards, under the circumstances of the case, as expressly or impliedly authorised by him to make them, are admissions.
(2) Statements made by—
(i) parties to suits suing or sued in a representative character, are not admissions,
unless they were made while the party making them held that character; or
(ii) (a) persons who have any proprietary or pecuniary interest in the subject matter of the proceeding, and who make the statement in their character of persons so 5 interested; or
(b) persons from whom the parties to the suit have derived their interest in the subject matter of the suit,
are admissions, if they are made during the continuance of the interest of the persons making the statements.
simplified_text:
Admissions in Legal Proceedings: When a party or their representative makes statements in court that are regarded as authorized by the party, these statements are considered admissions.

Exceptions to Admissions: However, statements made by parties who are representing others in a legal case are not considered admissions, unless they were made while acting in that representative capacity. Additionally, statements made by individuals with a financial or property interest in the case, or by those from whom the parties to the case derived their interest, are considered admissions if they are made while those interests are ongoing.

legal_text:
17. Statements made by persons whose position or liability, it is necessary to prove
as against any party to the suit, are admissions, if such statements would be relevant as against such persons in relation to such position or liability in a suit brought by or against them, and if they are made whilst the person making them occupies such position or is subject to such liability.
Illustration.
A undertakes to collect rents for B. B sues A for not collecting rent due from C to B. A denies that rent was due from C to B. A statement by C that he owed B rent is an admission, and is a relevant fact as against A, if A denies that C did owe rent to B.
simplified_text:
Statements by Relevant Persons:
Any statements made by individuals whose position or responsibility needs to be proven in a legal case will be considered as admissions if those statements would be relevant in proving their position or responsibility in a case brought against them. This applies if the statements are made while the person holds that position or has that responsibility.
Illustration:
If A has agreed to collect rent for B, and B later sues A for not collecting rent owed by C to B, and A denies that C owed any rent to B, then a statement by C admitting that he owed rent to B is considered an admission and is relevant evidence against A, if A denies that C owed rent to B.

legal_text:
18. Statements made by persons to whom a party to the suit has expressly referred for information in reference to a matter in dispute are admissions.
Illustration.
The question is, whether a horse sold by A to B is sound.
A says to B—"Go and ask C, C knows all about it". C's statement is an admission.
simplified_text:
Statements by Referred Persons: If someone involved in a legal case tells another person to ask someone else for information about the dispute, the information given by that other person is considered as an admission in the case.

Example:
If A sells a horse to B and tells B to ask C about the horse's condition, C's statement about the horse is considered an admission in the case.

legal_text: 20. Oral admissions as to the contents of a document are not relevant, unless and until the party proposing to prove them shows that he is entitled to give secondary evidence of the contents of such document under the rules hereinafter contained, or unless the genuineness of a document produced is in question.
simplified_text: Admissions about Document Contents: What someone says about the contents of a document is not important, unless they prove that they have the right to provide alternative evidence of the document's contents, as per the following rules. The only exception is if the authenticity of a document that has been presented is being questioned.

legal_text:
21. In civil cases no admission is relevant, if it is made either upon an express condition that evidence of it is not to be given, or under circumstances from which the Court can infer that the parties agreed together that evidence of it should not be given.
Explanation.—Nothing in this section shall be taken to exempt any advocate from giving evidence of any matter of which he may be compelled to give evidence under sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 132.
simplified_text:
In civil cases, any admission is not considered relevant if it is made with the condition that evidence of it is not to be presented, or if it is made under circumstances that suggest the parties agreed not to present evidence of it.

Explanation: This rule does not prevent a lawyer from giving evidence if they are required to do so under other sections of the law.

legal_text:
22. A confession made by an accused person is irrelevant in a criminal proceeding, if the making of the confession appears to the Court to have been caused by any inducement, threat, coercion or promise having reference to the charge against the accused person, proceeding from a person in authority and sufficient, in the opinion of the Court, to give the accused person grounds which would appear to him reasonable for supposing that by making it he would gain any advantage or avoid any evil of a temporal nature in reference to the proceedings against him:
Provided that if the confession is made after the impression caused by any such inducement, threat, coercion or promise has, in the opinion of the Court, been fully removed, it is relevant:
Provided further that if such a confession is otherwise relevant, it does not become irrelevant merely because it was made under a promise of secrecy, or in consequence of a deception practised on the accused person for the purpose of obtaining it, or when he was drunk, or because it was made in answer to questions which he need not have answered, whatever may have been the form of those questions, or because he was not warned that he was not bound to make such confession, and that evidence of it might be given against him.
simplified_text: Confession in Criminal Proceedings: If an accused person makes a confession in a criminal trial because they were induced, threatened, coerced, or promised an advantage or to avoid harm by a person in authority, the confession is not considered relevant to the case. However, if the influence has been removed, the confession becomes relevant. Even if the confession was made under a promise of secrecy, as a result of deception, while intoxicated, in response to unnecessary questions, or without being warned about its implications, it may still be relevant if it meets other criteria of relevance.

legal_text:
23. (1) No confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence.
(2) No confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer, unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate shall be proved against him:Provided that when any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of any offence, in the custody of a police officer, so much of such information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered, may be proved.
simplified_text:
23. (1) Confessions to police officers cannot be used as evidence against someone accused of a crime.
(2) Confessions made by a person while in police custody, unless made in the presence of a Magistrate, cannot be used as evidence against them. However, information obtained from the accused that leads to the discovery of a fact can be used as evidence in a case, even if it includes a confession.

legal_text:
24. When more persons than one are being tried jointly for the same offence, and a confession made by one of such persons affecting himself and some other of such persons
is proved, the Court may take into consideration such confession as against such other person as well as against the person who makes such confession.
Explanation I.—"Offence", as used in this section, includes the abetment of, or attempt to commit, the offence.
Explanation II.—A trial of more persons than one held in the absence of the accused who has absconded or who fails to comply with a proclamation issued under section 84 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 shall be deemed to be a joint trial for the purpose of this section.
Illustrations. (a) A and B are jointly tried for the murder of C. It is proved that A said—"B and I murdered C". The Court may consider the effect of this confession as against B.
(b) A is on his trial for the murder of C. There is evidence to show that C was murdered
by A and B, and that B said—"A and I murdered C". This statement may not be taken into consideration by the Court against A, as B is not being jointly tried.
simplified_text:
Joint Trial Confession: When multiple people are tried together for the same crime, and one of them confesses, the court can consider that confession as evidence against the other person involved in the confession, in addition to the person who made the confession.

Definitions: The term "offence" in this section includes helping someone commit a crime or attempting to commit a crime. Also, if the trial is held for multiple people in the absence of an accused person who has run away or failed to comply with a issued proclamation, it will be considered a joint trial under this section.

Examples:
(a) A and B are tried together for the murder of C. If it is proven that A confessed, "B and I murdered C," the court may consider this confession as evidence against B.
(b) If A is on trial for the murder of C, and there is evidence that C was murdered by both A and B, and B confessed, "A and I murdered C," this statement may not be used as evidence against A, since B is not being tried together with A.

legal_text:
25. Admissions are not conclusive proof of the matters admitted but they may operate as estoppels under the provisions hereinafter contained.
Statements by persons who cannot be called as witnesses
simplified_text:
Admissions do not prove the matters admitted, but they may prevent the party from arguing otherwise as explained in the following provisions.
Statements by people who cannot testify.

legal_text:
27. Evidence given by a witness in a judicial proceeding, or before any person authorised by law to take it, is relevant for the purpose of proving, in a subsequent judicial proceeding, or in a later stage of the same judicial proceeding, the truth of the facts which
it states, when the witness is dead or cannot be found, or is incapable of giving evidence,
or is kept out of the way by the adverse party, or if his presence cannot be obtained without an amount of delay or expense which, under the circumstances of the case, the Court considers unreasonable:
Provided that the proceeding was between the same parties or their representatives in interest; that the adverse party in the first proceeding had the right and opportunity to cross-examine and the questions in issue were substantially the same in the first as in the second proceeding.
Explanation.—A criminal trial or inquiry shall be deemed to be a proceeding between the prosecutor and the accused within the meaning of this section.
simplified_text:
Relevant Witness Testimony: If a witness gives evidence in a court case, or to someone authorized by law, that evidence can be used in a later stage of the same case, or in a new case, to prove the truth of what the witness said if:

the witness has died, can't be found, or can't give evidence

the adverse party has deliberately kept the witness away, or it would be too difficult or expensive to bring the witness to court, as long as the court thinks the delay or cost is unreasonable.

This applies if the new case involves the same parties or their representatives and the adverse party had the chance to question the witness in the original case, and if the issues in the two cases are similar.

Note: This rule also applies to criminal trials or investigations involving a prosecutor and an accused person.

legal_text:
28. Entries in the books of account, including those maintained in an electronic form, regularly kept in the course of business are relevant whenever they refer to a matter into which the Court has to inquire, but such statements shall not alone be sufficient evidence
to charge any person with liability.
Illustration.
A sues B for one thousand rupees, and shows entries in his account books showing B to be indebted to him to this amount. The entries are relevant, but are not sufficient, without other evidence, to prove the debt.
simplified_text:
Keeping and using business account records
Business account records, whether in physical or electronic form, that are regularly maintained, are important when the court needs to investigate a matter. However, these records alone are not enough evidence to hold someone responsible for a debt. 
For example:
A sues B for one thousand rupees and presents entries from his account books that show B owes him that amount. The entries are important, but more evidence is needed to prove the debt.

legal_text:
29. An entry in any public or other official book, register or record or an electronic record, stating a fact in issue or relevant fact, and made by a public servant in the discharge
of his official duty, or by any other person in performance of a duty specially enjoined by the law of the country in which such book, register or record or an electronic record, is kept, is itself a relevant fact.
simplified_text: Entry in Official Record: If a public servant or another person, as instructed by the law, makes a statement about a fact that is important to the matter at hand in a public or official record book, register, or electronic record, then that statement itself is important to the issue.

legal_text: 30. Statements of facts in issue or relevant facts, made in published maps or charts generally offered for public sale, or in maps or plans made under the authority of the Central Government or any State Government, as to matters usually represented or stated in such maps, charts or plans, are themselves relevant facts.
simplified_text: 30. Facts stated in publicly available maps or charts, or in maps and plans authorized by the Central Government or a State Government, about typical information found in such maps, charts, or plans, are considered relevant facts.

legal_text:
31. When the Court has to form an opinion as to the existence of any fact of a public nature, any statement of it, made in a recital contained in any Central Act or State Act or in
a Central Government or State Government notification appearing in the respective Official Gazette or in any printed paper or in electronic or digital form purporting to be such Gazette, is a relevant fact.
simplified_text: When the Court needs to determine if a fact relating to the public is true, it can consider any statement about it found in an official publication, such as a Central or State Act, a Government notification in the Official Gazette, or in a printed or electronic form that claims to be the Official Gazette.

legal_text: 32. When the Court has to form an opinion as to a law of any country, any statement of such law contained in a book purporting to be printed or published including in electronic or digital form under the authority of the Government of such country and to contain any such law, and any report of a ruling of the Courts of such country contained in a book including in electronic or digital form purporting to be a report of such rulings, is relevant.
simplified_text: When the Court needs to understand the law of a specific country, it can consider a statement of that law found in a book or electronic publication authorized by the government of that country, as well as any reports of court rulings in a book or electronic publication that claims to be a report of those rulings.

legal_text: 33. When any statement of which evidence is given forms part of a longer statement, or of a conversation or part of an isolated document, or is contained in a document which forms part of a book, or is contained in part of electronic record or of a connected series of letters or papers, evidence shall be given of so much and no more of the statement, conversation, document, electronic record, book or series of letters or papers as the Court considers necessary in that particular case to the full understanding of the nature and effect of the statement, and of the circumstances under which it was made.
simplified_text: When presenting evidence in court, only the necessary part of a statement or conversation, a document, electronic record, book, or series of letters or papers will be provided to ensure a full understanding of the nature and impact of the statement and the circumstances in which it was made.

legal_text: 34. The existence of any judgment, order or decree which by law prevents any Court from taking cognizance of a suit or holding a trial, is a relevant fact when the question is whether such Court ought to take cognizance of such suit or to hold such trial.
simplified_text: The presence of a judgment, order, or decree that legally stops a court from hearing a case or conducting a trial is important to consider when deciding if that court should handle the case or trial.

This legal text can be simplified as follows:
 
A final ruling from a competent Court or Tribunal in probate, matrimonial, admiralty, or insolvency cases is relevant if it confers or removes a legal status from a person or declares that a person is entitled to something. This ruling is considered as conclusive evidence of the following:
1. Any legal status granted by the ruling comes into effect when the ruling itself is enforced.
2. Any legal status declared by the ruling as belonging to a person is recognized from the time stated in the ruling.
3. Any legal status taken away from a person ends at the time specified in the ruling.
4. Anything that the ruling declares a person to be entitled to is confirmed to have been the person's property from the time specified in the ruling.

legal_text:
36. Judgments, orders or decrees other than those mentioned in section 35 are relevant if they relate to matters of a public nature relevant to the enquiry; but such judgments, orders or decrees are not conclusive proof of that which they state.
Illustration.
A sues B for trespass on his land. B alleges the existence of a public right of way over the land, which A denies. The existence of a decree in favour of the defendant, in a suit by A against C for a trespass on the same land, in which C alleged the existence of the same right of way, is relevant, but it is not conclusive proof that the right of way exists.
simplified_text:
Relevant Judgments: Judgments, orders, or decrees that are not mentioned in section 35 can be considered if they pertain to public matters that are relevant to the investigation. However, these judgments, orders, or decrees are not definite proof of what they state.

Example: If A sues B for trespass on his land, and B claims there is a public right of way over the land which A denies, a court decree in favor of B in a separate case, where C alleged the same right of way, can be considered but does not definitively prove the existence of the right of way.

legal_text:
37. Judgments or orders or decrees, other than those mentioned in sections 34, 35 and 36, are irrelevant, unless the existence of such judgment, order or decree is a fact in issue, or is relevant under some other provision of this Adhiniyam.
Illustrations.
(a) A and B separately sue C for a libel which reflects upon each of them. C in each case says that the matter alleged to be libellous is true, and the circumstances are such that
it is probably true in each case, or in neither. A obtains a decree against C for damages on the ground that C failed to make out his justification. The fact is irrelevant as between B and C.
(b) AprosecutesBforstealingacowfromhim.Bisconvicted.AafterwardssuesC
for the cow, which B had sold to him before his conviction. As between A and C, the judgment against B is irrelevant.
(c) AhasobtainedadecreeforthepossessionoflandagainstB.C,B'sson,murders A in consequence. The existence of the judgment is relevant, as showing motive for a crime.
(d) A is charged with theft and with having been previously convicted of theft. The previous conviction is relevant as a fact in issue.
(e) AistriedforthemurderofB.ThefactthatBprosecutedAforlibelandthatAwas convicted and sentenced is relevant under section 6 as showing the motive for the fact in issue.
simplified_text:
Relevant Judgments, Orders, and Decrees:
  
  Only judgments, orders, or decrees mentioned in sections 34, 35, and 36 are important unless their existence is a fact in question or is relevant under another part of this law.
  
  Examples:
  (a) A and B separately sue C for libel, and C claims the alleged libel is true in each case. A gets a ruling against C on the basis that C failed to prove the truth of the libel. This ruling is not relevant for the case between B and C.
  (b) A accuses B of stealing a cow, and B is convicted. A later sues C for the cow that B had sold to him before the conviction. In the case between A and C, the judgment against B is not relevant.
  (c) A obtains a decree for the possession of land against B. Later, B's son murders A. The existence of the decree is relevant as it shows a motive for the crime.
  (d) A is charged with theft and with a previous theft conviction. The previous conviction is relevant to prove the current charge.
  (e) A is tried for the murder of B. The fact that B prosecuted A for libel, and A was convicted and sentenced, is relevant under section 6 as it shows the motive for the matter in question.

legal_text: 38. Any party to a suit or other proceeding may show that any judgment, order or decree which is relevant under section 34, 35 or 36, and which has been proved by the adverse party, was delivered by a Court not competent to deliver it, or was obtained by fraud or collusion.
simplified_text: Challenging Judgments: Any person involved in a legal case can argue that a judgment, order, or decree, relevant under certain sections of the law, provided by the opposing party, was issued by a court that didn't have the authority to issue it, or was obtained through deceit or cooperation between the parties.

legal_text:
39. (1) When the Court has to form an opinion upon a point of foreign law or of science or art, or any other field, or as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions, the 25 opinions upon that point of persons specially skilled in such foreign law, science or art, or any other field, or in questions as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions are relevant facts and such persons are called experts.
Illustrations.
(a) The question is, whether the death of A was caused by poison. The opinions of experts as to the symptoms produced by the poison by which A is supposed to have died,
are relevant.
(b) The question is, whether A, at the time of doing a certain act, was, by reason of unsoundness of mind, incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he was doing what was either wrong or contrary to law. The opinions of experts upon the question whether the symptoms exhibited by A commonly show unsoundness of mind, and whether such unsoundness of mind usually renders persons incapable of knowing the nature of the acts which they do, or of knowing that what they do is either wrong or contrary to law, are relevant.
(c) The question is, whether a certain document was written by A. Another document is produced which is proved or admitted to have been written by A. The opinions of expertson the question whether the two documents were written by the same person or by different persons, are relevant.
(2) When in a proceeding, the court has to form an opinion on any matter relating to any information transmitted or stored in any computer resource or any other electronic or digital form, the opinion of the Examiner of Electronic Evidence referred to in section 79A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, is a relevant fact.
Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-section, an Examiner of Electronic Evidence shall be an expert.
simplified_text:
Opinions of Experts: When the court needs to determine a point of foreign law, science, art, or any other field, or has to identify handwriting or finger impressions, the opinions of individuals who have specialized knowledge in these areas are considered relevant facts. These individuals are known as experts.

Examples:
(a) For example, if the issue is whether A's death was caused by poison, the opinions of experts on the symptoms produced by the supposed poison are relevant.
(b) Similarly, if the question is whether A, due to unsoundness of mind, was incapable of understanding the nature of an act or the wrongfulness of the act, the opinions of experts on whether the symptoms displayed by A indicate unsoundness of mind and whether such condition usually renders individuals incapable of understanding the nature of their acts or the wrongfulness of their actions are relevant.
(c) Additionally, if there is a question of whether a document was written by A, the opinions of experts on whether two documents were authored by the same person or different people are relevant, especially if one document is proven or admitted to have been written by A.

Relevant Evidence from Electronic Sources: In legal proceedings involving information stored in a computer resource or in electronic or digital form, the opinion of the Examiner of Electronic Evidence referred to in section 79A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, is a relevant fact. An Examiner of Electronic Evidence is considered an expert for the purpose of this provision.

legal_text:
40. Facts, not otherwise relevant, are relevant if they support or are inconsistent with the opinions of experts, when such opinions are relevant.
Illustrations.
(a) The question is, whether A was poisoned by a certain poison. The fact that other persons, who were poisoned by that poison, exhibited certain symptoms which experts affirm or deny to be the symptoms of that poison, is relevant.
(b) The question is, whether an obstruction to a harbour is caused by a certain sea-wall. The fact that other harbours similarly situated in other respects, but where there were no such sea-walls, began to be obstructed at about the same time, is relevant.
simplified_text:
Relevance of Facts Supporting Expert Opinions

Facts that are not otherwise important become relevant if they support or contradict the opinions of experts when those opinions are important.

Examples:
a) If we are asking whether A was poisoned by a specific poison, it is relevant to consider the symptoms shown by other people who were poisoned by the same poison and whether those symptoms are confirmed or denied by experts to be caused by that poison.
b) If we are investigating whether a sea-wall is causing an obstruction in a harbour, it is relevant to take into account other harbours in similar situations, where no sea-walls were present but still started to become obstructed at roughly the same time.

legal_text:
41. (1) When the Court has to form an opinion as to the person by whom any document was written or signed, the opinion of any person acquainted with the handwriting of the person by whom it is supposed to be written or signed that it was or was not written or signed by that person, is a relevant fact.
Explanation.—A person is said to be acquainted with the handwriting of another person when he has seen that person write, or when he has received documents purporting to be written by that person in answer to documents written by himself or under his authority and addressed to that person, or when, in the ordinary course of business, documents purporting to be written by that person have been habitually submitted to him.
Illustration.
The question is, whether a given letter is in the handwriting of A, a merchant in Itanagar. B is a merchant in Bengaluru, who has written letters addressed to A and received letters purporting to be written by him. C, is B's clerk whose duty it was to examine and file B's correspondence. D is B's broker, to whom B habitually submitted the letters purporting to be written by A for the purpose of advising him thereon. The opinions of B, C and D on the question whether the letter is in the handwriting of A are relevant, though neither B, C nor D ever saw A write.
(2) When the Court has to form an opinion as to the electronic signature of any person, the opinion of the Certifying Authority which has issued the Electronic Signature Certificate is a relevant fact.
simplified_text:
Determining Handwriting Authenticity:
When a court needs to decide if a document was written or signed by a particular person, the opinion of someone who is familiar with that person's handwriting is important. This person might have seen the individual write, received documents purportedly written by that person in response to their own documents, or may have regularly reviewed documents supposedly written by that person in the course of business.
Example:
For instance, if there is a question about whether a letter was written by A, a merchant in Itanagar, the opinions of B, C, and D are relevant. B, who has corresponded with A, C, who was responsible for organizing B's letters, and D, to whom B regularly showed A's letters for advice, can provide their opinions on whether the letter is in A's handwriting, even if none of them witnessed A actually writing.
Electronic Signature:
When the Court needs to determine the authenticity of an electronic signature, the opinion of the Certifying Authority that issued the Electronic Signature Certificate is important.

legal_text:
42. When the Court has to form an opinion as to the existence of any general custom or right, the opinions, as to the existence of such custom or right, of persons who would be likely to know of its existence if it existed, are relevant.
Explanation.—The expression "general custom or right" includes customs or rights common to any considerable class of persons.
Illustration.
The right of the villagers of a particular village to use the water of a particular well is a general right within the meaning of this section.
simplified_text:
Opinion on General Custom or Right: When the court needs to decide if a common custom or right exists, the opinions of people who would probably know about it if it existed are important. This includes customs or rights that are common to a large group of people.

Example: The right of the people in a specific village to use water from a specific well is considered a general right as per this law.

legal_text:
43. When the Court has to form an opinion as to—
(i) the usages and tenets of any body of men or family;(ii) the constitution and governance of any religious or charitable foundation; or
(iii) the meaning of words or terms used in particular districts or by particular classes of people,
the opinions of persons having special means of knowledge thereon, are relevant facts.
simplified_text:
Opinions in Court:
When the Court needs to understand:
1. The customs and beliefs of a group or family;
2. The rules and management of a religious or charitable organization; or
3. The meaning of words used in specific areas or by certain groups,
the opinions of people with special knowledge about these things are important for the Court to consider.

legal_text:
44. When the Court has to form an opinion as to the relationship of one person to another, the opinion, expressed by conduct, as to the existence of such relationship, of any person who, as a member of the family or otherwise, has special means of knowledge on the subject, is a relevant fact:
Provided that such opinion shall not be sufficient to prove a marriage in proceedings under the Divorce Act, 1869, or in prosecution under sections 82 and 84 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
Illustrations.
(a) The question is, whether A and B were married. The fact that they were usually
received and treated by their friends as husband and wife, is relevant.
(b) The question is, whether A was the legitimate son of B. The fact that A was always treated as such by members of the family, is relevant.
simplified_text:
Forming Opinions about Relationships: When a court needs to determine the relationship between two people, the opinion of someone with special knowledge, expressed through their actions, is important. This applies to family members or others who have special insight into the relationship.

Exceptions: However, in certain legal proceedings related to divorce or specific prosecutions, such opinions are not enough to prove a marriage.

Examples:
(a) If the court needs to know if A and B were married, how their friends usually treated them as a married couple is relevant.
(b) If the court needs to establish if A was the legitimate son of B, how A was always treated by family members is relevant.

legal_text: 45. Whenever the opinion of any living person is relevant, the grounds on which such opinion is based are also relevant.An expert may give an account of experiments performed by him for the purpose of forming his opinion.
simplified_text: Opinions and Expert Testimony: When the opinion of a living person is important, the reasons for that opinion are also important. An expert can talk about the experiments they did in order to form their opinion.

legal_text:
In civil cases character to prove conduct imputed, irrelevant.
46. In civil cases the fact that the character of any person concerned is such as to render probable or improbable any conduct imputed to him, is irrelevant, except in so far as such character appears from facts otherwise relevant.
simplified_text: In civil cases, the character of a person involved is not important in proving whether they are likely to behave a certain way, unless their character is shown through other relevant facts.

legal_text:
In criminal cases previous good character relevant.
47. In criminal proceedings the fact that the person accused is of a good character, is relevant.
simplified_text: Considering Good Character in Criminal Cases: In criminal court cases, the fact that the accused person has a good character is important and can be taken into account.

legal_text: 48. In a prosecution for an offence under section 64, section 65, section 66, section 67, section 68, section 69, section 70, section 71, section 74, section 75, section 76, section 77 or section 78 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 or for attempt to commit any such offence, where the question of consent is in issue, evidence of the character of the victim or of such person's previous sexual experience with any person shall not be relevant on the issue of such consent or the quality of consent.
simplified_text: In any case where someone is being prosecuted for breaking the law as stated in sections 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 69, 70, 71, 74, 75, 76, 77, or 78 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, or trying to commit such an offense, evidence of the victim's character or their past sexual experiences with anyone is not relevant to the question of whether the victim consented or the nature of that consent.

legal_text:
49. In criminal proceedings, the fact that the accused has a bad character, is irrelevant, unless evidence has been given that he has a good character, in which case it becomes relevant.
Explanation 1.—This section does not apply to cases in which the bad character of any person is itself a fact in issue.
Explanation 2.—A previous conviction is relevant as evidence of bad character.
simplified_text: In criminal cases, a person's bad character is not important unless evidence is presented to show that the person has a good character. If it's relevant that a person has a bad character, such as in cases where the person's character is an issue itself, this rule doesn't apply. Also, a previous conviction can be used as evidence of a person's bad character.

legal_text:
50. In civil cases, the fact that the character of any person is such as to affect the amount of damages which he ought to receive, is relevant.
Explanation.—In this section and sections 46, 47 and 49, the word "character" includes both reputation and disposition; but, except as provided in section 49, evidence may be given only of general reputation and general disposition, and not of particular acts by which reputation or disposition has been shown.
simplified_text: In civil cases, a person's character can be considered when deciding how much compensation they should receive. And when we talk about "character," we mean both their reputation and their general behavior. However, evidence can only be given about a person's general reputation and behavior, and not about specific acts that might have affected their reputation or behavior.

legal_text:
Fact judicially noticeable need not be proved.
51. No fact of which the Court will take judicial notice need be proved.
simplified_text: It is not necessary to prove facts that are already known by the court. If the court recognizes a fact as being common knowledge, it does not need to be proven.

legal_text:
53. No fact needs to be proved in any proceeding which the parties thereto or their agents agree to admit at the hearing, or which, before the hearing, they agree to admit by any writing under their hands, or which by any rule of pleading in force at the time they are deemed to have admitted by their pleadings:
Provided that the Court may, in its discretion, require the facts admitted to be proved 5 otherwise than by such admissions
simplified_text:
Simplified text:
In any legal proceeding, if both parties or their representatives agree to a fact, there is no need to prove it. This agreement can be made during the hearing or in writing before the hearing. If the court chooses, it can still ask for proof of the admitted facts in a different way.

legal_text:
56. The contents of documents may be proved either by primary or by secondary evidence.
57. Primary evidence means the document itself produced for the inspection of the Court.
Explanation 1.—Where a document is executed in several parts, each part is primary evidence of the document.
Explanation 2.—Where a document is executed in counterpart, each counterpart being executed by one or some of the parties only, each counterpart is primary evidence as against the parties executing it.
Explanation 3.—Where a number of documents are all made by one uniform process, as in the case of printing, lithography or photography, each is primary evidence of the contents of the rest; but, where they are all copies of a common original, they are not primary evidence of the contents of the original.
Explanation 4.—Where an electronic or digital record is created or stored, and such storage occurs simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, each such file is primary evidence.
Explanation 5.—Where an electronic or digital record is produced from proper custody, such electronic and digital record is primary evidence unless it is disputed.
Explanation 6.—Where a video recording is simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted or broadcast or transferred to another, each of the stored recordings is primary evidence.
Explanation 7.—Where an electronic or digital record is stored in multiple storage spaces in a computer resource, each such automated storage, including temporary files, is primary evidence.
simplified_text:
Proof of Documents: Document contents can be proven with either primary or secondary evidence. 

Primary Evidence: This means the actual document presented to the court for review. 

Additional Clarifications: 
- If a document is made up of multiple parts, each part is considered primary evidence of the whole document.
- If a document is executed in counterpart (separate identical documents), each counterpart is primary evidence against the parties executing it.
- When multiple documents are created using the same process like printing, each is considered primary evidence of the others. However, if they are all copies of an original, they are not considered primary evidence of the original.
- In the case of electronic or digital records, each file created or stored simultaneously or sequentially is considered primary evidence.
- A properly stored electronic or digital record is considered primary evidence unless it is disputed.
- If a video recording is stored electronically and transmitted or broadcasted, each stored recording is primary evidence.
- For electronic or digital records stored in multiple areas in a computer, each automated storage, including temporary files, is considered primary evidence.

Where an order is made under section 152 for the purpose of preventing
obstruction, nuisance or danger to the public in the use of any way, river, channel or place,
the Magistrate shall, on the appearance before him of the person against whom the order
was made, question him as to whether he denies the existence of any public right in respect
of the way, river, channel or place, and if he does so, the Magistrate shall, before proceeding
under section 157, inquire into the matter.
(2) If in such inquiry the Magistrate finds that there is any reliable evidence in support
of such denial, he shall stay the proceedings until the matter of the existence of such right
has been decided by a competent Court; and, if he finds that there is no such evidence, he
shall proceed as laid down in section 157
(3) A person who has, on being questioned by the Magistrate under sub-section (1),
fail to deny the existence of a public right of the nature therein referred to, or who, having
made such denial, has failed to adduce reliable evidence in support thereof, shall not in the
subsequent proceedings be permitted to make any such denial.
simplified_text:
Order Inquiry: If an order is issued under section 152 to prevent obstruction, nuisance, or danger to the public in using a pathway, river, channel, or place, the Magistrate will question the person the order is against. If the person denies the existence of any public right in relation to the pathway, river, channel, or place, the Magistrate will investigate before taking further action under section 157.

Stay Proceedings: If during the investigation, the Magistrate finds reliable evidence supporting the denial of public rights, the proceedings will be put on hold until a competent court decides on the existence of such rights. If no such evidence is found, the Magistrate will proceed as specified in section 157.

Consequences of Denial: A person who, when questioned by the Magistrate, does not deny the existence of a public right as mentioned, or who denies it but fails to provide reliable evidence to support the denial, cannot later deny the existence of such public rights in the subsequent proceedings.

Decision on the Order: If the Magistrate believes that the original order, or a modified version, is fair and appropriate, the order will be finalized without any changes or with the agreed modifications.

Conclusion of Proceedings: If the Magistrate does not approve of the order, the case will not progress any further. However, the proceedings under this section must be concluded within 90 days, and can be extended to 120 days with a written explanation.

simplified_text:
Notice and Enforcement of Court Orders:

After a court order becomes final, the Magistrate will notify the person it applies to and give them a deadline to comply. The notice will also warn of the penalty for not obeying the order.

If the person does not comply within the deadline, the Magistrate can enforce the order and recover the costs from the person's property through sale or seizure.

No legal action can be taken against the Magistrate for actions taken in good faith under this section.

(1) In cases where, in the opinion of a District Magistrate, a Sub-divisional
Magistrate or any other Executive Magistrate specially empowered by the State Government
in this behalf, there is sufficient ground for proceeding under this section and immediate
prevention or speedy remedy is desirable, such Magistrate may, by a written order stating
the material facts of the case and served in the manner provided by section 153, direct any
person to abstain from a certain act or to take certain order with respect to certain property
in his possession or under his management, if such Magistrate considers that such direction
is likely to prevent, or tends to prevent, obstruction, annoyance or injury to any person
lawfully employed, or danger to human life, health or safety or a disturbance of the public
tranquility, or a riot, or an affray.
(2) An order under this section may, in cases of emergency or in cases where the
circumstances do not admit of the serving in due time of a notice upon the person against
whom the order is directed, be passed ex parte.
(3) An order under this section may be directed to a particular individual, or to persons
residing in a particular place or area, or to the public generally when frequenting or visiting
a particular place or area.
(4) No order under this section shall remain in force for more than two months from
the making thereof:

danger to human life, health or safety or for preventing a riot or any affray, it may, by

notification.

aggrieved, rescind or alter any order made under this section by himself or any Magistrate
subordinate to him or by his predecessor-in-office.

person aggrieved, rescind or alter any order made by it under the proviso to sub-section (4).

Order to Abstain or Act: If a District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate, or any other specially authorized Executive Magistrate believes there are sufficient grounds and immediate action is needed, they can issue a written order to a person to stop doing something or to take certain actions regarding their property, if the Magistrate thinks it will prevent obstruction, annoyance, injury, danger to human life, health, safety, public disturbance, riot, or affray.

Emergency or Ex Parte Orders: In urgent situations or when there isn’t enough time to notify the person involved, the order can be given without their input.

Scope of Order: The order can be directed to a specific person, people in a certain area, or the general public at a particular place.

Duration of Order: An order under this section can only be valid for two months, unless the State Government extends it for up to six months if necessary to prevent danger or riot.

Rescinding or Changing Orders: Any Magistrate or the State Government can cancel or change an order made under this section, and they must provide a chance for the affected person to explain why.

Handling Land and Water Disputes: 
When a local magistrate gets a report from a police officer or any other information, about a disagreement over using a piece of land or water that might lead to trouble, the magistrate will write an order. This order will explain why the magistrate thinks there's a problem and tell the people involved in the disagreement to come to court on a set date and time. They should also write down their arguments.

Reviewing Arguments: 
The magistrate will read the written arguments and listen to the parties. The magistrate will also look at any evidence that the parties bring and decide if the right to use the land or water exists. The rules in section 164 will apply to this decision. The magistrate might also decide if someone can't interfere with the right to use the land or water, and might order something to be moved if it's in the way.

Decision Based on Timing: 
If the magistrate finds that the right to use the land or water exists, the magistrate might say that no one can interfere with it. But this won't happen if the right has not been used recently.  

Handling Other Disputes: 
If the magistrate finds out during a proceeding that the dispute is related to using land or water, the magistrate can continue with the case. Likewise, if the magistrate finds that the dispute should be handled differently, the magistrate can decide to handle it that way.

If a person dies or disappears, or if a woman alleges rape, while in custody authorized by the Magistrate or the Court, an inquiry must be held by the Judicial Magistrate within the area where the offense occurred, in addition to any police inquiry or investigation.

3) Recording Evidence:
The Magistrate conducting the inquiry must record the evidence in the manner appropriate to the case.

4) Examination of Deceased:
If the Magistrate considers it necessary to examine the body of a person who has already been buried to determine the cause of death, they can order the body to be exhumed and examined.

5) Involvement of Relatives:
The Magistrate should, when possible, inform known relatives of the deceased and allow them to be present at the inquiry.

6) Medical Examination:
The Magistrate, Executive Magistrate, or police officer conducting an inquiry must, within 24 hours of the death, send the body for examination by a qualified medical practitioner, unless this is not possible, for reasons that must be documented.

Who can make a complaint:
Only a person who has been affected by an offense under Chapter V of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 can file a complaint in court. However, there are special rules for certain situations:
- If the affected person is under 18 years old, has a serious mental disability, illness, or is unable to make a complaint due to sickness or infirmity, or is a woman who should not be forced to appear in public according to local customs, then someone else can make a complaint on their behalf with the court's permission.
- If the affected person is the husband and is serving in the Armed Forces under conditions making it impossible for him to make a complaint in person, someone else authorized by the husband can make a complaint on his behalf.
- If the affected person is the wife, her family members or another person related to her can make a complaint on her behalf with the court's permission.
- Only the husband can make a complaint for an offense under section 83 on behalf of the wife, unless he is absent, in which case another person who had care of the woman at the time of the offense can make the complaint with the court's permission.

Special rules for making a complaint:
- If the complaint is for a person under 18 or a person with mental illness, and the person making the complaint is not their appointed guardian, the court must notify the appointed guardian and allow them to be heard before granting permission for the complaint.
- If a husband cannot make the complaint in person due to his military service, the authorization for someone else to make the complaint must be in writing, signed by the husband, and certified by his Commanding Officer.
- Documents that meet the requirements for authorization and certification are considered genuine unless proven otherwise.

Limitation on taking legal action:
No court can take action for an offense under section 64 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 if the offense involves sexual intercourse by a man with his wife who is under 18, and more than one year has passed since the offense occurred.
These rules also apply to attempts to commit an offense or to help someone commit an offense.

constitute the offence alleged, the nature of such offence and such other particulars as are
reasonably sufficient to give notice to the accused of the offence alleged to have been
committed by him.
(4) No complaint under sub-section (2) shall be made by the Public Prosecutor except
with the previous sanction—
(a) of the State Government,—
(i) in the case of a person who is or has been the Governor of that State or
a Minister of that Government;
(ii) in the case of any other public servant employed in connection with
the affairs of the State;
(b) of the Central Government, in any other case.
(5) No Court of Session shall take cognizance of an offence under sub-section (2)
unless the complaint is made within six months from the date on which the offence is alleged
to have been committed.
(6) Nothing in this section shall affect the right of the person against whom the
offence is alleged to have been committed, to make a complaint in respect of that offence
before a Magistrate having jurisdiction or the power of such Magistrate to take cognizance

simplified_text:
Legal Simplification:

1. Offence Complaint: No court can consider a crime punishable under Chapter XIX of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 unless a complaint is made by an affected person. However, in certain circumstances, another person can make the complaint with the court's permission on behalf of the affected person.

2. Exceptional Cases: In situations where the offence is alleged to have been committed against high-ranking officials or public servants, a Court of Session can consider the offence upon a written complaint by the Public Prosecutor, without the case being referred to it.

3. Complaint Details: Every complaint made by the Public Prosecutor must include specific details about the alleged offence to inform the accused.

4. Sanction Requirement: The Public Prosecutor can only make a complaint under exceptional circumstances with the previous consent of the State Government or the Central Government, depending on the case.

5. Time Limit: No Court of Session can consider an offence under exceptional circumstances unless the complaint is made within six months from the date of the alleged offence.

6. Right to Complaint: This section does not affect the affected person's right to make a complaint before a Magistrate, nor does it affect the Magistrate's authority to consider the offence based on that complaint.

A Magistrate having jurisdiction while taking cognizance of an offence on
complaint shall examine upon oath the complainant and the witnesses present, if any, and
the substance of such examination shall be reduced to writing and shall be signed by the
complainant and the witnesses, and also by the Magistrate:
Provided that no cognizance of an offence under this section shall be taken by the
Magistrate without giving the accused an opportunity of being heard:
Provided further that, when the complaint is made in writing, the Magistrate need not
examine the complainant and the witnesses—
(a) if a public servant acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official
duties or a Court has made the complaint; or
(b) if the Magistrate makes over the case for inquiry or trial to another Magistrate
under section 212:
Provided further that if the Magistrate makes over the case to another Magistrate

Provided further that in case of a complaint against a public servant, the Magistrate

simplified_text:
When a Magistrate with the authority to do so starts looking into a complaint about an offense, they must swear in the person who made the complaint and any witnesses who are there, if there are any. What they say during the questioning should be written down and signed by the person who made the complaint and the witnesses, as well as the Magistrate.

But, the Magistrate can't start looking into the offense without giving the accused person a chance to speak up.

If the complaint is written down, the Magistrate doesn't have to question the person who made the complaint or the witnesses in these cases:

(a) if it's a public servant or a Court that made the complaint, or
(b) if the Magistrate has passed the case on to another Magistrate for investigation or trial under section 212.

If the Magistrate passes the case on to another Magistrate after questioning the person who made the complaint and the witnesses, the new Magistrate doesn't need to question them again.

When there's a complaint against a public servant, the Magistrate should follow the procedure set out in section 217.

Magistrate's Powers to Handle Offence Complaints:

However, if the accused resides outside the Magistrate's jurisdiction, the process against the accused can be postponed. This is mandatory in such cases.

Conditions on Investigation:
During the investigation, the Magistrate may gather evidence from witnesses and oath if they think it's necessary. If the offense is only triable by the Court of Session, the Magistrate must ask the complainant to bring and examine all of their witnesses under oath.


Powers of Non-Police Officer Investigator:
If the investigation is assigned to a person who is not a police officer, they will have all the necessary powers for investigation, except for the power to arrest someone without a warrant.

Issuing Summons and Warrants: If a Magistrate believes there are sufficient grounds to proceed with a case, they can:

Filing of Prosecution Witness List: Before issuing a summons or warrant, the prosecution must file a list of their witnesses for the case.

simplified_text:
Providing Documents to the Accused and Victim: If the legal case is started based on a police report, the Magistrate must promptly, and no later than fourteen days from the date the accused appears in court, provide, free of charge, copies of the following to the accused and to the victim if they are being represented by a lawyer:

1. The police report
2. The first information report filed under section 193
3. Statements of all persons that the prosecution plans to call as witnesses, except for any parts specifically requested for exclusion by the police officer
