legal_text:
. (1) Every charge under this Sanhita shall state the offence with which the accused
is charged.
(2) If the law which creates the offence gives it any specific name, the offence may be
described in the charge by that name only.
(3) If the law which creates the offence does not give it any specific name, so much of
the definition of the offence must be stated as to give the accused notice of the matter with
which he is charged.
(4) The law and section of the law against which the offence is said to have been
committed shall be mentioned in the charge.
(5) The fact that the charge is made is equivalent to a statement that every legal
condition required by law to constitute the offence charged was fulfilled in the particular
case.
(6) The charge shall be written in the language of the Court.
(7) If the accused, having been previously convicted of any offence, is liable, by
reason of such previous conviction, to enhanced punishment, or to punishment of a different
kind, for a subsequent offence, and it is intended to prove such previous conviction for the
purpose of affecting the punishment which the Court may think fit, to award for the
subsequent offence, the fact, date and place of the previous conviction shall be stated in
the charge; and if such statement has been omitted, the Court may add it at any time before
sentence is passed.
Illustrations.
(a) A is charged with the murder of B. This is equivalent to a statement that A's act fell
within the definition of murder given in sections 98 and 99 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,
2023; that it did not fall within any of the general exceptions of the said Sanhita; and that it
did not fall within any of the five exceptions to section 99, or that, if it did fall within
Exception 1, one or other of the three provisos to that exception applied to it.
(b) A is charged under section 116 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, with
voluntarily causing grievous hurt to B by means of an instrument for shooting. This is
equivalent to a statement that the case was not provided for by section 120 of the said
Sanhita, and that the general exceptions did not apply to it.
(c) A is accused of murder, cheating, theft, extortion, adultery or criminal intimidation,
or using a false property-mark. The charge may state that A committed murder, or
cheating, or theft, or extortion, or adultery, or criminal intimidation, or that he used a false
property-mark, without reference to the definitions, of those crimes contained in the Bharatiya
Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; but the sections under which the offence is punishable must, in each
instance be referred to in the charge.
(d) A is charged under section 220 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, with
intentionally obstructing a sale of property offered for sale by the lawful authority of a
public servant. The charge should be in those words.
simplified_text:
Every charge in this statute must clearly state the offense the accused is being charged with. If the law naming the offense, it should be mentioned in the charge by that name. If the law does not name the offense, the charge should include enough details of the offense to notify the accused. The law and section against which the offense is said to have been committed should be mentioned in the charge. When a charge is made, it is taken as a statement that every legal requirement to constitute the offense was met. The charge must be written in the language of the Court. If the accused has a previous conviction that can lead to enhanced or different punishment for a subsequent offense, the fact, date, and place of the previous conviction should be stated in the charge. If this is initially omitted, it can be added by the Court before sentencing.

Illustrations:
(a) A is charged with the murder of B. This means that A's act fits within the definition of murder, as given in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and did not fall within any exceptions given.
(b) A is charged with causing grievous hurt to B by means of an instrument for shooting. This means that the case was not provided for by a specific section of the Sanhita, and that the general exceptions did not apply.
(c) A is accused of several crimes. The charge may state that A committed murder, cheating, theft, extortion, adultery, criminal intimidation, or using a false property-mark, without defining the crimes, but each must be referred to the specific sections of the law.
(d) A is charged with intentionally obstructing a sale of property offered for sale by the lawful authority of a public servant. The charge should be in those words.

legal_text:
(1) The charge shall contain such particulars as to the time and place of the
alleged offence, and the person (if any) against whom, or the thing (if any) in respect of
which, it was committed, as are reasonably sufficient to give the accused notice of the
matter with which he is charged.
(2) When the accused is charged with criminal breach of trust or dishonest
misappropriation of money or other movable property, it shall be sufficient to specify the
gross sum or, as the case may be, describe the movable property in respect of which the
offence is alleged to have been committed, and the dates between which the offence is
alleged to have been committed, without specifying particular items or exact dates, and the
charge so framed shall be deemed to be a charge of one offence within the meaning of
section 242:
Provided that the time included between the first and last of such dates shall not
exceed one year
simplified_text:
Providing Information in Charges:

The charge must include enough details about the time and place of the alleged offense, as well as the person or thing involved, to give the accused a clear understanding of the accusation.

When the accused is charged with criminal breach of trust or dishonest misappropriation of money or property, it is enough to specify the total amount of money or describe the property, without listing individual items or exact dates. The charge should cover a period of up to one year between the first and last dates.

legal_text:
When the nature of the case is such that the particulars mentioned in
sections 234 and 235 do not give the accused sufficient notice of the matter with which he
is charged, the charge shall also contain such particulars of the manner in which the alleged
offence was committed as will be sufficient for that purpose.
Illustrations.
(a) A is accused of the theft of a certain article at a certain time and place. The charge
need not set out the manner in which the theft was effected.
(b) A is accused of cheating B at a given time and place. The charge must set out the
manner in which A cheated B.
(c) A is accused of giving false evidence at a given time and place. The charge must
set out that portion of the evidence given by A which is alleged to be false.
(d) A is accused of obstructing B, a public servant, in the discharge of his public
functions at a given time and place. The charge must set out the manner in which A obstructed
B in the discharge of his functions.
(e) A is accused of the murder of B at a given time and place. The charge need not
state the manner in which A murdered B.
(f) A is accused of disobeying a direction of the law with intent to save B from
punishment. The charge must set out the disobedience charged and the law infringed
simplified_text:
When the accused is not given enough notice of the matter with which he is charged, the charge should also contain enough details about how the alleged offense was committed.

Examples:
- If A is accused of stealing something at a certain time and place, the charge doesn't need to describe how the theft happened.
- If A is accused of cheating B at a certain time and place, the charge must describe how A cheated B.
- If A is accused of giving false evidence at a certain time and place, the charge must describe the portion of A's evidence that is alleged to be false.

No error in stating either the offence or the particulars required to be stated in
the charge, and no omission to state the offence or those particulars, shall be regarded at
any stage of the case as material, unless the accused was in fact misled by such error or
omission, and it has occasioned a failure of justice.
Illustrations.
(a) A is charged under section 178 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, with "having
been in possession of counterfeit coin, having known at the time when he became possessed
thereof that such coin was counterfeit," the word "fraudulently" being omitted in the charge.
Unless it appears that A was in fact misled by this omission, the error shall not be regarded
as material.
(b) A is charged with cheating B, and the manner in which he cheated B is not set out
in the charge or is set out incorrectly. A defends himself, calls witnesses and gives his own
account of the transaction. The Court may infer from this that the omission to set out the
manner of the cheating is not material.
(c) A is charged with cheating B, and the manner in which he cheated B is not set out
in the charge. There were many transactions between A and B, and A had no means of
knowing to which of them the charge referred, and offered no defence. The Court may infer
from such facts that the omission to set out the manner of the cheating was, in the case, a
material error.
(d) A is charged with the murder of Khoda Baksh on the 21st January, 2023. In fact, the
murdered person's name was Haidar Baksh, and the date of the murder was the 20th January,
2023. A was never charged with any murder but one, and had heard the inquiry before the
Magistrate, which referred exclusively to the case of Haidar Baksh. The Court may infer
from these facts that A was not misled, and that the error in the charge was immaterial.
(e) A was charged with murdering Haidar Baksh on the 20th January, 2023, and Khoda
Baksh (who tried to arrest him for that murder) on the 21st January, 2023. When charged for
the murder of Haidar Baksh, he was tried for the murder of Khoda Baksh. The witnesses
present in his defence were witnesses in the case of Haidar Baksh. The Court may infer from
this that A was misled, and that the error was material

No error in stating either the offense or the details required in the charge, and no omission to state the offense or those details, shall be considered important in the case unless it actually misled the accused and led to a miscarriage of justice.

Examples:
(a) A is charged with being in possession of counterfeit coins, knowing they were counterfeit, but the charge does not include the word "fraudulently." Unless it is shown that A was in fact misled by this omission, the error is not important.
(b) A is charged with cheating B, but the charge does not specify how A cheated B or does so incorrectly. A presents a defense, calls witnesses, and gives his own version of the events. From this, the court may conclude that the omission of the cheating method is not important.
(c) A is charged with cheating B, but the charge does not specify how. There were many transactions between A and B, and A had no way of knowing which one the charge referred to and did not offer any defense. In this case, the court may infer that the omission of the cheating details was significant.
(d) A is charged with the murder of Khoda Baksh on January 21, 2023, but the actual victim's name was Haidar Baksh, and the date of the murder was January 20, 2023. A was only charged with one murder and was aware of the proceedings. The court may infer from these facts that A was not misled, and the error in the charge was not important.
(e) A was charged with murdering Haidar Baksh on January 20, 2023, and Khoda Baksh on the following day. During the trial for Haidar Baksh's murder, A was tried for Khoda Baksh's murder, and the defense witnesses were for Haidar Baksh's case. In this instance, the court may infer that A was misled, and the error was significant.

accused of them may be charged with, and tried at one trial for, each of such offences.
(4) If several acts, of which one or more than one would by itself or themselves
constitute an offence, constitute when combined a different offence, the person accused of
them may be charged with, and tried at one trial for the offence constituted by such acts
when combined, and for any offence constituted by any one, or more, of such acts.
(5) Nothing contained in this section shall affect section 12 of the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023.
Illustrations to sub-section (1)
(a) A rescues B, a person in lawful custody, and in so doing causes grievous hurt to
C, a constable in whose custody B was. A may be charged with, and convicted of, offences
under sections 261 and 119 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
(b) A commits house-breaking by day with intent to commit adultery, and commits, in
the house so entered, adultery with B's wife. A may be separately charged with, and convicted
of, offences under section 330 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
(c) A entices B, the wife of C, away from C, with intent to commit adultery with B, and
then commits adultery with her. A may be separately charged with, and convicted of, offences
under section 83 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
(d) A has in his possession several seals, knowing them to be counterfeit and intending
to use them for the purpose of committing several forgeries punishable under section 335 of
the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. A may be separately charged with, and convicted of, the
possession of each seal under section 339 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
(e) With intent to cause injury to B, A institutes a criminal proceeding against him,
knowing that there is no just or lawful ground for such proceeding, and also falsely accuses
B of having committed an offence, knowing that there is no just or lawful ground for such
charge. A may be separately charged with, and convicted of, two offences under section
246 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
(f) A, with intent to cause injury to B, falsely accuses him of having committed an
offence, knowing that there is no just or lawful ground for such charge. On the trial, A gives
false evidence against B, intending thereby to cause B to be convicted of a capital offence.
A may be separately charged with, and convicted of, offences under sections 246 and 228
of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
(g) A, with six others, commits the offences of rioting, grievous hurt and assaulting a
public servant endeavouring in the discharge of his duty as such to suppress the riot. A
may be separately charged with, and convicted of, offences under sections 189, 115 and 193
of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
(h) A threatens B, C and D at the same time with injury to their persons with intent to
cause alarm to them. A may be separately charged with, and convicted of, each of the three
offences under section 309 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
The separate charges referred to in illustrations (a) to (h), respectively, may be tried
at the same time.

separately charged with, and convicted of, offences under sections 323, 392 and 394 of the

have committed, although he was not charged with it.
Illustrations.
(a) A is accused of an act which may amount to theft, or receiving stolen property, or
criminal breach of trust or cheating. He may be charged with theft, receiving stolen property,
criminal breach of trust and cheating, or he may be charged with having committed theft, or
receiving stolen property, or criminal breach of trust or cheating.
(b) In the case mentioned, A is only charged with theft. It appears that he committed
the offence of criminal breach of trust, or that of receiving stolen goods. He may be convicted
of criminal breach of trust or of receiving stolen goods (as the case may be), though he was
not charged with such offence.
(c) A states on oath before the Magistrate that he saw B hit C with a club. Before the
Sessions Court A states on oath that B never hit C. A may be charged in the alternative and
convicted of intentionally giving false evidence, although it cannot be proved which of

simplified_text:
Charging for Multiple Offences: If the evidence suggests that the accused may have committed more than one offense, they can be charged with any or all of those offenses. Alternatively, they can be charged with one offense, and if it turns out in the trial that they committed a different offense that could have been included in the original charge, they can still be convicted of that offense.

Examples:
- A is accused of an act that could be considered theft, receiving stolen property, criminal breach of trust, or cheating. They can be charged with any or all of these offenses, or charged with having committed theft, receiving stolen property, criminal breach of trust, or cheating.
- If A is only charged with theft but it comes out in the trial that they committed the offense of criminal breach of trust or receiving stolen goods, they can still be convicted of the offense they committed, even if it wasn't the one they were originally charged with.

1. If a person is charged with an offense that includes multiple parts, some of which make up a complete minor offense, and those parts are proven, the person can be convicted of the minor offense even if it was not specifically charged.
2. If a person is charged with an offense and evidence is presented that reduces it to a minor offense, they can be convicted of the minor offense even if it was not charged.
3. If a person is charged with an offense, they can be convicted of attempting to commit that offense even if the attempt was not separately charged.
4. However, this does not allow for conviction of a minor offense if the necessary requirements for initiating proceedings for that minor offense have not been met.

Example:
(a) A is charged with criminal breach of trust as a carrier. It is found that A did commit criminal breach of trust, but the property was not entrusted to him as a carrier. A may be convicted of criminal breach of trust.

Legal Text Simplified:

1. Trial Procedure: If a Court of Session is handling a case under section 222, it will follow the same trial process as for non-police report warrant-cases before a Magistrate Court. The person accused of the offence will usually be examined as a witness for the prosecution, unless the Court directs otherwise for specific reasons.

2. Confidential Trials: The trial may be held in private if either party requests it or if the Court finds it appropriate.

3. Discharge and Compensation: If the Court discharges or acquits the accused and believes there was no good reason for the accusation, it can order the accuser (excluding certain high-ranking officials) to justify why they should not compensate the accused. The Court will then consider the justification and may order the accuser to pay compensation, up to a certain amount.

4. Recovery of Compensation: Any compensation ordered by the Court will be recovered in the same way as a fine imposed by a Magistrate.

5. Legal Liability: The order for compensation does not exempt the accuser from civil or criminal liability related to the complaint. Any compensation already paid to the accused would be considered in any subsequent civil suit on the same matter.

6. Right to Appeal: The person ordered to pay compensation can appeal the order, specifically regarding the compensation, to the High Court.

7. Payment Timing: The compensator cannot pay the compensation until the period for filing an appeal has passed, or if an appeal is submitted, until the appeal has been decided.

simplified_text:
Charging and Trying the Accused: When the Magistrate believes that there is reason to think the accused has committed a crime that falls under the Magistrate's jurisdiction and can be adequately punished by them, the Magistrate must formally accuse the accused in writing.

Reading and Explaining the Charge: The charge will then be read and explained to the accused, who will be asked to enter a plea or present a defense.

Handling the Plea: If the accused pleads guilty, the Magistrate can choose to convict them. If the accused refuses to plead, or does not plead, or claims to be tried, the Magistrate will ask if they want to cross-examine any of the prosecution's witnesses.

Cross-Examination of Witnesses: If the accused wishes to cross-examine the witnesses, they will be recalled, questioned, and released. The evidence of any remaining prosecution witnesses will then be recorded.

Proceeding Without Witness Attendance: If the prosecution witnesses cannot be brought for cross-examination despite reasonable efforts, the Magistrate may proceed with the case based on the available evidence, and this decision will be explained in writing.

(1) If, in any case instituted upon complaint or upon information given to a
police officer or to a Magistrate, one or more persons is or are accused before a Magistrate
of any offence triable by a Magistrate, and the Magistrate by whom the case is heard
discharges or acquits all or any of the accused, and is of opinion that there was no reasonable
ground for making the accusation against them or any of them, the Magistrate may, by his
order of discharge or acquittal, if the person upon whose complaint or information the
accusation was made is present, call upon him forthwith to show cause why he should not
pay compensation to such accused or to each or any of such accused when there are more
than one; or, if such person is not present, direct the issue of a summons to him to appear
and show cause as aforesaid.
(2) The Magistrate shall record and consider any cause which such complainant or
informant may show, and if he is satisfied that there was no reasonable ground for making
the accusation, may, for reasons to be recorded, make an order that compensation to such
amount, not exceeding the amount of fine he is empowered to impose, as he may determine,
be paid by such complainant or informant to the accused or to each or any of them.
(3) The Magistrate may, by the order directing payment of the compensation under
sub-section (2), further order that, in default of payment, the person ordered to pay such
compensation shall undergo simple imprisonment for a period not exceeding thirty days.
(4) When any person is imprisoned under sub-section (3), the provisions of
sections 68 and 69 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 shall, so far as may be, apply.
(5) No person who has been directed to pay compensation under this section shall,
by reason of such order, be exempted from any civil or criminal liability in respect of the
complaint made or information given by him:
Provided that any amount paid to an accused person under this section shall be taken
into account in awarding compensation to such person in any subsequent civil suit relating
to the same matter.
(6) A complainant or informant who has been ordered under sub-section (2) by a
Magistrate of the second class to pay compensation exceeding one thousand rupees, may
appeal from the order, as if such complainant or informant had been convicted on a trial held
by such Magistrate.
(7) When an order for payment of compensation to an accused person is made in a
case which is subject to appeal under sub-section (6), the compensation shall not be paid to
him before the period allowed for the presentation of the appeal has elapsed, or, if an appeal
is presented, before the appeal has been decided; and where such order is made in a case
which is not so subject to appeal the compensation shall not be paid before the expiration
of one month from the date of the order.
(8) The provisions of this section apply to summons-cases as well as to
warrant-cases.
simplified_text:
Ordering Compensation for False Accusations: If a person is accused of a crime in a case brought by a complaint or information given to a police officer or Magistrate, and the Magistrate finds that there was no reasonable basis for the accusation, the Magistrate can order the person who made the complaint or gave the information to pay compensation to the accused. The Magistrate can determine the amount of compensation, not exceeding the maximum fine the Magistrate is allowed to impose. If the person ordered to pay compensation does not do so, they may be imprisoned for up to thirty days.
If a person is imprisoned for not paying the compensation, certain laws will apply. If someone is ordered to pay compensation under this section, it does not exempt them from any civil or criminal liability for the complaint or information made by them. However, any amount paid to an accused person under this section will be taken into account in a subsequent civil suit related to the same matter.
If a complainant or informant is ordered to pay compensation exceeding one thousand rupees by a Magistrate of the second class, they have the right to appeal the order as if they had been convicted in a trial. If an order for payment of compensation is made in a case subject to appeal, the compensation cannot be paid until a certain period has elapsed or until the appeal has been decided. If the order is made in a case not subject to appeal, the compensation cannot be paid until one month has passed from the date of the order.
These rules apply to cases brought by either summons or warrants.

Summary Trial of Offences:

- Receiving or retaining stolen property

- Offenses like insult with intent to provoke a breach of the peace, criminal intimidation, abetment, and attempts to commit these offenses

Additionally, the magistrate, after giving the accused a fair chance to be heard, can conduct a summary trial for other offenses not punishable by death or imprisonment exceeding three years. (3) After receiving the application under sub-section (1), the Court shall issue notice
to the Public Prosecutor or the complainant of the case and to the accused to appear on the
date fixed for the case.
(4) When the Public Prosecutor or the complainant of the case and the accused
appear on the date fixed under sub-section (3), the Court shall examine the accused in
camera, where the other party in the case shall not be present, to satisfy itself that the
accused has filed the application voluntarily and where—
(a) the Court is satisfied that the application has been filed by the accused
voluntarily, it shall provide time, not exceeding sixty days, to the Public Prosecutor or
the complainant of the case and the accused to work out a mutually satisfactory
disposition of the case which may include giving to the victim by the accused the
compensation and other expenses during the case and thereafter fix the date for
further hearing of the case;
(b) the Court finds that the application has been filed involuntarily by the
accused or he has previously been convicted by a Court in a case in which he had
been charged with the same offence, it shall proceed further in accordance with the
provisions of this Sanhita from the stage such application has been filed under
sub-section (1).
simplified_text:
Plea Bargaining Process:

1. Timeframe: If a person is accused of an offense, they have thirty days from the date the charges are made to apply for plea bargaining in the court where the case is being tried.

2. Application Requirements: The application must describe the case, specify the offense, and be accompanied by a sworn affidavit from the accused. The affidavit should state that the accused has chosen plea bargaining voluntarily, understands the potential punishment for the offense, and has not been previously convicted in a similar case.

3. Notice: After receiving the application, the court will notify the Public Prosecutor or the complainant, and the accused, about the date for the case.

4. Examination: When all parties appear in court, the accused will be examined in private to ensure that the application for plea bargaining was voluntary. If satisfied, the court can provide up to sixty days for the parties to reach a mutually agreeable resolution, including compensation to the victim. If the application was not voluntary or if the accused has a previous conviction for the same offense, the court will proceed with the case as per the relevant legal provisions.

legal_text:
In working out a mutually satisfactory disposition under clause (a) of
sub-section (4) of section 290, the Court shall follow the following procedure, namely:—
(a) in a case instituted on a police report, the Court shall issue notice to the
Public Prosecutor, the police officer who has investigated the case, the accused and
the victim of the case to participate in the meeting to work out a satisfactory disposition
of the case:
Provided that throughout such process of working out a satisfactory disposition
of the case, it shall be the duty of the Court to ensure that the entire process is
completed voluntarily by the parties participating in the meeting:
Provided further that the accused, if he so desires, participate in such meeting
with his pleader, if any, engaged in the case;
(b) in a case instituted otherwise than on police report, the Court shall issue
notice to the accused and the victim of the case to participate in a meeting to work out
a satisfactory disposition of the case:
Provided that it shall be the duty of the Court to ensure, throughout such
process of working out a satisfactory disposition of the case, that it is completed
voluntarily by the parties participating in the meeting
Provided further that if the victim of the case or the accused so desires, he may
participate in such meeting with his pleader engaged in the case
simplified_text:
Simplified text:
When trying to come to an agreement under clause (a) of sub-section (4) of section 290, the Court will follow this process:
(a) In cases where the police have filed a report, the Court will send notice to the Public Prosecutor, the police officer who investigated the case, the accused, and the victim of the case to attend a meeting to work out an agreeable solution for the case. Throughout this process, the Court's responsibility is to ensure that all parties are participating in the meeting voluntarily. If the accused wishes, he can attend this meeting with his lawyer.
(b) In cases not started by the police, the Court will send notice to the accused and the victim to attend a meeting to work out an agreeable solution for the case. Throughout this process, the Court's responsibility is to ensure that both parties are participating voluntarily. If the victim or the accused wishes, they can attend this meeting with their lawyer.

legal_text:
Where in a meeting under section 291, a satisfactory disposition of the case has
been worked out, the Court shall prepare a report of such disposition which shall be signed
by the presiding officer of the Court and all other persons who participated in the meeting
and if no such disposition has been worked out, the Court shall record such observation
and proceed further in accordance with the provisions of this Sanhita from the stage the
application under sub-section (1) of section 290 has been filed in such case.
simplified_text: In a meeting under section 291, if a satisfactory solution to the case is reached, the Court will prepare a report on the decision. This report must be signed by the presiding officer of the Court and all others involved in the meeting. If no solution is reached, the Court will note this and continue in line with the rules of this Sanhita from the point when the application under sub-section (1) of section 290 was filed.

legal_text:
Where a satisfactory disposition of the case has been worked out under
section 292, the Court shall dispose of the case in the following manner, namely:—
(a) the Court shall award the compensation to the victim in accordance with the
disposition under section 292 and hear the parties on the quantum of the punishment,
releasing of the accused on probation of good conduct or after admonition under
section 401 or for dealing with the accused under the provisions of the Probation of
Offenders Act, 1958 or any other law for the time being in force and follow the procedure
specified in the succeeding clauses for imposing the punishment on the accused;
(b) after hearing the parties under clause (a), if the Court is of the view that
section 401 or the provisions of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 or any other law
for the time being in force are attracted in the case of the accused, it may release the
accused on probation or provide the benefit of any such law;
(c) after hearing the parties under clause (b), if the Court finds that minimum
punishment has been provided under the law for the offence committed by the accused,
it may sentence the accused to half of such minimum punishment, and where the
accused is a first-time offender and has not been convicted of any offence in the past,
it may sentence the accused to one-fourth of such minimum punishment;
(d) in case after hearing the parties under clause (b), the Court finds that the
offence committed by the accused is not covered under clause (b) or clause (c), then,
it may sentence the accused to one-fourth of the punishment provided or extendable,
as the case may be, for such offence and where the accused is a first-time offender
and has not been convicted of any offence in the past, it may sentence the accused to
one-sixth of the punishment provided or extendable, as the case may be, for such
offence.
simplified_text:
Resolving Cases: When a satisfactory resolution has been reached under section 292, the Court will handle the case as follows:
(a) The Court will award compensation to the victim based on the resolution reached under section 292. The Court will also hear from both parties regarding the punishment for the accused, including the option of releasing the accused on probation or after a warning under section 401, or applying the provisions of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958, or any other applicable law. The Court will follow the specified procedure for imposing the punishment on the accused.
(b) After hearing from both parties in clause (a), if the Court determines that section 401 or the provisions of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958, or any other applicable law apply to the accused, it may release the accused on probation or provide the benefit of such law.
(c) After hearing from both parties in clause (b), if the Court finds that the minimum punishment specified by law for the offence committed by the accused has been provided, it may sentence the accused to half of such minimum punishment. If the accused is a first-time offender with no past convictions, the Court may sentence the accused to one-fourth of such minimum punishment.
(d) If, after hearing from both parties in clause (b), the Court finds that the offence committed by the accused is not covered under clause (b) or (c), it may sentence the accused to one-fourth of the punishment provided or extendable for such offence. If the accused is a first-time offender with no past convictions, the Court may sentence the accused to one-sixth of the punishment provided or extendable for such offence.

The Court shall deliver its judgment in terms of section 293 in the open Court and

simplified_text: The Court will announce its decision in open court as per section 293, and the presiding officer will sign the judgment.

simplified_text: In order to carry out its duties as outlined in this Chapter, a Court has the authority to use all the powers it has regarding bail, trial of offenses, and other matters related to handling a case within the scope of this law.

legal_text:
The provisions of section 469 shall apply, for setting off the period of detention

simplified_text: Applying Time Served: The rules in section 469 will be used to subtract the time the accused has already spent in custody from the prison sentence given under this law, just like they are used for other prison sentences under this law.

The provisions of this Chapter shall have effect notwithstanding anything

simplified_text: Regardless of any existing law, any statements or facts provided by an accused person in an application for plea bargaining cannot be used for any purpose other than for the process of plea bargaining.

(1) Whenever, in the course of an inquiry, trial or proceeding under this Sanhita,
it appears to a Criminal Court,—
(a) that a person confined or detained in a prison should be brought before the
Court for answering to a charge of an offence, or for the purpose of any proceedings
against him; or
(b) that it is necessary for the ends of justice to examine such person as a
witness,
the Court may make an order requiring the officer in charge of the prison to produce
such person before the Court answering to the charge or for the purpose of such
proceeding or for giving evidence.
(2) Where an order under sub-section (1) is made by a Magistrate of the second class,
it shall not be forwarded to, or acted upon by, the officer in charge of the prison unless it is
countersigned by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, to whom such Magistrate is subordinate.
(3) Every order submitted for countersigning under sub-section (2) shall be
accompanied by a statement of the facts which, in the opinion of the Magistrate, render the

considering such statement, decline to countersign the order.
simplified_text:
Here is a simplified version of the legal text:

Bringing Detained Persons to Court

(1) If during an inquiry, trial, or legal proceeding, a Criminal Court believes that a person held in prison needs to appear before the Court to answer charges or provide evidence, the Court can order the prison officer to produce that person.

(2) If a second-class Magistrate issues the order, it must be approved by the Chief Judicial Magistrate before the prison officer is required to act on it.

(3) The second-class Magistrate must provide a statement to the Chief Judicial Magistrate explaining why the order is necessary, and the Chief Judicial Magistrate has the authority to refuse to approve the order after reviewing the statement.

legal_text:
3. (1) The State Government or the Central Government, as the case may be, may, at
any time, having regard to the matters specified in sub-section (2), by general or special
order, direct that any person or class of persons shall not be removed from the prison in
which he or they may be confined or detained, and thereupon, so long as the order remains
in force, no order made under section 302, whether before or after the order of the State
Government, shall have effect in respect of such person or class of persons.
(2) Before making an order under sub-section (1), the State Government or the Central
Government in the cases instituted by its central agency, as the case may be, shall have
regard to the following matters, namely:—
(a) the nature of the offence for which, or the grounds on which, the person or
class of persons has been ordered to be confined or detained in prison;
(b) the likelihood of the disturbance of public order if the person or class of

(c) the public interest, generally.
simplified_text:
Simplified Text:
Government Orders Restriction on Prison Removal
The State Government or the Central Government can, at any time, decide that a person or a group of people should not be moved from the prison where they are held, based on certain considerations. While this decision is in place, any other orders related to the person or group's detention cannot be enforced.
Before making this decision, the State Government or the Central Government must consider:
- The nature of the offense or grounds for which the person or group is detained.
- The potential for public disturbance if the person or group is allowed to leave prison.
- The overall public interest.

legal_text:
Where the person in respect of whom an order is made under section 302—
(a) is by reason of sickness or infirmity unfit to be removed from the prison; or
(b) is under committal for trial or under remand pending trial or pending a
preliminary investigation; or
(c) is in custody for a period which would expire before the expiration of the time
required for complying with the order and for taking him back to the prison in which
he is confined or detained; or
(d) is a person to whom an order made by the State Government under
section 303 applies,
the officer in charge of the prison shall abstain from carrying out the Court's order and
shall send to the Court a statement of reasons for so abstaining:
Provided that where the attendance of such person is required for giving evidence at
a place not more than twenty-five kilometres distance from the prison, the officer in charge
of the prison shall not so abstain for the reason mentioned in clause (b).
simplified_text:
When to Refrain from Carrying out a Court Order: If a person on whom a court order has been made under section 302 falls under any of the following situations:
   a) is too sick or infirm to be removed from the prison,
   b) is awaiting trial or under investigation,
   c) is in custody for a period that will end before the time needed to comply with the order and take him back to the prison where he is held, or
   d) is subject to an order made by the State Government under section 303,
then the prison officer must not carry out the court's order and must provide a statement to the court explaining the reasons for not doing so. However, if the person is required to appear as a witness at a location within 25 kilometers from the prison, the officer in charge of the prison is not required to refrain from carrying out the order.

legal_text:
Subject to the provisions of section 304, the officer in charge of the prison shall,
upon delivery of an order made under sub-section (1) of section 302 and duly countersigned,
where necessary, under sub-section (2) thereof, cause the person named in the order to be
taken to the Court in which his attendance is required, so as to be present there at the time
mentioned in the order, and shall cause him to be kept in custody in or near the Court until
he has been examined or until the Court authorises him to be taken back to the prison in
which he was confined or detained.
simplified_text: Transporting Prisoners to Court: The prison official in charge must ensure that a person named in an order, which has been properly approved, is brought to the court where their presence is needed. The person must be kept in custody near the court until they are examined or until the court allows them to be taken back to the prison they were held in.

legal_text:
. The provisions of this Chapter shall be without prejudice to the power of the
Court to issue, under section 319, a commission for the examination, as a witness, of any
person confined or detained in a prison; and the provisions of Part B of Chapter XXVI shall
apply in relation to the examination on commission of any such person in the prison as they
apply in relation to the examination on commission of any other person.
simplified_text: The rules in this section do not limit the court's authority to send a commission, under section 319, to question someone who is in prison as a witness. The rules in Part B of Chapter XXVI will be used for questioning someone in prison in the same way they are used for questioning any other person.

legal_text:
The State Government may determine what shall be, for purposes of this Sanhita,
the language of each Court within the State other than the High Court.
simplified_text: For this law, the state government can decide which language will be used in all courts in the state, except for the High Court.

legal_text:
Except as otherwise expressly provided, all evidence taken in the course of the
trial or other proceeding shall be taken in the presence of the accused, or, when his personal
attendance is dispensed with, in the presence of his pleader
Provided that where the evidence of a woman below the age of eighteen years who is

accused while at the same time ensuring the right of cross-examination of the accused.

proceeding under Chapter IX has been commenced under this Sanhita
simplified_text:
Recording Evidence in the Presence of the Accused: In general, all evidence collected during a trial or any other legal proceeding should be done in front of the accused person. If the accused person is not physically present, their lawyer should be present instead.

Protection for Underage Sexual Assault Victims: If the evidence of a girl below the age of eighteen who has been a victim of rape or another sexual offense needs to be recorded, the court can take steps to make sure that she does not have to face the accused directly. At the same time, the accused person still has the right to be cross-examined.

(1) In all summons-cases tried before a Magistrate, in all inquiries under sections
165 to 168 (both inclusive), and in all proceedings under section 493 otherwise than in the
course of a trial, the Magistrate shall, as the examination of each witness proceeds, make a
memorandum of the substance of the evidence in the language of the Court
Provided that if the Magistrate is unable to make such memorandum himself, he shall,

simplified_text:
1) When a Magistrate is handling summon-cases, inquiries, or certain proceedings, they must write down a summary of the evidence given by each witness in the language of the court. If the Magistrate cannot do it themselves, they must explain why and have it written down or dictated in the open court. 
2) The summary must be signed by the Magistrate and will be included in the official record of the case.

legal_text:
. (1) In all warrant-cases tried before a Magistrate, the evidence of each witness
shall, as his examination proceeds, be taken down in writing either by the Magistrate himself
or by his dictation in open Court or, where he is unable to do so owing to a physical or other
incapacity, under his direction and superintendence, by an officer of the Court appointed
by him in this behalf:
Provided that evidence of a witness under this sub-section may also be recorded by
audio-video electronic means in the presence of the advocate of the person accused of the
offence.
(2) Where the Magistrate causes the evidence to be taken down, he shall record a
certificate that the evidence could not be taken down by himself for the reasons referred to
in sub-section (1).
(3) Such evidence shall ordinarily be taken down in the form of a narrative; but the
Magistrate may, in his discretion take down, or cause to be taken down, any part of such
evidence in the form of question and answer.
(4) The evidence so taken down shall be signed by the Magistrate and shall form part

simplified_text: In criminal cases heard by a Magistrate, the testimony of each witness must be recorded in writing as they give their testimony. The Magistrate can write it down himself, have someone else write it down under his supervision, or use audio or video recording in the presence of the accused's lawyer. If the Magistrate is unable to write it down himself, he must state it in a certificate. The testimony is usually recorded as a narrative, but the Magistrate can choose to have it recorded as a question and answer session. Once recorded, the testimony is signed by the Magistrate and becomes part of the official record.

legal_text:
(1) In all trials before a Court of Session, the evidence of each witness shall, as
his examination proceeds, be taken down in writing either by the presiding Judge himself or
by his dictation in open Court, or under his direction and superintendence, by an officer of
the Court appointed by him in this behalf.
(2) Such evidence shall ordinarily be taken down in the form of a narrative, but the
presiding Judge may, in his discretion, take down, or cause to be taken down, any part of

(3) The evidence so taken down shall be signed by the presiding Judge and shall form

simplified_text:
Recording of Witness Testimony in Court: During trials at a Court of Session, the testimony of each witness will be recorded in writing. This can be done by the presiding Judge himself, by his verbal instruction in open Court, or by a Court-appointed officer under the Judge's oversight.

Format of Testimony: Normally, the testimony will be recorded in the form of a narrative. However, the presiding Judge has the discretion to record or have recorded any part of the testimony in a question and answer format.

Authentication and Inclusion in Record: The recorded testimony will be signed by the presiding Judge and will become a part of the official court record.

legal_text:
. In every case where evidence is taken down under sections 310 or 311,—
(a) if the witness gives evidence in the language of the Court, it shall be taken
down in that language;
(b) if he gives evidence in any other language, it may, if practicable, be taken

(c) where under clause (b) evidence is taken down in a language other than the

simplified_text:
Recording of Evidence: When a witness provides evidence in court, the following rules apply:

If the witness speaks in the language of the court, the evidence will be recorded in that language.
If the witness speaks in a different language, the evidence may be recorded in that language if possible. If that's not possible, a true translation in the language of the court will be prepared and signed by the Magistrate or presiding Judge as part of the record.
If evidence is initially recorded in a language other than the language of the court, a true translation in the language of the court will be prepared as soon as possible and will become part of the record, signed by the Magistrate or presiding Judge.
In cases where evidence is originally recorded in English and a translation in the language of the court is not requested by any party, the court may waive the requirement for such translation.

legal_text:
. (1) As the evidence of each witness taken under section 310 or section 311 is
completed, it shall be read over to him in the presence of the accused, if in attendance, or of
his pleader, if he appears by pleader, and shall, if necessary, be corrected.
(2) If the witness denies the correctness of any part of the evidence when the same is
read over to him, the Magistrate or presiding Judge may, instead of correcting the evidence,
make a memorandum thereon of the objection made to it by the witness and shall add such
remarks as he thinks necessary.
(3) If the record of the evidence is in a language different from that in which it has

simplified_text: Reading Evidence to Witnesses: After the evidence of each witness is taken, it must be read to them in the presence of the accused or their attorney. If the witness disagrees with any part of the evidence, the Magistrate or Judge can make a note of the objection instead of correcting the evidence. If the record of the evidence is in a different language from what the witness speaks, it must be interpreted to them in a language they understand.

legal_text:
(1) Whenever any evidence is given in a language not understood by the accused,
and he is present in Court in person, it shall be interpreted to him in open Court in a
language understood by him.
(2) If he appears by pleader and the evidence is given in a language other than the
language of the Court, and not understood by the pleader, it shall be interpreted to such
pleader in that language.
(3) When documents are put for the purpose of formal proof, it shall be in the discretion

simplified_text:
Simplified text:
1) If a person accused of a crime is in court and does not understand the language being spoken, the evidence will be translated into a language the person understands.
2) If the accused is represented by a lawyer and the evidence is in a language the lawyer does not understand, it will be translated for the lawyer.
3) The court may decide to translate only the parts of documents that are needed for formal proof.

legal_text:
When a presiding Judge or Magistrate has recorded the evidence of a witness,
he shall also record such remarks (if any) as he thinks material respecting the demeanour of
such witness whilst under examination.
simplified_text: After a judge or magistrate has taken down a witness's testimony, they must also record any comments they have about the behavior or attitude of the witness during the questioning.

legal_text:
(1) Whenever the accused is examined by any Magistrate, or by a Court of
Session, the whole of such examination, including every question put to him and every
answer given by him, shall be recorded in full by the presiding Judge or Magistrate himself
or where he is unable to do so owing to a physical or other incapacity, under his direction
and superintendence by an officer of the Court appointed by him in this behalf.
(2) The record shall, if practicable, be in the language in which the accused is examined
or, if that is not practicable, in the language of the Court.
(3) The record shall be shown or read to the accused, or, if he does not understand the
language in which it is written, shall be interpreted to him in a language which he understands,
and he shall be at liberty to explain or add to his answers.
(4) It shall thereafter be signed by the accused and by the Magistrate or presiding
Judge, who shall certify under his own hand that the examination was taken in his presence
and hearing and that the record contains a full and true account of the statement made by
the accused:
Provided that where the accused is in custody and is examined through electronic
communication, his signature shall be taken within seventy-two hours of such examination.
(5) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to apply to the examination of an accused
person in the course of a summary trial.
simplified_text:
Recording and Interpretation of Accused's Statements: When the accused person is questioned by a Judge or Magistrate, the entire conversation, including the questions asked and the answers given, must be written down. This will be done by the presiding Judge or Magistrate or by a court officer appointed by them.

Language of the Record: If possible, the conversation will be written down in the same language in which the accused is being questioned. If this is not possible, it will be written in the language of the Court.

Reading and Signing of the Record: The recorded conversation will be shown or read to the accused person. If the accused person does not understand the language in which it is written, it will be translated to a language they understand. The accused person will have the opportunity to explain or add to their answers. After this, the accused person and the Magistrate or presiding Judge will sign the record, and the Judge will certify that the conversation was recorded in their presence and that the record is accurate.

Signature of Accused Person in Custody: If the accused person is in custody and is questioned through electronic communication, their signature must be obtained within 72 hours of the questioning.

Exception for Summary Trials: These rules do not apply to the questioning of an accused person during a summary trial.

legal_text:
7. When the services of an interpreter are required by any Criminal Court for the
interpretation of any evidence or statement, he shall be bound to state the true interpretation

simplified_text: Interpreter Services: If a Criminal Court needs an interpreter to understand any evidence or statement, the interpreter must accurately explain the true meaning of that evidence or statement.

Every High Court may, by general rule, prescribe the manner in which the evidence

simplified_text:
High Court Rules on Taking Evidence:
The High Court can make rules about how witnesses give evidence and how the accused is questioned in cases before it. The evidence and questioning must follow these rules.

legal_text:
(1) Whenever, in the course of any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this
Sanhita, it appears to a Court or Magistrate that the examination of a witness is necessary

(1) A person who has once been tried by a Court of competent jurisdiction for an
offence and convicted or acquitted of such offence shall, while such conviction or acquittal
remains in force, not be liable to be tried again for the same offence, nor on the same facts
for any other offence for which a different charge from the one made against him might have
been made under sub-section (1) of section 244, or for which he might have been convicted
under sub-section (2) thereof.
(2) A person acquitted or convicted of any offence may be afterwards tried, with the
consent of the State Government, for any distinct offence for which a separate charge might
have been made against him at the former trial under sub-section (1) of section 243.
(3) A person convicted of any offence constituted by any act causing consequences
which, together with such act, constituted a different offence from that of which he was
convicted, may be afterwards tried for such last-mentioned offence, if the consequences
had not happened, or were not known to the Court to have happened, at the time when he
was convicted.
(4) A person acquitted convicted of any offence constituted by any acts may,
notwithstanding such acquittal or conviction, be subsequently charged with, and tried for,
any other offence constituted by the same acts which he may have committed if the Court
by which he was first tried was not competent to try the offence with which he is subsequently
charged.
(5) A person discharged under section 281 shall not be tried again for the same
offence except with the consent of the Court by which he was discharged or of any other
Court to which the first-mentioned Court is subordinate.
(6) Nothing in this section shall affect the provisions of section 26 of the General
Clauses Act, 1897 or of section 208 of this Sanhita.
Explanation.—The dismissal of a complaint, or the discharge of the accused, is not
an acquittal for the purposes of this section.
Illustrations.
(a) A is tried upon a charge of theft as a servant and aquitted. He cannot afterwards,
while the acquittal remains in force, be charged with theft as a servant, or, upon the same
facts, with theft simply, or with criminal breach of trust.
(b) A is tried for causing grievous hurt and convicted. The person injured afterwards
dies. A may be tried again for culpable homicide.
(c) A is charged before the Court of Session and convicted of the culpable homicide
of B. A may not afterwards be tried on the same facts for the murder of B.
(d) A is charged by a Magistrate of the first class with, and convicted by him of,
voluntarily causing hurt to B. A may not afterwards be tried for voluntarily causing grievous
hurt to B on the same facts, unless the case comes within sub-section (3) of this section.
(e) A is charged by a Magistrate of the second class with, and convicted by him of,
theft of property from the person of B. A may subsequently be charged with, and tried for,
robbery on the same facts.
(f) A, B and C are charged by a Magistrate of the first class with, and convicted by him
of, robbing D. A, B and C may afterwards be charged with, and tried for, dacoity on the same
facts
simplified_text:
Once a person has been tried in court and either convicted or acquitted of an offense, they cannot be tried again for the same offense or for any other offense based on the same facts. However, there are some exceptions to this rule.

If a person has been acquitted or convicted of an offense, with the consent of the State Government, they may be tried for a different offense for which a separate charge could have been made in the previous trial.

If a person has been convicted of an offense and the consequences of their actions constituted a different offense, they may be tried for the second offense if the consequences had not happened or were not known to the court at the time of the first trial.

If a person has been acquitted or convicted of an offense but the court that first tried them was not competent to try the particular offense, they can be subsequently charged and tried for the appropriate offense.

If a person has been discharged, they cannot be tried again for the same offense except with the consent of the court that discharged them or a higher court.

These rules do not affect certain provisions of the law. It's important to note that dismissing a complaint or discharging the accused does not count as an acquittal under these rules.

Examples:
- If someone is acquitted of theft as a servant, they cannot be charged with the same theft offense while the acquittal stands, nor can they be charged with a different theft offense based on the same facts.
- If someone is convicted of causing grievous hurt and the injured person later dies, they can be tried for culpable homicide.
- If someone is charged and convicted of culpable homicide, they cannot be tried for murder based on the same facts.
- Someone convicted of theft of property may later be charged with and tried for robbery based on the same facts.
- If three individuals are convicted of robbing someone, they may later be charged and tried for dacoity based on the same facts.

- If a representative of a corporation does not appear, the requirements mentioned in the previous point will not apply.

- If there is a question about whether a person appearing as the representative of a corporation is actually the representative, the court will make the decision.

3. (1) With a view to obtaining the evidence of any person supposed to have been
directly or indirectly concerned in or privy to an offence to which this section applies, the
Chief Judicial Magistrate at any stage of the investigation or inquiry into, or the trial of, the
offence, and the Magistrate of the first class inquiring into or trying the offence, at any
stage of the inquiry or trial, may tender a pardon to such person on condition of his making
a full and true disclosure of the whole of the circumstances within his knowledge relative to
the offence and to every other person concerned, whether as principal or abettor, in the
commission thereof.
(2) This section applies to—
(a) any offence triable exclusively by the Court of Session or by the Court of a
Special Judge appointed under any other law for the time being in force;
(b) any offence punishable with imprisonment which may extend to seven years
or with a more severe sentence.
(3) Every Magistrate who tenders a pardon under sub-section (1) shall record—
(a) his reasons for so doing;
(b) whether the tender was or was not accepted by the person to whom it was
made,
and shall, on application made by the accused, furnish him with a copy of such record free
of cost.
(4) Every person accepting a tender of pardon made under sub-section (1)—
(a) shall be examined as a witness in the Court of the Magistrate taking cognizance
of the offence and in the subsequent trial, if any;
(b) shall, unless he is already on bail, be detained in custody until the termination
of the trial.
(5) Where a person has accepted a tender of pardon made under sub-section (1) and
has been examined under sub-section (4), the Magistrate taking cognizance of the offence
shall, without making any further inquiry in the case—
(a) commit it for trial—
(i) to the Court of Session if the offence is triable exclusively by that
Court or if the Magistrate taking cognizance is the Chief Judicial Magistrate;
(ii) to a Court of Special Judge appointed under any other law for the time
being in force, if the offence is triable exclusively by that Court;
(b) in any other case, make over the case to the Chief Judicial Magistrate who
shall try the case himself
simplified_text:
Offer of Pardon:
If someone is believed to have been involved in a certain offense, the Chief Judicial Magistrate during the investigation or trial, and the Magistrate of the first class during the inquiry or trial, can offer them a pardon if they agree to fully and truthfully disclose all the facts they know about the offense and the involvement of any other person, whether as the main offender or an accomplice.

Applicability:
This rule applies to offenses that are exclusively tried by the Court of Session or by a Special Judge appointed under another law, as well as offenses punishable by imprisonment up to seven years or a more severe sentence.

Procedure and Consequences:

The magistrate offering the pardon must record the reasons for doing so and whether or not the person accepts the offer, and provide a copy of the record to the accused upon request, free of cost.

The person accepting the pardon will be examined as a witness in court and, if not already on bail, will be detained until the trial is over.

After the person has accepted the pardon and been examined, the Magistrate will either send the case to the Court of Session or to a Special Judge if it's exclusively triable by that court, or to the Chief Judicial Magistrate if it's not.

legal_text:

to which the commitment is made may, with a view to obtaining at the trial the evidence of
any person supposed to have been directly or indirectly concerned in, or privy to, any such

simplified_text: Offering Pardon before Judgment: The court handling a case can offer a pardon to anyone involved in the offense with the condition that they provide evidence during the trial. This offer can be made anytime between the case being committed to the court and the judgment being delivered.

Provided further that such person shall not be tried for the offence of giving false
evidence except with the sanction of the High Court, and nothing contained in section 215
or section 379 shall apply to that offence.
(2) Any statement made by such person accepting the tender of pardon and recorded
by a Magistrate under section 183 or by a Court under sub-section (4) of section 343 may be
given in evidence against him at such trial.
(3) At such trial, the accused shall be entitled to plead that he has complied with the
condition upon which such tender was made; in which case it shall be for the prosecution
to prove that the condition has not been complied with.
(4) At such trial, the Court shall—
(a) if it is a Court of Session, before the charge is read out and explained to the
accused;
(b) if it is the Court of a Magistrate, before the evidence of the witnesses for the
prosecution is taken,
ask the accused whether he pleads that he has complied with the conditions on which the
tender of pardon was made.
(5) If the accused does so plead, the Court shall record the plea and proceed with the
trial and it shall, before passing judgment in the case, find whether or not the accused has
complied with the conditions of the pardon, and, if it finds that he has so complied, it shall,

simplified_text:
Acceptance of Pardon and Trial: If someone accepts a pardon under a specific law, and the Public Prosecutor believes that the person has not followed the conditions of the pardon by purposefully hiding important information or providing false evidence, that person can be tried for the original offense for which the pardon was offered, any related offense, and the offense of giving false evidence. However, they cannot be tried together with any other accused individuals. Additionally, they cannot be tried for giving false evidence without the High Court's approval.

Statements made by the person when accepting the pardon can be used as evidence in their trial.

In the trial, the accused can argue that they have followed the conditions of the pardon, and then it is up to the prosecution to prove otherwise.

During the trial, the court will ask the accused about their plea before proceeding. If the accused pleads that they have followed the conditions of the pardon, the court will record the plea and continue with the trial. If it is found that the accused has followed the conditions of the pardon, the court will issue a judgment of acquittal.

it necessary or advisable to postpone the commencement of, or adjourn, any inquiry or trial,
it may, from time to time, for reasons to be recorded, postpone or adjourn the same on such
terms as it thinks fit, for such time as it considers reasonable, and may by a warrant remand
the accused if in custody:
Provided that no Court shall remand an accused person to custody under this
section for a term exceeding fifteen days at a time:
Provided further that when witnesses are in attendance, no adjournment or
postponement shall be granted, without examining them, except for special reasons to be
recorded in writing:
Provided also that no adjournment shall be granted for the purpose only of enabling
the accused person to show cause against the sentence proposed to be imposed on him:
Provided also that—
(a) no adjournment shall be granted at the request of a party, except where the
circumstances are beyond the control of that party;
(b) where the circumstances are beyond the control of a party, not more than
two adjournments may be granted by the Court after hearing the objections of the
other party and for the reasons to be recorded in writing;
(c) the fact that the advocate of a party is engaged in another Court, shall not be
a ground for adjournment;
(d) where a witness is present in Court but a party or his advocate is not present
or the party or his advocate though present in Court, is not ready to examine or
cross-examine the witness, the Court may, if thinks fit, record the statement of the
witness and pass such orders as it thinks fit dispensing with the examination-in-chief
or cross-examination of the witness, as the case may be.
Explanation 1.—If sufficient evidence has been obtained to raise a suspicion that
the accused may have committed an offence, and it appears likely that further evidence may
be obtained by a remand, this is a reasonable cause for a remand.
Explanation 2.—The terms on which an adjournment or postponement may be granted
include, in appropriate cases, the payment of costs by the prosecution or the accused
simplified_text:
Ensuring Prompt Proceedings: In every inquiry or trial, the process will continue day by day until all the present witnesses have been questioned, unless the Court decides an adjournment is necessary for specific reasons. For cases related to certain offenses, the inquiry or trial must be concluded within two months from the date of filing charges.

Flexibility in Postponing or Adjournment: If the Court, after taking notice of an offense, deems it necessary or advisable to delay or adjourn the inquiry or trial, it can do so for a reasonable period, with reasons recorded. The accused may be remanded in custody by warrant, but not for more than fifteen days at a time.

Conditions for Adjournment: The Court cannot postpone without examining witnesses, unless there are special reasons. The Court also has specific conditions for granting adjournments, and it can take necessary action if a party is not ready for the examination or cross-examination of a witness.

Explanation of Remand: If there is enough evidence to suspect the accused of an offense and it seems likely that further evidence may be obtained by remanding, this is considered a reasonable cause for remand.

Costs for Adjournment or Postponement: The terms for an adjournment or postponement may include the payment of costs by the prosecution or the accused in appropriate cases.

simplified_text: Summoning and Examining Witnesses: During any legal proceeding under this law, a court has the power to call someone to testify as a witness, question someone who is present but not summoned as a witness, or bring back and question someone who has already testified. The court must call, question, or recall someone if their testimony is crucial to making a fair decision in the case.

order relates shall be produced or shall attend at the time and place specified in such order
and shall give his specimen signatures or finger impressions or handwriting or voice sample:
Provided that no order shall be made under this section unless the person has at some

simplified_text: If a first-class Magistrate believes it is necessary for an investigation or legal process under this law, they can order any person, including a suspect, to provide signature specimens, fingerprints, handwriting samples, or voice samples. The person must comply with the order and provide the samples at the specified time and place. However, the Magistrate can only make this order if the person has been previously arrested in connection with the investigation or legal proceeding. The Magistrate can also order someone to provide samples even if they have not been arrested, but they must provide written reasons for doing so.

Transfer to Lower Court:
If, after considering the case and holding a hearing, the Judge believes there are grounds to suspect the accused has committed a non-exclusive offense, they can write up a charge and send the case to the Chief Judicial Magistrate or another first-class Judicial Magistrate. The accused will have to appear before the chosen Magistrate on a date set by the Judge, and the Magistrate will then conduct the trial following the procedure for such cases.

Exclusive Offense:
If the offense is exclusively triable by the Court, the Judge must write up a charge against the accused within 60 days from the first hearing on the charge.

Reading and Explaining Charge:

simplified_text: If the accused admits that they are guilty, the Judge will officially note the admission and has the option to declare them guilty.

The Judge can also, if the prosecution requests, issue any necessary orders to make sure witnesses come to court and any documents or evidence are provided.

When the appointed date arrives, the Judge will gather and consider all evidence presented in support of the prosecution. It is allowed for a witness to give their evidence using audio or video electronic methods.

The Judge has the authority to allow the evidence of a police officer or public servant to be recorded using audio or video electronic means.

Additionally, the Judge can decide to delay the cross-examination of a witness until after other witnesses have given their evidence, or recall a witness for further cross-examination.

Make Visits and Record Facts:

Any Judge or Magistrate has the authority to, at any point during an investigation, trial, or other legal process, visit and inspect a location where an offense is said to have occurred, or any other location necessary to properly understand the evidence presented during the investigation or trial. After the visit, they must promptly make a written record of any important observations.

Inclusion in Record and Provision of Copy:

352. (1) Any party to a proceeding may, as soon as may be, after the close of his 20 evidence, address concise oral arguments, and may, before he concludes the oral arguments,

simplified_text:
Summary:
After presenting their evidence, any party involved in a legal proceeding can give brief oral arguments and submit a concise written memorandum to the court, outlining their case under distinct headings. A copy of the memorandum must be provided to the opposing party. The court will not grant an adjournment for filing written arguments unless there are specific reasons for doing so. The court has the authority to regulate oral arguments if they are not deemed concise or relevant.

Provided that—
(a) he shall not be called as a witness except on his own request in writing;
(b) his failure to give evidence shall not be made the subject of any comment by any of the parties or the Court or give rise to any presumption against himself or any person charged together with him that the same trial.
(2) Any person against whom proceedings are instituted in any Criminal Court under section 101, or section 126 or section 127, or section 128, or section 129, or under Chapter X
or under Part B, Part C or Part D of Chapter XI, may offer himself as a witness in such proceedings:

simplified_text: Witness Testimony: A person accused of a crime in court can choose to testify and give evidence under oath to disprove the charges against them or anyone else on trial with them. However, they can only testify if they request to do so in writing. If they choose not to testify, nobody in the court can comment on it or assume anything against them or other defendants. The same rules apply for a person involved in proceedings under specific sections or chapters. If they choose not to testify, no one can make any comments or assumptions because of their decision.

legal_text: 354. Except as provided in sections 343 and 344, no influence, by means of any promise or threat or otherwise, shall be used to an accused person to induce him to disclose or withhold any matter within his knowledge.

simplified_text:
Attendance of Accused: During any investigation or trial under this law, if the Judge or Magistrate believes, for reasons they write down, that the accused's presence in court is not needed for the sake of justice, or if the accused is disrupting the court proceedings consistently, and if the accused has a lawyer, the Judge or Magistrate can allow the accused not to be present and continue with the investigation or trial. They can also, at a later stage, decide that the accused must attend in person.

If the accused does not have a lawyer, or if the Judge or Magistrate believes the person's attendance is necessary, they can, if they think it's appropriate and they give reasons for it, either delay the investigation or trial, or order that the case for that accused person be dealt with separately.

Note: This section considers the accused person's attendance to include attending through audio or video electronic methods.

simplified_text:
Bringing Additional Offenders to Trial:
  
When, during an investigation or trial of a crime, it becomes apparent that someone other than the accused has also committed an offense that could be tried together with the accused, the Court can take action against that person for the offense they seem to have committed.

If that person is not attending the Court, they can be arrested or summoned as necessary for this purpose. 

Whether or not under arrest or summons, a person attending the Court can be held by the Court for the investigation or trial of the offense they appear to have committed.

In cases where the Court proceeds against a person under the first point, the proceedings for that person will start again, and the witnesses will be re-heard. The case may continue as if that person had been accused when the Court first took notice of the offense under investigation or trial.
