496. When the person required by any Court, or officer to execute a bond is a minor,
such Court or officer may accept, in lieu thereof, a bond executed by a surety or sureties
only.
simplified_text: When a minor is required to execute a bond by a court or officer, the court or officer can accept a bond executed by a surety or sureties only instead.

legal_text:
497. All orders passed under section 493 shall be appealable,—
(i) in the case of an order made by a Magistrate, to the Sessions Judge;
(ii) in the case of an order made by a Court of Session, to the Court to which an
appeal lies from an order made by such Court.
simplified_text:
All decisions made under section 493 can be appealed:
- If a Magistrate issues an order, it can be appealed to the Sessions Judge.
- If a Court of Session issues an order, it can be appealed to the court that hears appeals from that Court.

legal_text:
498. The High Court or Court of Sessions may direct any Magistrate to levy the
amount due on a bond for appearance or attendance at such High Court or Court of Session.
simplified_text: Directing Magistrates to Collect Bond Amount: The High Court or Court of Sessions can instruct a Magistrate to collect the owed amount on a bond for appearing or attending the High Court or Court of Session.

legal_text:
499. When any property is produced before any Criminal Court or the Magistrate
empowered to take cognizance or commit the case for trial during any investigation, inquiry
or trial, the Court or the Magistrate may make such order as it thinks fit for the proper
custody of such property pending the conclusion of the investigation, inquiry or trial, and,
if the property is subject to speedy and natural decay, or if it is otherwise expedient so to do,
the Court or the Magistrate may, after recording such evidence as it thinks necessary, order
it to be sold or otherwise disposed of.
Explanation.—For the purposes of this section, "property" includes—
(a) property of any kind or document which is produced before the Court or
which is in its custody;
(b) any property regarding which an offence appears to have been committed
or which appears to have been used for the commission of any offence.
(2) The Court or the Magistrate shall, within a period of fourteen days from the
production of the property referred to in sub-section (1) before it, prepare a statement of
such property containing its description in such form and manner as the State Government
may, by rules, provide.
(3) The Court or the Magistrate shall cause to be taken the photograph and if necessary,
videograph on mobile phone or any electronic media, of the property referred to in
sub-section (1).
(4) The statement prepared under sub-section (2) and the photograph or the
videography taken under sub-section (3) shall be used as evidence in any inquiry, trial or
other proceeding under the Sanhita.
(5) The Court or the Magistrate shall, within a period of thirty days after the statement
has been prepared under sub-section (2) and the photograph or the videography has been
taken under sub-section (3), order the disposal, destruction, confiscation or delivery of the
property in the manner specified hereinafter.
simplified_text:
Custody and Disposal of Property: When any property is presented in a Criminal Court or before a Magistrate during an investigation, inquiry, or trial, the Court or Magistrate can make an appropriate decision to keep the property safe until the investigation, inquiry, or trial is complete. If the property is likely to decay quickly or if it is necessary for other reasons, the Court or Magistrate can, after gathering relevant evidence, order the property to be sold or disposed of in another way.
  
Definition of Property: For the purpose of this section, "property" includes any type of property or document presented in the Court, or in its custody, and any property that seems to be related to a crime or used in the commission of a crime.

Statement and Documentation: Within 14 days of the property being presented, the Court or Magistrate must prepare a description of the property in a format specified by the State Government. The Court or Magistrate must also take a photograph or video of the property.

Use of Evidence: The statement prepared and the photograph or video taken will be used as evidence in any inquiry, trial, or legal proceedings.

Disposal of Property: Within 30 days of preparing the statement and taking the photograph or video, the Court or Magistrate will decide on the disposal, destruction, confiscation, or delivery of the property as specified by the law.

legal_text:
500. (1) When an investigation, inquiry or trial in any Criminal Court is concluded, the
Court or the Magistrate may make such order as it thinks fit for the disposal, by destruction,
confiscation or delivery to any person claiming to be entitled to possession thereof or
otherwise, of any property or document produced before it or in its custody, or regarding
which any offence appears to have been committed, or which has been used for the
commission of any offence.
(2) An order may be made under sub-section (1) for the delivery of any property to
any person claiming to be entitled to the possession thereof, without any condition or on
condition that he executes a bond, with or without securities, to the satisfaction of the
Court or the Magistrate, engaging to restore such property to the Court if the order made
under sub-section (1) is modified or set aside on appeal or revision.
(3) A Court of Session may, instead of itself making an order under sub-section (1),
direct the property to be delivered to the Chief Judicial Magistrate, who shall thereupon
deal with it in the manner provided in sections 505, 506 and 507.
(4) Except where the property is livestock or is subject to speedy and natural decay,
or where a bond has been executed in pursuance of sub-section (2), an order made under
sub-section (1) shall not be carried out for two months, or when an appeal is presented,
until such appeal has been disposed of.
(5) In this section, the term "property" includes, in the case of property regarding
which an offence appears to have been committed, not only such property as has been
originally in the possession or under the control of any party, but also any property into or
for which the same may have been converted or exchanged, and anything acquired by such
conversion or exchange, whether immediately or otherwise.
simplified_text: Disposal of Property: When a criminal investigation, inquiry, or trial concludes in any Criminal Court, the Court or the Magistrate may issue an order for the destruction, confiscation, or delivery of any property or document that was presented before it or is in its custody, or that appears to be connected to an offense or used to commit an offense. The order may require the delivery of property to a person claiming ownership, with or without conditions such as providing a bond, which must be returned to the Court if the order is changed or canceled on appeal. If the Court of Session doesn't make the order, it can direct the property to be delivered to the Chief Judicial Magistrate, who will handle it according to specific provisions. The order for disposal of property is usually delayed for two months, or until the disposal is appealed, except for cases involving livestock or items that decay quickly, or if a bond has been provided. The term "property" in this section includes not only the original property in the possession or control of any party, but also anything it has been converted into or exchanged for, and anything acquired through the conversion or exchange.

legal_text:
501. When any person is convicted of any offence which includes, or amounts to,
theft or receiving stolen property, and it is proved that any other person bought the stolen
property from him without knowing or having reason to believe that the same was stolen,
and that any money has on his arrest been taken out of the possession of the convicted
person, the Court may, on the application of such purchaser and on the restitution of the
stolen property to the person entitled to the possession thereof, order that out of such
money a sum not exceeding the price paid by such purchaser be delivered to him within six
months from the date of such order
simplified_text: Compensation for Innocent Purchasers: If someone is convicted of theft or receiving stolen property, and it is proven that another person bought the stolen property without knowing it was stolen, the Court may, upon the application of the purchaser and the return of the stolen property to its rightful owner, order that a portion of any money taken from the convicted person be given to the innocent purchaser, up to the amount they paid, within six months of the order.

legal_text:
502. (1) Any person aggrieved by an order made by a Court under section 500 or
section 501, may appeal against it to the Court to which appeals ordinarily lie from convictions
by the former Court.
(2) On such appeal, the Appellate Court may direct the order to be stayed pending
disposal of the appeal, or may modify, alter or annul the order and make any further orders
that may be just.
(3) The powers referred to in sub-section (2) may also be exercised by a Court of
appeal, confirmation or revision while dealing with the case in which the order referred to in
sub-section (1) was made.
simplified_text:
Appealing Court Orders: If someone is unhappy with an order made by a Court under section 500 or section 501, they can appeal to the Court that usually handles appeals from the Court that issued the original order.

Appellate Court Decisions: The Appellate Court has the power to suspend the original order while the appeal is being considered. Additionally, they can change, adjust, or cancel the order and also issue any other necessary orders.

Court Powers: The powers mentioned in subsection (2) can also be used by an appellate, confirmation, or revision court when they are handling the case in which the original order was issued.

legal_text:
503. (1) On a conviction under section 292, section 293, section 354 of the Bhartiya
Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the Court may order the destruction of all the copies of the thing in
respect of which the conviction was had, and which are in the custody of the Court or
remain in the possession or power of the person convicted.
(2) The Court may, in like manner, on a conviction under section 272, section 273,
section 274 or section 275 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, order the food, drink, drug
or medical preparation in respect of which the conviction was had, to be destroyed.
simplified_text: Ordering Destruction of Illegal Items: If someone is found guilty under specific sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the Court has the authority to order the destruction of all copies of the item related to the conviction that are in the custody of the Court or still in the possession of the convicted person. Additionally, the Court has the power to order the destruction of food, drink, drugs, or medical preparations related to certain convictions under the same law.

legal_text:
504. (1) When a person is convicted of an offence by use of criminal force or show of
force or by criminal intimidation, and it appears to the Court that, by such use of force or
show of force or intimidation, any person has been dispossessed of any immovable property,
the Court may, if it thinks fit, order that possession of the same be restored to that person
after evicting by force, if necessary, any other person who may be in possession of the
property:
Provided that no such order shall be made by the Court more than one month after the
date of the conviction.
(2) Where the Court trying the offence has not made an order under sub-section (1),
the Court of appeal, confirmation or revision may, if it thinks fit, make such order while
disposing of the appeal, reference or revision, as the case may be.
(3) Where an order has been made under sub-section (1), the provisions of
section 502 shall apply in relation thereto as they apply in relation to an order under section 501.
(4) No order made under this section shall prejudice any right or interest to or in such
immovable property which any person may be able to establish in a civil suit.
simplified_text:
Restoring Possession: If a person is convicted of a crime involving the use of force or intimidation, and it's found that someone has been deprived of property as a result, the Court has the authority to order the return of that property to the rightful person. They can use force to evict anyone else in possession of the property if necessary, but this order must be made within one month of the conviction.

Appeals and Revisions: If the original court did not make the possession order, the Court of appeal, confirmation, or revision can do so during the appeal process. If an order is made, it will be subject to the same rules as outlined in section 502. Furthermore, any order made under this section does not affect anyone's rights or interests in the property as they may be able to establish in a separate civil case.

legal_text:
505. (1) Whenever the seizure of property by any police officer is reported to a
Magistrate under the provisions of this Sanhita, and such property is not produced before
a Criminal Court during an inquiry or trial, the Magistrate may make such order as he thinks
fit respecting the disposal of such property or the delivery of such property to the person
entitled to the possession thereof, or if such person cannot be ascertained, respecting the
custody and production of such property.
(2) If the person so entitled is known, the Magistrate may order the property to be
delivered to him on such conditions (if any) as the Magistrate thinks fit and if such person
is unknown, the Magistrate may detain it and shall, in such case, issue a proclamation
specifying the articles of which such property consists, and requiring any person who may
have a claim thereto, to appear before him and establish his claim within six months from the
date of such proclamation.
simplified_text: Disposal of Seized Property: If a police officer seizes property and it is not presented in a criminal court during an investigation or trial, a magistrate can decide what to do with the property. This may include giving it to the rightful owner, if known, or keeping it safe until the owner is identified. If the owner is not known, the magistrate can issue a public notice asking anyone who claims the property to come forward within six months.

legal_text:
506. (1) If no person within such period establishes his claim to such property, and if
the person in whose possession such property was found is unable to show that it was
legally acquired by him, the Magistrate may by order direct that such property shall be at
the disposal of the State Government and may be sold by that Government and the proceeds
of such sale shall be dealt with in such manner as the State Government may, by rules,
provide.
(2) An appeal shall lie against any such order to the Court to which appeals ordinarily
lie from convictions by the Magistrate.
simplified_text: Disposal of Unclaimed Property: If no one claims the property within a certain period, and the person in possession of the property cannot prove that it was legally obtained, the Magistrate can order that the property be given to the state government. The state government can then sell the property and use the proceeds according to its rules. An appeal can be made against this order to the regular appeals court for cases handled by the Magistrate.

legal_text:
507. If the person entitled to the possession of such property is unknown or absent
and the property is subject to speedy and natural decay, or if the Magistrate to whom its
seizure is reported is of opinion that its sale would be for the benefit of the owner, or that the
value of such property is less than ten thousand rupees, the Magistrate may at any time
direct it to be sold; and the provisions of sections 505 and 506 shall, as nearly as may be
practicable, apply to the net proceeds of such sale.
simplified_text: If the owner of the property cannot be identified or is not present, and if the property is at risk of decay, or if the Magistrate believes that selling the property would benefit the owner, or if the value of the property is less than ten thousand rupees, the Magistrate can order the property to be sold. The rules in sections 505 and 506 will be applied to the money received from the sale as much as possible.

If a Magistrate mistakenly, but in good faith, does something he is not legally allowed to do, like issue a search warrant or order a police investigation, his actions will not be invalidated just because he did not have the legal authority to do so.

Unauthorized Actions by Magistrate:
If a Magistrate, who is not legally authorized to do so, takes any of the following actions:
- Seizes and sells property under section 85
- Issues a search warrant for items held by postal or telegraph authorities
- Requires security for maintaining peace or good behavior
- Releases a person from the obligation to maintain good behavior
- Cancels a bond to maintain peace
- Issues a maintenance order
- Issues an order regarding a local nuisance under section 152
- Prohibits the repetition or continuation of a public nuisance under section 162
- Makes an order under Part C or Part D of Chapter XI
- Takes action on an offense under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 210
- Conducts a trial
- Conducts a summary trial
- Imposes a sentence under section 364 based on proceedings recorded by another Magistrate
- Makes a decision on an appeal
- Calls for proceedings under section 438
- Revises an order passed under section 493
Then, those actions taken by the Magistrate will be invalid.

legal_text:
510. No finding, sentence or order of any Criminal Court shall be set aside merely on
the ground that the inquiry, trial or other proceedings in the course of which it was arrived
at or passed, took place in a wrong sessions division, district, sub-division or other local
area, unless it appears that such error has in fact occasioned a failure of justice.
simplified_text: Setting Aside Criminal Court Decisions: A finding, sentence, or order of any Criminal Court cannot be overturned just because the proceedings took place in the wrong local area. The decision can only be set aside if it is proven that the error actually caused an injustice.

legal_text:
511. (1) If any Court before which a confession or other statement of an accused
person recorded, or purporting to be recorded under section 183 or section 316, is tendered,
or has been received, in evidence finds that any of the provisions of either of such sections
have not been complied with by the Magistrate recording the statement, it may,
notwithstanding anything contained in section 94 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adiniyam 2023,
take evidence in regard to such non-compliance, and may, if satisfied that such
non-compliance has not injured the accused in his defence on the merits and that he duly
made the statement recorded, admit such statement.
(2) The provisions of this section apply to Courts of appeal, reference and revision.
simplified_text: If a confession or statement from an accused person is recorded under specific legal sections and the Court finds that the Magistrate did not follow the proper procedures in recording the statement, the Court has the authority to take additional evidence regarding the non-compliance. If the Court determines that the accused was not harmed in their defense and that the statement was made voluntarily, the statement may still be admitted as evidence. This rule applies to appellate, reference, and revision Courts.

legal_text:
512. (1) No finding, sentence or order by a Court of competent jurisdiction shall be
deemed invalid merely on the ground that no charge was framed or on the ground of any
error, omission or irregularity in the charge including any misjoinder of charges, unless, in
the opinion of the Court of appeal, confirmation or revision, a failure of justice has in fact
been occasioned thereby.
(2) If the Court of appeal, confirmation or revision, is of opinion that a failure of justice
has in fact been occasioned, it may,—
(a) in the case of an omission to frame a charge, order that a charge be framed,
and that the trial be recommended from the point immediately after the framing of the
charge;
(b) in the case of an error, omission or irregularity in the charge, direct a new trial
to be had upon a charge framed in whatever manner it thinks fit:
Provided that if the Court is of opinion that the facts of the case are such that no valid
charge could be preferred against the accused in respect of the facts proved, it shall quash
the conviction.
simplified_text:
Challenging Court Decisions: A ruling or order from a competent court won't be considered invalid just because a charge was not formally presented or because there were errors or irregularities in the charge, such as combining different charges together. However, if the Court of appeal, confirmation, or revision believes that a miscarriage of justice has occurred, it has the power to:
(a) if a charge was not framed, instruct that a charge is framed and a new trial is conducted from that point forward; or
(b) if there were errors, omissions, or irregularities in the charge, order a new trial with a charge framed in a different manner.

Note: If the Court determines that no valid charge could have been filed based on the facts, it will cancel the conviction.

legal_text:
513. (1) Subject to the provisions hereinbefore contained, no finding, sentence or
order passed by a Court of competent jurisdiction shall be reversed or altered by a Court of
appeal, confirmation of revision on account of any error, omission or irregularity in the
complaint, summons, warrant, proclamation, order, judgment or other proceedings before or
during trial or in any inquiry or other proceedings under this Sanhita, or any error, or
irregularity in any sanction for the prosecution, unless in the opinion of that Court, a failure
of justice has in fact been occasioned thereby.
(2) In determining whether any error, omission or irregularity in any proceeding under
this Sanhita, or any error, or irregularity in any sanction for the prosecution has occasioned
a failure of justice, the Court shall have regard to the fact whether the objection could and
should have been raised at an earlier stage in the proceedings.
simplified_text:
Simplified text:
 
Court Decisions:
A Court of appeal, confirmation, or revision cannot reverse or change a finding, sentence, or order made by a competent court due to any errors or irregularities in the legal process, unless the Court believes that a failure of justice has actually occurred.
Determining Failure of Justice:
When deciding if an error or irregularity has caused a failure of justice, the Court will consider whether the objection could and should have been raised earlier in the legal process.

legal_text:
514. No attachment made under this Sanhita shall be deemed unlawful, nor shall any
person making the same be deemed a trespasser, on account of any defect or want of form
in the summons, conviction, writ of attachment or other proceedings relating thereto.
simplified_text: 514. No attachment made under this law shall be considered illegal, and no person making the attachment will be considered a trespasser due to any errors or lack of proper form in the legal documents related to the attachment process.

legal_text:
515. For the purposes of this Chapter, unless the context otherwise requires, "period
of limitation" means the period specified in section 517 for taking cognizance of an offence.
simplified_text: Defining Period of Limitation: In this section, "period of limitation" refers to the duration specified in section 517 for prosecuting an offense.

legal_text:
516. (1) Except as otherwise provided in this Sanhita, no Court shall take cognizance
of an offence of the category specified in sub-section (2), after the expiry of the period of
limitation.
(2) The period of limitation shall be—
(a) six months, if the offence is punishable with fine only;
(b) one year, if the offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term not
exceeding one year;
(c) three years, if the offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term
exceeding one year but not exceeding three years.
(3) For the purposes of this section, the period of limitation, in relation to offences
which may be tried together, shall be determined with reference to the offence which is
punishable with the more severe punishment or, as the case may be, the most severe
punishment.
Explanation.—For the purpose of computing the period of limitation, the relevant
date shall be the date of filing complaint under section 223 or the date of recording of
information under section 173.
simplified_text:
Time Limit for Taking Legal Action: Except as provided in this law, no court can hear a certain type of offense after a certain time limit has passed.

Time Limits:
- 6 months if the offense is punishable by a fine only
- 1 year if the offense is punishable by up to 1 year in prison
- 3 years if the offense is punishable by more than 1 but less than 3 years in prison

Determining the Time Limit: If multiple offenses are related, the time limit is based on the offense with the harshest punishment.

Explanation: The relevant date for calculating the time limit is the date when a complaint is filed or when information is recorded.

legal_text:
517. (1) The period of limitation, in relation to an offender, shall commence,—
(a) on the date of the offence; or
(b) where the commission of the offence was not known to the person aggrieved
by the offence or to any police officer, the first day on which such offence comes to
the knowledge of such person or to any police officer, whichever is earlier; or
(c) where it is not known by whom the offence was committed, the first day on
which the identity of the offender is known to the person aggrieved by the offence or
to the police officer making investigation into the offence, whichever is earlier.
(2) In computing the said period, the day from which such period is to be computed
shall be excluded.
simplified_text:
Limitation Period: The time limit for prosecuting an offender starts from:

  the date of the offense, or
  the first day when the victim or any police officer becomes aware of the offense, or
  the first day when the offender's identity is known to the victim or the investigating police officer, whichever comes first.

When calculating this time limit, the starting day is not included.

legal_text:
518. (1) In computing the period of limitation, the time during which any person has
been prosecuting with due diligence another prosecution, whether in a Court of first instance
or in a Court of appeal or revision, against the offender, shall be excluded:
Provided that no such exclusion shall be made unless the prosecution relates to the
same facts and is prosecuted in good faith in a Court which from defect of jurisdiction or
other cause of a like nature, is unable to entertain it.
(2) Where the institution of the prosecution in respect of an offence has been stayed
by an injunction or order, then, in computing the period of limitation, the period of the
continuance of the injunction or order, the day on which it was issued or made, and the day
on which it was withdrawn, shall be excluded.
(3) Where notice of prosecution for an offence has been given, or where, under any
law for the time being in force, the previous consent or sanction of the Government or any
other authority is required for the institution of any prosecution for an offence, then, in
computing the period of limitation, the period of such notice or, as the case may be, the time
required for obtaining such consent or sanction shall be excluded.
Explanation.—In computing the time required for obtaining the consent or sanction
of the Government or any other authority, the date on which the application was made for
obtaining the consent or sanction and the date of receipt of the order of the Government or
other authority shall both be excluded.
(4) In computing the period of limitation, the time during which the offender—
(a) has been absent from India or from any territory outside India which is
under the administration of the Central Government; or
(b) has avoided arrest by absconding or concealing himself,
shall be excluded.
simplified_text:
Time Limit Exceptions in Legal Proceedings:

1. Prosecution Delays: If someone is actively pursuing legal action against an offender in court, the time taken for such legal action will not be counted towards the time limit for filing a case, provided that the legal action is genuine and related to the same facts.

2. Stayed Prosecution: If legal proceedings have been temporarily stopped due to a court order, the time during which the proceedings are paused and the day the order is issued or withdrawn will not be counted towards the time limit for filing a case.

3. Notice or Consent Requirements: If a notice of prosecution is given, or if government consent or sanction is required for initiating legal proceedings, the time taken for these notifications or obtaining of consent will not be counted towards the time limit for filing a case.

4. Offender's Absence or Avoidance: The time during which the offender is absent from India or avoiding arrest by absconding will not be counted towards the time limit for filing a case.

legal_text:
519. Where the period of limitation expires on a day when the Court is closed, the
Court may take cognizance on the day on which the Court reopens.
Explanation.—A Court shall be deemed to be closed on any day within the meaning
of this section, if, during its normal working hours, it remains closed on that day.
simplified_text:
Simplified text:
If the time limit for filing a case ends on a day when the Court is closed, the Court can accept the case when it reopens. A Court is considered closed if it remains closed during its normal working hours on any particular day.

legal_text:
520. In the case of a continuing offence, a fresh period of limitation shall begin to run
at every moment of the time during which the offence continues.
simplified_text: Continuing Offence: If an offence is ongoing, the time limit for taking legal action will restart at every moment that the offence continues.

legal_text:
521. Notwithstanding anything contained in the foregoing provisions of this Chapter,
any Court may take cognizance of an offence after the expiry of the period of limitation, if it
is satisfied on the facts and in the circumstances of the case that the delay has been
properly explained or that it is necessary so to do in the interests of justice.
simplified_text:
Legal Simplified Text:

Even if the time limit for taking action on a crime has passed, a court can still decide to take up the case if it believes there is a good reason for the delay or if it is necessary for the sake of justice.

legal_text:
522. When an offence is tried by the High Court otherwise than under section 448, it
shall, in the trial of the offence, observe the same procedure as a Court of Sessions would
observe if it were trying the case.
simplified_text:
Simplified text:
  If a crime is tried in the High Court, except under section 448, the court must follow the same procedures as a Sessions Court would for the trial.

legal_text:
523. (1) The Central Government may make rules consistent with this Sanhita and the
Army Act, 1950, the Navy Act, 1957, and the Air Force Act, 1950, and any other law, relating
to the Armed Forces of the Union, for the time being in force, as to cases in which persons
subject to military, naval or air-force law, or such other law, shall be tried by a Court to which
this Sanhita applies, or by a Court-martial; and when any person is brought before a Magistrate
and charged with an offence for which he is liable to be tried either by a Court to which this
Sanhita applies or by a Court-martial, such Magistrate shall have regard to such rules, and
shall in proper cases deliver him, together with a statement of the offence of which he is
accused, to the commanding officer of the unit to which he belongs, or to the commanding
officer of the nearest military, naval or air-force station, as the case may be, for the purpose
of being tried by a Court-martial.
Explanation.—In this section—
(a) "Unit" includes a regiment, corps, ship, detachment, group, battalion or
Company;
(b) "Court-martial" includes any Tribunal with the powers similar to those of a
Court-martial constituted under the relevant law applicable to the Armed Forces of
the Union.
(2) Every Magistrate shall, on receiving a written application for that purpose by the
commanding officer of any unit or body of soldiers, sailors or airmen stationed or employed
at any such place, use his utmost endeavours to apprehend and secure any person accused
of such offence.
(3) A High Court may, if it thinks fit, direct that a prisoner detained in any jail situate
within the State be brought before a Court-martial for trial or to be examined touching any
matter pending before the Court-martial.
simplified_text:
Court Proceedings for Military Personnel:

The central government has the authority to create rules in line with this law and other related laws regarding the armed forces. These rules determine whether military personnel should be tried in a civilian court or a military court for certain offenses. If a person is charged with an offense that could be tried in either a civilian court or a military court, the magistrate must follow these rules. In some cases, the magistrate may deliver the accused, along with a statement of the offense, to their commanding officer for trial by a military court.

Explanation: In this section:
- "Unit" includes various military groups and divisions.
- "Court-martial" includes any tribunal with similar powers to a military court under the relevant laws for the armed forces.

Additionally, every magistrate must make every effort to arrest and detain any person accused of an offense who is stationed or employed at a military location when requested by the commanding officer.

Furthermore, a High Court has the authority to order that a prisoner held in a state jail be brought before a military court for trial or examination relating to an ongoing matter before the military court.

legal_text:
524. Subject to the power conferred by article 227 of the Constitution, the forms set
forth in the Second Schedule, with such variations as the circumstances of each case
require, may be used for the respective purposes therein mentioned, and if used shall be
sufficient.
simplified_text: Using Approved Forms: Unless specifically allowed by article 227 of the Constitution, the forms listed in the Second Schedule can be used for their intended purposes. If used, these forms will be considered valid, as long as they are adjusted as needed for each particular situation.

legal_text:
525. (1) Every High Court may, with the previous approval of the State Government,
make rules—
(a) as to the persons who may be permitted to act as petition-writers in the
Criminal Courts subordinate to it;
(b) regulating the issue of licences to such persons, the conduct of business by
them, and the scale of fees to be charged by them;
(c) providing a penalty for a contravention of any of the rules so made and
determining the authority by which such contravention may be investigated and the
penalties imposed;
(d) any other matter which is required to be, or may be, provided by rules made
by the State Government.
(2) All rules made under this section shall be published in the Official Gazette.
simplified_text:
High Court Rules on Petition-Writers: Each High Court, with prior approval from the State Government, can create regulations regarding the following:
1. Who is allowed to work as petition-writers in its subordinate Criminal Courts
2. Issuing licenses to these individuals, their business conduct, and the fees they can charge
3. Imposing penalties for breaking these rules and determining the authority to investigate and enforce these penalties
4. Any other matters that the State Government requires or permits to be addressed through rules.
All rules created under this section must be published in the Official Gazette.

legal_text:
526. If the Legislative Assembly of a State by a resolution so permits, the State
Government may, after consultation with the High Court, by notification, direct that references
in sections 127, 128, 129, 164 and 166 to an Executive Magistrate shall be construed as
references to a Judicial Magistrate of the first class.
simplified_text: If the State Legislative Assembly passes a resolution allowing it, the State Government can, after talking to the High Court, officially decide that in certain sections of the law, the term "Executive Magistrate" will be understood to mean "Judicial Magistrate of the first class."

legal_text:
527. No Judge or Magistrate shall, except with the permission of the Court to which
an appeal lies from his Court, try or commit for trial any case to or in which he is a party, or
personally interested, and no Judge or Magistrate shall hear an appeal from any judgment
or order passed or made by himself.
Explanation.—A Judge or Magistrate shall not be deemed to be a party to, or
personally interested in, any case by reason only that he is concerned therein in a public
capacity, or by reason only that he has viewed the place in which an offence is alleged to
have been committed, or any other place in which any other transaction material to the case
is alleged to have occurred, and made an inquiry in connection with the case.
simplified_text:
527. Restrictions on Judges and Magistrates' Personal Involvement
No Judge or Magistrate may hear a case or make a decision if they are personally involved or have a personal interest in the case, unless the higher court gives permission. They also cannot hear an appeal from a judgment or order they made. 
Explanation: A Judge or Magistrate is not considered personally involved in a case just because they are involved in a public capacity or have conducted an inquiry related to the case.

legal_text:
528. No advocate who practices in the Court of any Magistrate shall sit as a Magistrate
in that Court or in any Court within the local jurisdiction of that Court.
simplified_text: Advocates who practice in a Magistrate's Court cannot also serve as a Magistrate in that Court or in any Court nearby.

legal_text:
529. A public servant having any duty to perform in connection with the sale of any
property under this Sanhita shall not purchase or bid for the property.
simplified_text: A public servant involved in selling any property under this law cannot buy or bid for the property.

legal_text:
530. Nothing in this Sanhita shall be deemed to limit or affect the inherent powers of
the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under
this Sanhita, or to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the
ends of justice.
simplified_text: The Sanhita does not limit the High Court's power to make orders to enforce orders under the Sanhita or prevent abuse of the legal process, or to ensure justice is served.

legal_text:
531. Every High Court shall so exercise its superintendence over the Courts of Sessions
and Courts of Judicial Magistrates subordinate to it as to ensure that there is an expeditious
and proper disposal of cases by the Judges and Magistrates.
simplified_text: Overseeing Lower Courts: Each High Court must supervise the Sessions Courts and Judicial Magistrates under it to ensure that cases are dealt with promptly and correctly by the Judges and Magistrates.

All legal processes under this Code, including summoning, holding inquiries, examining complainants and witnesses, trials before different courts, recording evidence, appellate proceedings, and other related procedures, can be conducted electronically through electronic communication or audio-video electronic means.

Secondary Evidence:
When the original document cannot be produced, secondary evidence can still be used to prove its existence, condition, or contents in the following situations:
- If the original is in possession of someone who is not producing it despite notice.
- If the original has been admitted in writing by the person against whom it is being used.
- If the original has been destroyed, lost, or cannot be produced in a reasonable time for reasons not due to negligence.
- If the original is not easily movable.
- If the original is a public document.
- If the original can be replaced by a certified copy.
- If the original consists of numerous accounts or documents that cannot be conveniently examined in court.

Additionally:
- In cases (a), (c), and (d), any secondary evidence of the document's contents is allowed.
- In case (b), written admissions are admissible.
- In case (e) or (f), only certified copies are admissible as secondary evidence.
- In case (g), evidence of the general result of the documents can be provided by a skilled person who has examined them.

legal_text:
61. Nothing in this Adhiniyam shall apply to deny the admissibility of an electronic
or digital record in the evidence on the ground that it is an electronic or digital record and
such record shall, subject to section 63, have the same legal effect, validity and enforceability
as other document.
simplified_text:
Electronic Records Admissibility:

This law does not stop electronic or digital records from being used as evidence just because they are electronic or digital. These records will have the same legal importance, validity, and enforceability as any other document, except as specified in section 63.

legal_text:
62. The contents of electronic records may be proved in accordance with the
provisions of section 63.
simplified_text: Proof of Electronic Records: The information in electronic records can be proven as per the rules in section 63.

legal_text:
64. Secondary evidence of the contents of the documents referred to in clause (a) of
section 60, shall not be given unless the party proposing to give such secondary evidence
has previously given to the party in whose possession or power the document is, or to his
advocate or representative, such notice to produce it as is prescribed by law; and if no
notice is prescribed by law, then such notice as the Court considers reasonable under the
circumstances of the case:
Provided that such notice shall not be required in order to render secondary evidence
admissible in any of the following cases, or in any other case in which the Court thinks fit to
dispense with it: —
(a) when the document to be proved is itself a notice;
(b) when, from the nature of the case, the adverse party must know that he will
be required to produce it;
(c) when it appears or is proved that the adverse party has obtained possession
of the original by fraud or force;
(d) when the adverse party or his agent has the original in Court;
(e) when the adverse party or his agent has admitted the loss of the document;
(f) when the person in possession of the document is out of reach of, or not
subject to, the process of the Court.
simplified_text:
Evidence of Documents: In order to present secondary evidence of the contents of the documents referred to in section 60(a), the party wishing to do so must have given prior notice to the party who has the document, or to their legal representative. If the law does not specify a notice period, the court will determine a reasonable notice period based on the circumstances. However, there are exceptions where notice is not required:
When the document itself is a notice.
When it is reasonable to assume that the other party knows they will be asked to produce it.
When it is evident or proven that the other party obtained the original document through fraud or force.
When the other party or their representative has the original document in court.
When the other party or their representative has admitted the loss of the document.
When the person in possession of the document is beyond the court's jurisdiction.

legal_text:
65. If a document is alleged to be signed or to have been written wholly or in part by
any person, the signature or the handwriting of so much of the document as is alleged to be
in that person's handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting.
simplified_text: If someone claims that a document was signed or written by a particular person, they need to prove that the signature or the handwriting in question is indeed that person's.

legal_text:
66. Except in the case of a secure electronic signature, if the electronic signature of
any subscriber is alleged to have been affixed to an electronic record, the fact that such
electronic signature is the electronic signature of the subscriber must be proved.
simplified_text: Electronic Signatures: Unless it's a secure electronic signature, in cases where it's claimed that an electronic signature was added to an electronic record, it must be proven that the electronic signature belongs to the person who is said to have signed it.

legal_text:
67. If a document is required by law to be attested, it shall not be used as evidence
until one attesting witness at least has been called for the purpose of proving its execution,
if there be an attesting witness alive, and subject to the process of the Court and capable of
giving evidence:
Provided that it shall not be necessary to call an attesting witness in proof of the
execution of any document, not being a will, which has been registered in accordance with
the provisions of the Indian Registration Act, 1908, unless its execution by the person by
whom it purports to have been executed is specifically denied.
simplified_text: If a document must be witnessed by law, it cannot be used as evidence until at least one witness who saw it being signed is called to confirm its execution, provided that the witness is alive, can testify in court, and subject to the court's processes. However, if a document, other than a will, has been registered according to the Indian Registration Act, 1908, it's not necessary to call an attesting witness unless the person who allegedly signed the document denies doing so.

legal_text:
68. If no such attesting witness can be found, it must be proved that the attestation
of one attesting witness at least is in his handwriting, and that the signature of the person
executing the document is in the handwriting of that person.
simplified_text: If there is no witness available to verify the document, it must be proven that at least one witness wrote the attestation and that the signature on the document matches the handwriting of the person who signed it.

legal_text:
69. The admission of a party to an attested document of its execution by himself
shall be sufficient proof of its execution as against him, though it be a document required by
law to be attested.
simplified_text: Admitting to signing an official document is enough to prove that it was signed by that person, even if the law says it needs to be witnessed.

legal_text:
70. If the attesting witness denies or does not recollect the execution of the document,
its execution may be proved by other evidence.
simplified_text: 70. If the witness who signed the document denies being present at its execution or cannot remember it, the document's execution can be proven using other evidence.

legal_text:
71. An attested document not required by law to be attested may be proved as if it
was unattested.
simplified_text: An unattested document can be proven in the same way as if it had been attested, even if it was not required by law to be attested.

legal_text:
72. (1) In order to ascertain whether a signature, writing or seal is that of the person
by whom it purports to have been written or made, any signature, writing, or seal admitted
or proved to the satisfaction of the Court to have been written or made by that person may
be compared with the one which is to be proved, although that signature, writing or seal has
not been produced or proved for any other purpose.
(2) The Court may direct any person present in Court to write any words or figures for
the purpose of enabling the Court to compare the words or figures so written with any
words or figures alleged to have been written by such person.
(3) This section applies also, with any necessary modifications, to finger impressions.
simplified_text: To determine if a signature, writing, or seal is genuine, the Court can compare it to another signature, writing, or seal known to be genuine, even if the latter has not been presented for any other reason. The Court can also ask someone in the courtroom to write specific words or numbers to compare with the disputed writing. This rule also applies, with necessary changes, to fingerprint impressions.

legal_text:
73. In order to ascertain whether a digital signature is that of the person by whom it
purports to have been affixed, the Court may direct—
(a) that person or the Controller or the Certifying Authority to produce the
Digital Signature Certificate;
(b) any other person to apply the public key listed in the Digital Signature
Certificate and verify the digital signature purported to have been affixed by that
person.
simplified_text:
To check if a digital signature is authentic, the court can:

Ask the person or the Controller or the Certifying Authority to show the Digital Signature Certificate.
Request any other person to use the public key listed in the Digital Signature Certificate to verify that the digital signature belongs to the person who claims to have applied it.

legal_text:
74. (1) The following documents are public documents:—
(a) documents forming the acts, or records of the acts—
(i) of the sovereign authority;
(ii) of official bodies and tribunals; and
(iii) of public officers, legislative, judicial and executive of India or of a
foreign country;
(b) public records kept in any State or Union territory of private documents.
(2) All other documents except the documents referred to in sub-section (1) are
private.
simplified_text:
Public Documents: The following documents are considered public and can be accessed by anyone:
 
Documents that record the actions of the government, official bodies, and tribunals, as well as public officers, whether they are part of the legislative, judicial, or executive branches of the Indian government or a foreign country.
 
Public records held in any State or Union territory that relate to private documents.

Private Documents: Any documents not mentioned in the previous section are considered private.

legal_text:
75. Every public officer having the custody of a public document, which any person
has a right to inspect, shall give that person on demand a copy of it on payment of the legal
fees therefor, together with a certificate written at the foot of such copy that it is a true copy
of such document or part thereof, as the case may be, and such certificate shall be dated and
subscribed by such officer with his name and his official title, and shall be sealed, whenever
such officer is authorised by law to make use of a seal; and such copies so certified shall be
called certified copies.
Explanation.—Any officer who, by the ordinary course of official duty, is authorised
to deliver such copies, shall be deemed to have the custody of such documents within the
meaning of this section.
simplified_text:
Providing Copies of Public Documents: Any public officer who is responsible for a public document that can be inspected by the public must give a copy of it to any person who requests it. The person making the request must pay the legal fees for the copy. The officer must also provide a certificate at the bottom of the copy, confirming that it is a true copy of the document or part of the document. The certificate must include the date, the officer's name and official title, and must be sealed if the officer is required to use a seal by law. These certified copies are then referred to as certified copies.

Further Explanation: Any officer who is regularly required to provide such copies in the course of their official duties is considered to have custody of the documents referred to in this section.

legal_text:
76. Such certified copies may be produced in proof of the contents of the public
documents or parts of the public documents of which they purport to be copies.
simplified_text: Certified copies are valid as evidence of the information in public documents or parts of public documents that they claim to represent.

legal_text:
77. The following public documents may be proved as follows:—
(a) Acts, orders or notifications of the Central Government in any of its Ministries
and Departments or of any State Government or any Department of any State
Government or Union territory Administration—
(i) by the records of the Departments, certified by the head of those
Departments respectively; or
(ii) by any document purporting to be printed by order of any such
Government;
(b) the proceedings of Parliament or a State Legislature, by the journals of those
bodies respectively, or by published Acts or abstracts, or by copies purporting to be
printed by order of the Government concerned;
(c) proclamations, orders or Regulations issued by the President of India or the
Governor of a State or the Administrator or Lieutenant Governor of a Union territory,
by copies or extracts contained in the Official Gazette;
(d) the Acts of the Executive or the proceedings of the Legislature of a foreign
country, by journals published by their authority, or commonly received in that country
as such, or by a copy certified under the seal of the country or sovereign, or by a
recognition thereof in any Central Act;
(e) the proceedings of a municipal or local body in a State, by a copy of such
proceedings, certified by the legal keeper thereof, or by a printed book purporting to
be published by the authority of such body;
(f) public documents of any other class in a foreign country, by the original or
by a copy certified by the legal keeper thereof, with a certificate under the seal of a
Notary Public, or of an Indian Consul or diplomatic agent, that the copy is duly
certified by the officer having the legal custody of the original, and upon proof of the
character of the document according to the law of the foreign country.
simplified_text:
Proof of Public Documents: Certain public documents can be proven in the following ways:

Acts, orders, or notifications of the Central Government or any State Government can be proven using records certified by the head of the respective departments, or any document printed by order of the government.

The proceedings of Parliament or a State Legislature can be proven using their respective journals, published Acts, abstracts, or copies printed by order of the concerned government.

Proclamations, orders, or regulations issued by the President of India, a State Governor, or an Administrator or Lieutenant Governor of a Union territory can be proven using copies or extracts from the Official Gazette.

Acts of the Executive or the proceedings of the Legislature of a foreign country can be proven using journals published by their authority, copies certified under the seal of the country or sovereign, or by recognition thereof in any Central Act.

The proceedings of a municipal or local body in a state can be proven using certified copies of the proceedings or a printed book published by the authority of the body.

Public documents of any other class in a foreign country can be proven using the original or a certified copy with a certificate under the seal of a Notary Public, or an Indian Consul or diplomatic agent, stating that the copy is duly certified by the officer having the legal custody of the original, and proof of the document's character according to the law of the foreign country.

legal_text:
78. (1) The Court shall presume to be genuine every document purporting to be a
certificate, certified copy or other document, which is by law declared to be admissible as
evidence of any particular fact and which purports to be duly certified by any officer of the
Central Government or of a State Government:
Provided that such document is substantially in the form and purports to be executed
in the manner directed by law in that behalf.
(2) The Court shall also presume that any officer by whom any such document
purports to be signed or certified, held, when he signed it, the official character which he
claims in such paper.
simplified_text:
Presumption of Authenticity of Documents:
The court will assume that any document claiming to be a certificate, certified copy, or other document, and is declared admissible as evidence of a specific fact by law, is genuine. This is as long as it is certified by an officer of the Central Government or a State Government and follows the required legal form and execution.
Additionally, the court will also assume that the officer who signed or certified such a document held the official position they claim when they signed it.

legal_text:
79. Whenever any document is produced before any Court, purporting to be a record
or memorandum of the evidence, or of any part of the evidence, given by a witness in a
judicial proceeding or before any officer authorised by law to take such evidence or to be a
statement or confession by any prisoner or accused person, taken in accordance with law,
and purporting to be signed by any Judge or Magistrate, or by any such officer as aforesaid,
the Court shall presume that—
(i) the document is genuine;
(ii) any statements as to the circumstances under which it was taken, purporting
to be made by the person signing it, are true; and
(iii) such evidence, statement or confession was duly taken.
simplified_text:
Documentary Evidence: When a document is presented before a court, claiming to be a written record of a witness's testimony in a legal proceeding or a statement or confession by a prisoner or accused person, and it is signed by a judge, magistrate, or authorized officer, the court will assume that:

The document is authentic.
Statements regarding the circumstances in which it was obtained, as claimed by the person who signed it, are accurate.
The evidence, statement, or confession was lawfully obtained.

legal_text:
80. The Court shall presume the genuineness of every document purporting to be
the Official Gazette, or to be a newspaper or journal, and of every document purporting to be
a document directed by any law to be kept by any person, if such document is kept
substantially in the form required by law and is produced from proper custody.
Explanation.—For the purposes of this section and section 92, document is said to
be in proper custody if it is in the place in which, and looked after by the person with whom
such document is required to be kept; but no custody is improper if it is proved to have had
a legitimate origin, or if the circumstances of the particular case are such as to render that
origin probable.
simplified_text:
Presumption of Authenticity: The court will assume that any document claiming to be the Official Gazette, a newspaper or journal, or a document required by law to be kept by someone, is genuine if it is maintained in the correct form as required by law and is produced from the appropriate custody.

Explanation: For this rule and another related rule, a document is considered to be in proper custody if it is held and taken care of by the person who is required to keep it, in the place where it is supposed to be kept. However, custody will not be considered improper if it can be shown that the document has a legitimate origin, or if the circumstances of the case make this origin likely.

legal_text:
81. The Court shall presume the genuineness of every electronic or digital record
purporting to be the Official Gazette, or purporting to be electronic or digital record directed
by any law to be kept by any person, if such electronic or digital record is kept substantially
in the form required by law and is produced from proper custody.
Explanation.—For the purposes of this section and section 93 electronic records are
said to be in proper custody if they are in the place in which, and looked after by the person
with whom such document is required to be kept; but no custody is improper if it is proved
to have had a legitimate origin, or the circumstances of the particular case are such as to
render that origin probable.
simplified_text:
Every electronic or digital record that claims to be the Official Gazette, or that is required by law to be kept by someone, will be presumed to be genuine by the Court if it is kept in the correct form as required by law and is produced from the proper custody.

Explanation: Electronic records are considered to be in proper custody if they are kept in the place and under the care of the person responsible for keeping them. However, custody will not be considered improper if it can be proven to have a legitimate origin, or if the circumstances of the case make that origin likely.

legal_text:
82. The Court shall presume that maps or plans purporting to be made by the authority
of the Central Government or any State Government were so made, and are accurate; but
maps or plans made for the purposes of any cause must be proved to be accurate.
simplified_text: Maps or Plans: The Court will assume that maps or plans made by the Central Government or a State Government are accurate, unless there is proof otherwise. However, maps or plans made for a specific case must be proven to be accurate.

legal_text:
83. The Court shall presume the genuineness of, every book purporting to be printed
or published under the authority of the Government of any country, and to contain any of
the laws of that country, and of every book purporting to contain reports of decisions of the
Courts of such country
simplified_text: Presumption of Authenticity: The Court will assume that any book claiming to be published by a government and containing its laws, or claiming to contain court decisions of that country, is genuine.

legal_text:
84. The Court shall presume that every document purporting to be a
power-of-attorney, and to have been executed before, and authenticated by, a Notary Public,
or any Court, Judge, Magistrate, Indian Consul or Vice-Consul, or representative of the
Central Government, was so executed and authenticated.
simplified_text: Presumed Authenticity of Power-of-Attorney: The Court will assume that any document claiming to be a power-of-attorney, and certified by a Notary Public, Court, Judge, Magistrate, Indian Consul or Vice-Consul, or representative of the Central Government, was genuinely executed and certified as claimed.

legal_text:
85. The Court shall presume that every electronic record purporting to be an agreement
containing the electronic or digital signature of the parties was so concluded by affixing the
electronic or digital signature of the parties
simplified_text: The Court will assume that any electronic record claiming to be an agreement with the electronic or digital signatures of the parties was indeed concluded by the parties using those signatures.

legal_text:
86. (1) In any proceeding involving a secure electronic record, the Court shall presume
unless contrary is proved, that the secure electronic record has not been altered since the
specific point of time to which the secure status relates.
(2) In any proceeding, involving secure electronic signature, the Court shall presume
unless the contrary is proved that—
(a) the secure electronic signature is affixed by subscriber with the intention of
signing or approving the electronic record;
(b) except in the case of a secure electronic record or a secure electronic signature,
nothing in this section shall create any presumption, relating to authenticity and
integrity of the electronic record or any electronic signature.
simplified_text:
86. (1) When dealing with a secure electronic record in court, it will be assumed, unless proven otherwise, that the record has not been changed since the specific time it was secured.
(2) When dealing with a secure electronic signature, the court will assume, unless proven otherwise, that:
(a) the signature was intended by the person to sign or approve the electronic record;
(b) this section does not create any assumptions about the authenticity and integrity of the electronic record or any electronic signature, unless they are secure.

legal_text:
87. The Court shall presume, unless contrary is proved, that the information listed in
an Electronic Signature Certificate is correct, except for information specified as subscriber
information which has not been verified, if the certificate was accepted by the subscriber
simplified_text: The Court will assume that the information in an Electronic Signature Certificate is true, unless someone can prove otherwise. This is true for all information except for the subscriber information that has not been verified, if the certificate was accepted by the subscriber.

legal_text:
88. (1) The Court may presume that any document purporting to be a certified copy of
any judicial record of any country beyond India is genuine and accurate, if the document
purports to be certified in any manner which is certified by any representative of the Central
Government in or for such country to be the manner commonly in use in that country for the
certification of copies of judicial records.
(2) An officer who, with respect to any territory or place outside India is a Political
Agent therefor, as defined in clause (43) of section 3 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, shall,
for the purposes of this section, be deemed to be a representative of the Central Government
in and for the country comprising that territory or place.
simplified_text:
Presumption of Authenticity of Foreign Judicial Records:
The Court can assume that a document claiming to be a certified copy of a judicial record from a country outside India is genuine and accurate if it is certified in a way that is commonly used in that country for certifying copies of judicial records, as determined by a representative of the Central Government in that country.
Definition of Representative:
An officer serving as a Political Agent for a territory or place outside India, as defined in the General Clauses Act, 1897, will be considered a representative of the Central Government for the purposes of this section.

legal_text:
89. The Court may presume that any book to which it may refer for information on
matters of public or general interest, and that any published map or chart, the statements of
which are relevant facts, and which is produced for its inspection, was written and published
by the person, and at the time and place, by whom or at which it purports to have been
written or published.
simplified_text: Presumption of Reliability: The Court can assume that any book, map, or chart it refers to for public or general information, and which is relevant to the case, was actually written and published by the person and at the time and place it claims to have been.

legal_text:
90. The Court may presume that an electronic message, forwarded by the originator
through an electronic mail server to the addressee to whom the message purports to be
addressed corresponds with the message as fed into his computer for transmission; but the
Court shall not make any presumption as to the person by whom such message was sent.
simplified_text: Presumption About Electronic Messages: The court can assume that an electronic message sent by the sender through an email server to the recipient matches the message entered into the recipient's computer for sending. However, the court cannot make any assumptions about who sent the message.

legal_text:
91. The Court shall presume that every document, called for and not produced after
notice to produce, was attested, stamped and executed in the manner required by law.
simplified_text: Assuming a Document: If a document is requested in court but not provided after being asked for, the court will assume that it was properly witnessed, stamped, and signed as required by law.

legal_text:
92. Where any document, purporting or proved to be thirty years old, is produced
from any custody which the Court in the particular case considers proper, the Court may
presume that the signature and every other part of such document, which purports to be in
the handwriting of any particular person, is in that person's handwriting, and, in the case of
a document executed or attested, that it was duly executed and attested by the persons by
whom it purports to be executed and attested.
Explanation.—The Explanation to section 80 shall also apply to this section.
Illustrations.
(a) A has been in possession of landed property for a long time. He produces from
his custody deeds relating to the land showing his titles to it. The custody shall be proper.
(b) A produces deeds relating to landed property of which he is the mortgagee. The
mortgagor is in possession. The custody shall be proper.
(c) A, a connection of B, produces deeds relating to lands in B's possession, which
were deposited with him by B for safe custody. The custody shall be proper.
simplified_text:
Presumption of Authenticity of Old Documents: If a document that is at least thirty years old is produced from a suitable place of custody, the court can presume that the signature and any other part of the document that appears to be in the handwriting of a specific person is indeed written by that person. Additionally, in the case of a document that was signed or witnessed, the court can presume that it was properly signed and witnessed by the individuals identified in the document.

Example scenarios:
a) A person A has owned a piece of land for a long time and produces historical papers related to the property from their own custody. The court considers this to be appropriate custody.
b) A person A produces documents related to a piece of land for which they are the mortgage holder, and the original landowner possesses the property. The court deems this as proper custody.
c) A person A, who is related to person B, presents documents related to land that is in person B's possession. These documents were entrusted to A by B for safekeeping. The court considers this as proper custody.

The Explanation to section 80 of the law also applies to this section.

legal_text:
93. Where any electronic record, purporting or proved to be five years old, is produced
from any custody which the Court in the particular case considers proper, the Court may
presume that the electronic signature which purports to be the electronic signature of any
particular person was so affixed by him or any person authorised by him in this behalf.
Explanation.—The Explanation to section 81 shall also apply to this section.
simplified_text: Interpretation of Electronic Signatures: If an electronic record, which is claimed to be at least five years old, is presented from a source that the Court deems appropriate, the Court may assume that the electronic signature on the record was affixed by the person it claims to be from, or by someone authorized by that person. Note: The explanation to section 81 also applies to this section.

legal_text:
94. When the terms of a contract, or of a grant, or of any other disposition of property,
have been reduced to the form of a document, and in all cases in which any matter is
required by law to be reduced to the form of a document, no evidence shall be given in proof
of the terms of such contract, grant or other disposition of property, or of such matter,
except the document itself, or secondary evidence of its contents in cases in which secondary
evidence is admissible under the provisions hereinbefore contained.
Exception 1.—When a public officer is required by law to be appointed in writing,
and when it is shown that any particular person has acted as such officer, the writing by
which he is appointed need not be proved.
Exception 2.—Wills admitted to probate in India may be proved by the probate.
Explanation 1.—This section applies equally to cases in which the contracts, grants
or dispositions of property referred to are contained in one document, and to cases in which
they are contained in more documents than one.
Explanation 2.—Where there are more originals than one, one original only need be
proved.
Explanation 3.—The statement, in any document whatever, of a fact other than the
facts referred to in this section, shall not preclude the admission of oral evidence as to the
same fact.
Illustrations.
(a) If a contract be contained in several letters, all the letters in which it is contained
must be proved.
(b) If a contract is contained in a bill of exchange, the bill of exchange must be
proved.
(c) If a bill of exchange is drawn in a set of three, one only need be proved.
(d) A contracts, in writing, with B, for the delivery of indigo upon certain terms. The
contract mentions the fact that B had paid A the price of other indigo contracted for verbally
on another occasion. Oral evidence is offered that no payment was made for the other
indigo. The evidence is admissible.
(e) A gives B a receipt for money paid by B. Oral evidence is offered of the payment.
The evidence is admissible.
simplified_text:
Legal Text Simplification:

Documentary Evidence: When the terms of a contract, grant, or any other property arrangement are written down, or when the law requires something to be written down, only the written document itself can be used as proof of those terms or matters. Exceptions are:
1. If a public officer needs to be appointed in writing, and it can be shown that a specific person has acted as that officer, the written appointment does not need to be proven.
2. Wills approved in India can be proven by the approval document.
This rule applies whether the contracts, grants, or property arrangements are in one document or multiple documents. If there are multiple original documents, only one needs to be proven. This rule does not stop oral evidence about other facts mentioned in a document. Examples:
(a) If a contract is spread across several letters, all the letters containing it must be proven.
(b) If a contract is in a bill of exchange, the bill itself must be proven.
(c) If a bill of exchange exists in a set of three, only one needs to be proven.
(d) A contract between A and B in writing mentions that B paid A for other indigo verbally. Oral evidence can be presented to show that no payment was made for the other indigo.
(e) If A gives B a receipt for money, oral evidence can be presented to prove the payment.

legal_text:
97. When language used in a document is plain in itself, and when it applies accurately
to existing facts, evidence may not be given to show that it was not meant to apply to such
facts.
Illustration.
A sells to B, by deed, "my estate at Rampur containing one hundred bighas". A has an
estate at Rampur containing one hundred bighas. Evidence may not be given of the fact
that the estate meant to be sold was one situated at a different place and of a different size.
simplified_text:
When the language in a document is clear and accurately describes existing facts, evidence cannot be presented to claim that it was not intended to apply to those facts.

Example:
A sells to B, by deed, "my estate at Rampur containing one hundred bighas". A indeed has an estate at Rampur containing one hundred bighas. Evidence cannot be presented to show that the estate meant to be sold was located at a different place and of a different size.

legal_text:
98. When language used in a document is plain in itself, but is unmeaning in reference
to existing facts, evidence may be given to show that it was used in a peculiar sense.
Illustration.
A sells to B, by deed, "my house in Kolkata". A had no house in Kolkata, but it
appears that he had a house at Howrah, of which B had been in possession since the
execution of the deed. These facts may be proved to show that the deed related to the
house at Howrah.
simplified_text: When the language in a document seems clear but doesn't make sense in the context of existing facts, evidence can be presented to explain that the language was used in a special way. For example, if A sells "my house in Kolkata" to B in a written agreement, but it turns out that A didn't have a house in Kolkata, evidence may be presented to show that the agreement actually referred to A's house in Howrah, which B had been living in since the agreement was made.

legal_text:
99. When the facts are such that the language used might have been meant to apply
to any one, and could not have been meant to apply to more than one, of several persons or
things, evidence may be given of facts which show which of those persons or things it was
intended to apply to.
Illustrations.
(a) A agrees to sell to B, for one thousand rupees, "my white horse". A has two white
horses. Evidence may be given of facts which show which of them was meant.
(b) A agrees to accompany B to Ramgarh. Evidence may be given of facts showing
whether Ramgarh in Rajasthan or Ramgarh in Uttarakhand was meant.
simplified_text:
When the language used in a situation could apply to only one out of several persons or things, evidence can be given to show which specific person or thing it was meant to apply to.
Examples:
(a) If A agrees to sell "my white horse" to B for one thousand rupees, and A has two white horses, evidence can be provided to show which specific horse was meant.
(b) If A agrees to go with B to Ramgarh, evidence can be allowed to determine whether it was the Ramgarh in Rajasthan or the Ramgarh in Uttarakhand that was meant.

legal_text:
100. When the language used applies partly to one set of existing facts, and partly to
another set of existing facts, but the whole of it does not apply correctly to either, evidence
may be given to show to which of the two it was meant to apply.
Illustration.
A agrees to sell to B "my land at X in the occupation of Y". A has land at X, but not
in the occupation of Y, and he has land in the occupation of Y but it is not at X. Evidence
may be given of facts showing which he meant to sell.
simplified_text:
When a statement applies to some existing facts but not to others, evidence can be presented to determine which facts were meant to be covered. For example:
If A agrees to sell "my land at X in the occupation of Y" to B, but A has land at X that is not in the occupation of Y, and also has land that is in the occupation of Y but not at X, evidence can be presented to clarify which land A intended to sell.

legal_text:
101. Evidence may be given to show the meaning of illegible or not commonly
intelligible characters, of foreign, obsolete, technical, local and regional expressions, of
abbreviations and of words used in a peculiar sense.
Illustration.
A, sculptor, agrees to sell to B, "all my mods". A has both models and modelling tools.
Evidence may be given to show which he meant to sell.
simplified_text:
Simplified text:
Evidence can be presented to explain the meaning of unclear or not widely understandable characters, foreign, outdated, technical, local, and regional expressions, abbreviations, and words used in a specific way.
Example:
